en: In the *Tattvacintāmaṇi*, the section on the invalidity of verbal testimony (*śabdāprāmāṇyavāda*):
Now, the nature of verbal testimony (*śabda*) is investigated.

A word is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is produced by the knowledge of the reality of an object that serves as its instrumental cause (*prayogahetu*). Furthermore, that which is an instrument (*karaṇa*) is that in the presence of which the action (*kriyā*) necessarily occurs; however, it is not the case that valid cognition necessarily occurs whenever a word is present. Therefore, this word is not a means of valid cognition.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction regarding the validity or invalidity of the sentence "Sound is not a means of valid cognition" because, even if this [sentence] is invalid, it gives rise to a non-contradictory [cognition], we say: no. For a sentence possessing expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, which functions through the operation of recollecting word-meanings and the like, must necessarily be a means of valid cognition since a valid cognition arises from such [a sentence]; and if it were not of such a nature, its failure to produce a result would be identical to that of any other [defective] instrument.

Nevertheless, verbal testimony (*śabda*) is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), because the connection between word-meanings (*padārtha-saṃsarga*) is established through inference alone. To elaborate: the words "Bring the cow with a stick" or Vedic words are preceded by a cognition of the connection between the word-meanings as recalled through their intended purport (*tātparya-viṣaya-smārita-padārtha-saṃsarga-jñāna-pūrvakāṇi*), because they are a collection of words possessing expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, just like the sentence "Bring the jar. Furthermore, [the reason] is not [invalid], because they possess fitness (*yogyatā*) and proximity (*sattimatva*), and because they are directed toward a connected meaning (*saṃsṛṣṭārtha-paratvāt*), being accompanied by those [conditions] that are intent upon that [connection]. Thus, it is not [a case of] a fallacious reason (*hetu*).

For the fact that an object is connected, or that it possesses proximity to what is intended for that connection, is unestablished, since the connection itself is not cognized prior [to the sentence].

Furthermore, the intention to produce a cognition characterized by the mode of "being connected," or the possession of proximity to one who intends such a cognition, is fallacious in the case of the speech of an unreliable person and in the case of a sentence that is semantically complete (*nirākāṅkṣa*).

Even though a connection may have many modes, there is no establishment of the specific connection intended [by the speaker], because that [specific connection] is not the object of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*).
Otherwise, there would be no cognition of the intended connection even from words.
For this very reason, it is not to be proven that [words] possess meanings characterized by the relation of qualifier and qualified, or that they are preceded by the cognition thereof.
As for the claim that [the probandum] is "possessing a connection between the objects recalled [by the words],"...
And the meaning of the possessive suffix (*matvartha*) consists in being a signifier by way of its gender;
nor is there a circular dependency, because it is beginningless due to each preceding instance serving as the cause for the subsequent inference.
That is not so;
for the intended meaning is not established by mere indicatory power (*jñāpakatva*),
and because there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) even with that very [indicatory power] when it functions as a means of valid cognition (*pramāpaka*).

Furthermore, the relation is established by its being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the cognition, because there is a rule that the cognition of a cognition must have the same objects as the original cognition;
and in the case of a relation, it is the relata themselves that serve as the qualifiers.
By the force of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), there is the establishment of a specific relation even if it has not been apprehended as a pervader (*vyāpaka*).
Now, if this were so, even erroneous cognition would be an error;
yet, this is not an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).
Otherwise, it would follow that even the Lord is subject to error;

furthermore, just as from the error "this is silver," there is activity based on the cognition of the error "this person possesses the cognition of silver" regarding a mother-of-pearl shell, so too activity would result from the cognition of an erroneous knower.
As for the claim that a cognition is not valid simply because its object is erroneous—since the objects of error are undermined by whether they are established or not—it is [thus refuted].
And we shall explain that.

Do not say so; for error does not consist in having a non-existent object, since the objects of error do exist, but rather in having a qualifier that is in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇaprakārakatva*).
Nor is there a qualifier in a different locus within the cognition of an error.

Because even in an error (bhrama) where there is the property of having "silver-ness" as its qualifier (rajatatva-prakārakatva), that property exists; otherwise, errors would be abolished, as there is no evidence for such a thing.

Now, it might be argued that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of a sentence containing qualifiers, because through the perception of specific features (viśeṣadarśana), there is an absence of knowledge of the relation (saṃsarga-jñāna).
Nor can it be said that the construction of a sentence is impossible without cognizing a relation, and therefore an induced (āhārya) knowledge of that relation is possible [in such cases].

If it is argued that the formation of a sentence is possible from the knowledge of the words alone— just as in the case of a single word— and that this [knowledge] is the governing factor for other reasons as well, we say no; for a sentence is uttered with the intention, "This sentence will cause the cognition of the connection between these word-meanings," and thus that [sentence] also requires the knowledge of the connection, and furthermore, because of the absence of semantic competency (*yogyatā*).
For this very reason, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) when a non-concordant sentence is uttered as a single unit.
As for the cognition of a relation from a word, it arises due to an error regarding semantic competency (yogyatā).

Now, [one might ask]: how could there be a deviation in the case of either a concordant sentence or a sentence with an erroneous mode (bhrāntaprakāraka), in the absence of a cognition of the relation? Or else, how can that [sentence] be a valid cognition of the relation, given that the inference of the speaker’s cognition is impossible?
If not,

then if that were a valid cognition of connection (*saṃsarga-pramā*), it would follow that it is equal to the Veda, as has been stated. Furthermore, expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), and contiguity (*āsatti*) must be known to be effective [in the process].
"Otherwise, a verbal error would be inexplicable. To this it is replied:

If it is argued that it is the cognition of the object (*arthajñāna*) that prompts action, and not the cognition of that cognition (*tajjñānajñāna*), because the latter involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) and is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*),

and therefore [the cognition] has silver as its object— this is true; however, it is not the case that what prompts action is a cognition having "silver-ness" (*rajatatva*) as its qualifier (*prakāraka*).
And there would also be the consequence of a confusion between those two [the word-meaning and the sentence-meaning].

By this, the following view is refuted: that the apprehension of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*)—which is the cause of the cognition of the sentence-meaning—is dependent on the word-meanings and so forth; and that intention consists in having as its objective the cognition of a specific relation between word-meanings;
and thus, the relation is established through inference which grasps that intention, by virtue of being the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the knowledge of that intention.

Furthermore, since inference possesses the qualifier that is the delimiting condition of pervasion (*vyāpakatāvacchedaka*), it is preceded by a cognition of the relation between the objects remembered from words; therefore, the cognition that prompts action arises from the word alone.

For this very reason, the claim that the word is merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*) for the sake of prompting action is refuted, because verbal cognition and inferential cognition have different qualifiers and thus lack identity of object. [The objects of the sentence] possess a mutual relation within the scope of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), because they are remembered from words possessing expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, provided there is semantic competency (*yogyatā*) and contiguity (*āsatti*).

In the case of what is spoken by an unreliable person, there is no deviation [from the rule] because of the absence of semantic competency (*yogyatā*); and that [absence] is due to the existence of a sublation (*bādhaka*), since the cognition produced by it is an error. Even for a sentence of a single form, there is competency or lack of competency depending on whether a sublation exists or does not exist.

Now, the fitness (*yogyatā*) regarding the listener’s desire to know consists in the absence of a sublating cognition; fitness is the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), which takes the form of the prior non-existence of the comprehension of the relation to be produced in the listener; fitness is the absence of a sublating cognition; proximity (*āsatti*) is the knowledge of the relata of the immediately preceding relation; and these [expectancy, fitness, and proximity] are causes by virtue of their own existence (*svarūpasat*).

If it is argued that these [compatibility and so forth] are not qualifiers of the logical mark (*liṅga*) because they are not known due to their complexity—since there is no delay in the experience of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) without the cognition of them—and because they are difficult to ascertain at first since they are defined by the relation itself; we say no.

For even when compatibility and the rest are absent, a cognition of the relation occurs through the mere conceit (*abhimāna*) of their presence; otherwise, the possibility of verbal illusion (*śābdabhāsa*) would be abolished.
In the case of the doubt or misconception, "Does the king desire his son or a man?",

the cognition of the sentence-meaning is obstructed; therefore, the cause [of verbal comprehension] is merely the knowledge of semantic competency (*yogyatā*), which is common to both doubt and certainty.

The absence of a subverting cognition regarding both oneself and others is sometimes ascertained; for instance, when one ascertains the absence of a jar here through the non-apprehension of what is perceptible to oneself, the absence of a cognition of a jar in another person is also ascertained. In some cases, even when there is doubt regarding the mere absence of a subverting cognition, there is still a positive understanding (anvaya-bodha), because doubt concerning a subversion is not a defect.

Furthermore, for you as well, factors such as *yogyatā* (semantic competency) and so forth must be the determinants of validity (*prāmāṇya*), because if the state of being spoken by a reliable person (*āptoktatva*) were the determinant, it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), and because even in the case of what is spoken by an unreliable person, validity occurs through corroboration (*saṃvāda*). Thus, since the cognition of the means of knowledge (*jñāyamānakaraṇa*) is necessary as that which brings about validity, the cognition of those [factors] is the cause.
And that [expectancy] arises from specific co-utterance and so forth—
do not say so; for where one hears, "A buffalo roams on the bank of the river," without having heard, "The water is pure," expectancy and the like do exist there.
And there is no necessary connection between the two banks of a river,
because of the possibility of deviation;
for this very reason, that alone is the determinant of validity.

Now, if it is argued that even the phrase "as far as they are uttered together" (*yāvatsamabhivyāhṛta*) is a qualification of the mark (*liṅga*), and that for one who remembers only a few words, the cognition of the connection arises from a false attribution (*abhimāna*) of that mark—[we reply:
no, because the meaning of the sentence is understood even when there is doubt regarding those [words].
If it is further argued that in such a case there is an error (*bhrānti*) concerning the connection, [we reply: no.
Since there is an absence of any other cause, the word itself is what produces the error; and thus, being unvitiated, by what could that very same [word] be prevented from producing non-error?
If it is argued that this [error] consists in the non-apprehension of the connection [between word and object], we say no, because there is no sublation regarding the connection.
Now, if being spoken by a reliable person (*āptoktatva*) is a qualifier of the logical mark (*liṅga*), or if it is the logical mark itself,
then being spoken by a reliable person does not apply to the connection between the river and the marsh.

Furthermore, since being spoken by a reliable person is the determinant of validity, knowledge of that [qualifier] is necessary for that which is known as possessing it to function as a reason, just as in the case of a logical mark known as possessing pervasion (*vyāpti*).

If it is argued that the understanding of those [Vedic texts] in the world is based on the acceptance by great men (*mahājana*) because they are not rooted in error—and thus [the same applies] to the Veda and the Smṛti—[we reply]: No. For being an authoritative person (*āpta*) in some particular case does not mean one is an authoritative person in all cases; such authority is not established for one who is not inherently reliable, since error is a human trait. Furthermore, "authoritative personhood" consists in possessing a true cognition of the specific meaning of the sentence in question, and this is difficult to apprehend at the outset.

Since one cannot know whether error or its absence is the root [of a cognition], nor can one know the correspondence with successful activity (*pravṛtti-saṃvāda*) and so forth that would grasp it, activity proceeds even from doubt.

Furthermore, this person engaged in the act is either non-erroneous or possesses knowledge of reality; however, this cannot be known without cognizing the relation (*saṃsarga*), because the meaning of a sentence is something not previously known (*apūrva*).

We, however, say: fitness (*yogyatā*) is the absence of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*), and that [fitness] cannot be a qualification of the logical mark (*liṅga*), because it is impossible to ascertain the mere absence of a subverting means of valid cognition in all cases,
and because there is a comprehension of the connection from a word even when there is doubt regarding that [absence].

Regarding the authority of verbal testimony (*śabda*), however, it is held that verbal testimony is a means of valid cognition because mere knowledge—whether it be doubtful or certain—is the sole factor that determines semantic competency (*yogyatā*).

The ancient Mīmāṃsakas, on the other hand, maintain that in worldly discourse, since the meaning of a sentence is established either through the inference of the speaker’s cognition or through the inference of the connection [of word-meanings] based upon that [cognition], the word functions merely as a restatement (*anuvādaka*). In the Veda, however, because such [a speaker] is absent, its authority is independent.
They say this, but that is not so.

Since the causal complex for the cognition of a relation is established in the Veda, it would follow that even in common worldly usage, there could be no status as a restatement (anuvādakatā) because the cognition arises otherwise; for even if the logical mark (liṅga) exists previously, its cognition is delayed by the delay in the recollection of the pervasion (vyāpti).
If it is argued that even a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) equal to the Veda is not determinative because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the speech of an untrustworthy person, we say no;
for the eye and other sense organs function in that same way, and thus they remain means of valid cognition even when such doubt exists.
If it is further argued that an instrument known [to be fallible] is not determinative when there is doubt—just like a logical mark (*liṅga*)—we say no.

For doubt does not reside in the sentence, because that [sentence] is certain; nor does it reside in the validity of the cognition produced by it, because that [doubt] occurs subsequent to it; nor does it reside in its being spoken by a reliable person, because the certainty of that is not a factor [in the sentence itself].

[Objection: "But surely, in the world, when there is doubt regarding whether a statement was spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*), there is no cognition of the sentence-meaning; thus, the certainty of that [reliability] is the cause [of such cognition]. And so, the cognition of the sentence-meaning arises from inference—which depends upon the perception of the fact that the sentence was produced by a true knowledge of the sentence-meaning—rather than from the Veda itself. [Reply: No. For even one who lacks this [certainty of reliability] can ascertain the capacity [of the words]. Furthermore, even when there is no such certainty, the Gauḍa-Mīmāṃsaka—who presumes the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of sentences such as those of Manu because they are recited in imitation of the Veda—attains certainty regarding the meaning. Thus, the cognition of the sentence-meaning does not depend on the ascertainment of the speaker's reliability.
Nor is this an error, because there is no sublation; for even at the time when its human origin is ascertained, it remains just so.

Nor is that [cognition] merely the non-apprehension of non-relation; for even if the object exists in such a state, if there were no apprehension of non-relation, it would follow that all relations are abolished.

Nor can there be a sublation of the cognition of relation on the grounds that the cause—the certainty that the statement was uttered by a reliable person—is unimpaired; because such a cause is itself sublated when its causal efficacy is shown to be fallible. If it is argued that "it is a factor [in establishing truth] when it is known to be worldly," we say: no.

Because there is an absence of means of knowledge (*māna*), the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is something previously unknown (*apūrva*); thus, due to the absence of an inferential mark (*liṅga*), its apprehension is impossible.

Furthermore, if the cognition of meaning from the Veda occurs only when its non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) is ascertained, then let the establishment of the connection between word-meanings in the Veda proceed by way of being recalled by words possessing expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, provided they are not composed by a faulty person;
in that case, the Veda would likewise be merely repetitive (*anuvādaka*).

As it has been said: "Since these [words] are determined to be 'connected' by means of words that remind one of reality through the removal of doubts regarding individual defects, why would that [connection] not also apply to the Veda?
Nor, in this way, is the word itself a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

[The opponent argues: "Because the production of valid knowledge regarding the meaning of a sentence arises from inference alone. The Prābhākaras, however, maintain that one must accept a factor—distinct from erroneous words—that is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*), pervasive (*anugata*), and the instigator of valid knowledge (*pramā-prayojaka*). For, in the absence of this factor, there would be no invalid knowledge from sentences spoken by an unreliable person (*anāpta*), and otherwise, there would be no diversity in the effects [of verbal cognition].

Furthermore, this factor must be known to be effective, because it serves as an instrument of knowledge (*jñāpaka-karaṇa*) due to its distinction from deviant factors that contribute to knowledge, or because it is a cause of valid knowledge (*pramā-hetutva*), just like pervasion (*vyāpti*) or the expressive power of words (*śabda-śakti*).
Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of verbal appearances.

Nor is "being spoken by a reliable person" (āptoktatva) such [a means], because it is absent in the case of the Veda, in the words of a deluded deceiver that happen to coincide with the truth, and in the speech of Śuka; furthermore, there is no probans (liṅga) excluded from the fallacious that could serve as a basis for inferring "being spoken by a reliable person."
Or, even if [the object] exists, it is because the word itself, as possessing that [object], is the conveyor [of meaning]. By this,

[the claim that words are] a cause of invalid cognition is refuted, because error, negligence, deceit, and the incapacity of the instrument mutually exclude one another, and their combination is not universally applicable.

However, the view that the absence of being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*) is the cause of invalidity, and conversely, that being spoken by a reliable person is the cause of validity, is refuted;
for it is impossible to know at the outset whether something is spoken by a reliable person due to the absence of any inferential mark (*liṅga*).

Therefore, the absence of doubt regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is the cause [of validity], and since such doubt in the world arises from sources such as error, it is eliminated through the inference of being spoken by a reliable person.
And [the claim] that it is established by the ascertainment of the Veda’s being of human origin is refuted;

for since the intended meaning of the sentence is something previously unknown (*apūrva*), the probandum is unestablished. Furthermore, because the connection [of words] in the Veda would be established merely through being recalled by words not composed by a fallible person, it would result in the Veda being a mere restatement (*anuvādaka*).

Nor is there an absence of defects, because such an absence is lacking in the cognition produced by the words of a deluded or deceitful person when its correspondence has not been grasped through perception.

If it is argued that because the absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*) is the cause [of validity], the verbal testimony (*vākya*) in that case is merely mute, while conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) arises from perception (*pratyakṣa*); we say no.

This is because it would entail the denial of experience (*anubhava*), there is dispute regarding its being the cause, and it would result in the Veda being reduced to a mere restatement (*anuvādaka*).

Furthermore, if the absence of defects were the cause of valid cognition (*pramā*), then a defect (*doṣa*) would be the cause of invalidity (*apramā*); and if that [defect] were to function as a cause individually, [the following would ensue].

There is a logical inconsistency [if one holds that] the collection [of defects] constitutes [the cause of error]: if it were the case that the collection [is the cause], there would be no invalid cognition from a single [defect]; if each individual [defect such as] delusion and so forth were a defect, there would be a lack of commonality (ananugama);
but if the collection were the [cause], it follows that invalid cognition could not arise from a single [defect].

Therefore, by parsimony (lāghava), having a purport consistent with reality (*yathārthatātparyakatva*) is the cause of verbal valid cognition (*śābdapramā*). And this consists in having as its purpose the cognition of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-pratīti*) which accords with reality; this is common to both worldly and Vedic [utterances]. From the absence of this, there is invalid cognition.
That is indeed the fault; for no fault exists by its very nature as a genus,
and it is because they obstruct that [valid cognition] that errors and the like are considered faults.
For this very reason, the speech of a deluded deceiver and the speech of a parrot and the like are valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because they accord with reality.

For this same reason, when it is said "there is a jar in the house" with the intention of referring to one particular jar, if someone sees another jar there and brings that one, the word is not a valid means of knowledge in that case because its intent was directed elsewhere; however, the practical activity (*vyavahāra*) arises from perception itself. This is also the case in the expression, "Bring in the staffs."

And that *tātparya* (intention) is useful when it is known for the apprehension of the primary meaning; this is because, in the case of an instrument that is itself being cognized (*jñāyamāna-karaṇa*), it possesses a distinction from that which is merely useful for the cognition [of the result] but is variable, just like pervasion (*vyāpti*) and just like word-potency (*śakti*). Otherwise, there would be no comprehension of a connection with something other than what was intended, which would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total abolition of verbal fallacies (*śabdābhāsa*);
and from the error regarding that [intention], there arises verbal error (*śābdabhrama*).

For this very reason, in the expression "bring in the sticks" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*), there is no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) [of the persons], and the determining factor (*vinigamanā*) between the two [meanings] is rooted in the apprehension of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*).

Moreover, if the verbal cognition were to convey only that which is the actual intention, then indication would have no utility in cases where the primary meaning is incompatible with the syntactic connection (*anvaya*).
(Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p. 111)

For this very reason, when "he cooks" (*pacati*) is uttered, even if the word "kidney-bean" (*kalāya*) is presented—either by being explicitly mentioned or by being recalled from memory—the syntactic cognition "he cooks kidney-beans" (*kalāyaṃ pacati*) does not arise, because there is no ascertainment of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*).

Nor should it be argued that context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, which apprehend the intention, possess auxiliary status for the word because they are primary and necessary, whereas the apprehension of the intention itself does not.

This is because those [factors like context] are not uniform (*ananugata*) and thus lack causal efficacy due to mutual deviation (*vyabhicāra*); whereas the status of being an apprehender of intention belongs even to non-uniform factors, provided they are pervaded [by the cognition], just as smoke and other such signs are.
Furthermore, in the Veda, that intention (*tātparya*) is to be understood through reasoning; where the intention is determined by reasoning, that alone is the meaning of the Veda.
In the world, however, intention does not follow reasoning alone; it is not determined by reasoning, but rather is governed by the speaker’s own purpose.
Because human utterances produce cognition even regarding objects that are not within the scope of formal logic (nyāya), but are within the scope of human intention;
and a speaker utters a sentence with the desire to generate in another the knowledge of the meaning of that sentence;
and if that desire of the speaker is preceded by a correct knowledge of the meaning of the sentence, only then does that utterance [possess its validity].

At that very moment, the fact that the utterance of that [word] is directed toward the speaker’s intended knowledge of the true meaning of the sentence—which is pervaded by the desire for such true knowledge—is established; thus, without first ascertaining that the speaker possesses knowledge of the true meaning of the sentence, it is impossible to know that the utterance is directed toward a true cognition. Therefore, one must first infer the speaker's knowledge from the authoritative statement (āptavākya) and thereby ascertain the reality of the object.

Since it is impossible to know whether a statement is intent upon conveying the object as it truly is, one must first ascertain the speaker’s intention as being true to the facts by means of inferring the speaker’s cognition from the words of a reliable person (*āpta*). This inference is as follows: "This sentence is produced by either error or some other specific cognition, because it is a sentence. Based on this, one determines that the intention is indeed true to the facts.

Then, once error and other such defects have been excluded, there remains the inference of the knowledge of the sentence-meaning by means of elimination (*pariśeṣa*): "This person possesses a cognition of the meaning of the sentence he uttered that is in accordance with reality, because he is an utterer of a sentence not produced by error and so forth, just like myself.
This [inference] is not based on his being a trustworthy person (*āpta*), because that would constitute a specific qualification of the probandum (*sādhyaviśeṣa*).

From this follows: "These word-meanings possess the appropriate mutual relation, because they are objects of a cognition in accordance with reality, or because they are recalled by words spoken by a trustworthy person, just like the word-meanings spoken by a dull-witted person."

[Objection: Surely, the specific cognition of the speaker is what is to be inferred. And in cognition, the object itself is the specific feature (*viśeṣa*), and there is no other [feature] dependent on the object; thus, by the phrase "the specific feature is by means of the object alone," the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used figuratively. Consequently, the specific cognition of the sentence-meaning is what is to be inferred. Since that [specific cognition] is not previously established (*aprasiddhi*), the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is impossible. For this very reason, it is impossible to know whether this person is non-erroneous or authoritative regarding this sentence-meaning; therefore, the word itself must communicate that meaning. [Reply: No.

For the sake of ascertaining the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*), you too must necessarily admit that the cognition of a specific relation is indeed non-verbal (*aśābda*); otherwise, how could there be any determination of the intention?
For this very reason, it is also easy to determine whether there is a delusion regarding the excellence of the speaker or other such factors.
However, the verbal cognition of the relation does not occur first; rather, another kind of cognition occurs [prior to it].
Nor should it be said that "in this way, sound is not a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) because its object is already established beforehand," for the same applies to you as well.
If it is asked, "Even so, how is a specific object established, since no pervasion (vyāpti) is grasped with respect to a particular [object]?"—we reply: No.

Just as, from the observation of activity toward cooking and the like, there is an inference of a cognition of "being an effect" regarding the object of cooking—based on the general pervasion that whoever engages in something knows it—and just as, from observing a particular movement, there is a cognition of the intention to express the number ten, and from observing that same movement in a jar, there is a cognition of "tenness" in the jar; so too, by means of a general pervasion (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), the specific [object] is established.
(Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p. 126)
Alternatively, this sentence is caused by a single cognition whose object is its own meaning, because—while being spoken by a reliable person—it conveys that meaning, just like my own sentences.
From this, these word-meanings possess mutual connection, because—while being expectant—they are the objects of a single cognition, like the objects of a cognition of real silver.

Thus, when the speaker’s knowledge of the sentence-meaning as it truly is has been inferred, [one infers] through context and other means the speaker’s intended knowledge of the sentence-meaning as it truly is.

Through inference based on context and other factors, there arises the knowledge that the speaker intends a true cognition; subsequently, from the word, a cognition of the object occurs as if it were equal to the Veda.

However, the word is merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*), because the sentence-meaning is already established prior to this—either through the inference of a cognition of the relation [between word and object] by virtue of its delimiting the speaker’s cognition, or through the inference of the relation upon which that [speaker’s cognition] depends.

As for the claim that error (*bhrama*) consists in the non-apprehension of a relation (*saṃsargāgraha*), and the absence of that [error] is simply the apprehension of a relation— such that when the absence of error is inferred, it is the knowledge of the relation itself that is inferred, and thus the inference of the speaker’s cognition is included within the inference of reliability, rather than being a separate inference of the speaker’s cognition based on that [reliability] as its mark— that is not correct. For error is indeed two cognitions whose difference is not apprehended, and the absence of that [error] is the cognition of their difference.
For indeed, in deep sleep, where there is an absence of cognition, there is no linguistic usage based on error;
therefore, after ascertaining the absence of error, one infers the speaker's cognition.
If that is so, let the very same kind of mark (liṅga) be the means of comprehension.
To this it is replied:

the quality of being a lamp for the meaning of the sentence in accordance with reality is not known as that which produces valid cognition, because of its complexity (*gaurava*) and because it is impossible to know it first, since it is something previously unknown (*apūrva*).
(Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p. 137)

Furthermore, as for the claim that— in the world, after the elimination of error and the like— the speaker’s intention regarding the meaning of the sentence intended by the person is known through context and so forth, either as something that excludes [other] cognitions of the speaker’s knowledge or independently prior to that [sentence],
that is not correct.
Without knowing the meaning of the sentence, it is impossible to first ascertain that the speaker is not mistaken— given that, due to his being a human being, error and negligence are possible—
because one cannot grasp the fact that [the cognition] is not produced by error and so forth. Furthermore, since corroboration through action and the like occurs only after the cognition has arisen,

and because the word is not known as distinct from what is produced by error and so forth (or, if it were known, only that which possesses such a character could be the indicator), it is only that [specific feature] which conveys the meaning.

Because there is no deviation [from the truth], even in the case of the Veda, it is impossible—even by means of logic—to know that a sentence is intent upon the cognition of its true meaning without first understanding the sentence-meaning itself; for a cognition is determined by its object, and you yourself have accepted that, in order to determine *tātparya* (speaker’s intention) in ordinary worldly usage, one must first have a non-verbal cognition of the sentence-meaning.
Otherwise, the inference of the speaker’s knowledge would not be possible.

Nor can there be an understanding of that [Vedic meaning] through another means of knowledge as occurs in worldly matters, because the subject matter of the Veda is not within the scope of such other means, and because the Veda is initially mute [regarding its own meaning];
nor can there be a grasp of the purport regarding the Vedic meaning— which is established by logic— through another means of knowledge.
Otherwise, the Veda would fall into the status of being a mere restatement (*anuvādaka*), or the word itself would lose its character as a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇatva*).

Furthermore, since both reasoning (*tarka*) and doubt (*saṃśaya*) are impossible when the meaning of the sentence is unknown—because when there is either doubt or reasoning as to whether "this word-meaning is connected with another word-meaning" or not, the connection (*saṃsarga*) is not established as one of the two alternatives, and thus the intended meaning (*tātparya*) remains undetermined; and because those two [doubt and reasoning] do not have the sentence-meaning as their object, either because they concern a connection not yet grasped or because they concern an unreal object.

Otherwise, since even in common worldly usage the [meaning] would be presented by those two alone, what would be the point of inferring the speaker’s cognition? In reality, if the cognition of the speaker’s having a true intention (*yathārthatātparyakatva*) were the producer of verbal valid knowledge (*śabdapramā*), then, because it would be possible to infer the connection between word-meanings in both worldly and Vedic contexts through the fact that they are recalled by such words,
verbal testimony (*śabda*) would not be a distinct means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Moreover, when it is inferred that a human statement is produced by either a defect or a cognition qualified by a defect, at the stage where there is the certainty that it is not produced by a defect— by the method of elimination—

the causal complex (sāmagrī) identical to that of the Veda is present in the case of the human statement as well; therefore, since the ascertainment of the object arises from that very source, its validity is equal to that of the Veda,
because inference based on inference is delayed by the recollection of pervasion (vyāpti) and other factors.

By this, it is shown that having a subject matter whose meaning is uncontradicted (*abādhitārthaparatva*) is the means of establishing validity in both worldly and Vedic discourse. For in the world, it is observed that the meaning of a sentence may be contradicted;

thus, for a listener, the certainty that there is no contradiction cannot occur without the application of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). That [certainty] occurs in some cases through the listener's sense-perception (*indriya*), and in others through the inference of the speaker’s reliability (*āptatva*). In the case of the Veda, however, that certainty arises from reasoning (*nyāya*), because its subject matter is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition.

The claim that "there is no doubt in this case because the causal complex is different" is refuted; for it is impossible to ascertain either the absence of any initial error or the reliability [of the source], and it would result in the Veda being merely repetitive.

Therefore, whether it be the state of not being produced by error and the like, being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*), having an uncontradicted meaning, having a true intention, or the absence of any suspicion of deviation—whatever else it may be that produces valid knowledge and excludes deviant factors—that [cause] exists in its own right (*svarūpasat*) and is not known [as such].

Otherwise, since such [causes] would invariably correspond to the sentence-meaning, the relation (*saṃsarga*) would be established through the inferential mark (*liṅga*) alone, namely, through the fact of being recalled by words of that kind; thus, the Vaiśeṣikas would be victorious.

If it is argued that words possess the capacity to denote the related meaning because their causality is grasped with respect to the knowledge of the action related to the agent—which is inferred from linguistic usage—since such knowledge is present at that time, and since the word itself is not then presented as a logical mark (*liṅga*); we say no. For the cognition of the related meaning can be accounted for by the word alone through the absence of a [separate] logical mark; therefore, the status of being a cause does not belong to the word as possessing expectancy and so forth, due to the resulting complexity (*gaurava*).
If it is argued that although the word's status as an inferential mark (*liṅga*) is possible, it was not known by the child,
we shall explain that this is a defect of the child and not of the thing itself.
Furthermore, if this were the case, the Veda would also be merely repetitive (*anuvādaka*), just like worldly discourse.

By this, the Vaiśeṣika position—that verbal testimony is not a means of valid cognition because the sentence-meaning is established independently through an inference based on the grasp of the speaker’s intention (tātparya), which itself depends on an inference grasping that intention—is refuted; for the grasp of an intention that is merely factual (yathārtha) is not a cause for the cognition of the sentence-meaning.
As for the argument regarding "the instrument being known" (jñāyamāna-karaṇa):
That is not so;

for since it is impossible to know initially whether [the speaker] has a correspondence with reality as their intended meaning (*yathārthatātparyakatva*) and so forth, inference is sublated, and because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished.
Indeed, neither pervasion nor the power of words (*śabdaśakti*) is the cause [of such knowledge].
But that [meaning] is understood through the intellect, because we observe inference regarding what has passed,
and because there is comprehension of syntactic connection even from corrupt forms due to a misconception of expressive power (*śakti*).
Nor is it the case that the very same [cause] is useless,
for that is impossible at the outset.
Therefore, when a cause is known to be non-deviant with respect to its object, the cognition of its distinction from deviant causes is what is required.

Otherwise, since a word is known to deviate from its object, it would follow—like smearing mud on one's head—that it could not function as a signifier (*liṅga*) even when known [to be such], because it would lack the capacity to indicate.

It might be argued: "In the case of a statement by an unreliable person, one observes the absence of the object due to a sublation; therefore, there arises a doubt as to whether a sentence possessing expectancy and other [qualifiers] has a real object or a sublated object. A certainty regarding the object does not arise from that alone, for that which causes doubt cannot itself be a cause of certainty."
If it is argued that something more must be required [as a condition],
we say no; for doubt regarding the object or doubt regarding its sublation does not obstruct the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Even when there is doubt regarding fire and its sublation, the object is ascertained through perception, inference, and so forth; otherwise, all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be abolished, because prior to that [ascertainment], there is doubt concerning the object and its sublation. Furthermore, the composition of sentences can occur even without an object, such as: "Does this have this meaning, or not?"

Furthermore, because a doubt— such as "Does this possess a real object, or not? or "Is the cognition produced by this one possessed of a real object, or not?"— arises only after the meaning has been understood, therefore, whether it be being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*), not being produced by error and the like, having an uncontradicted object, or having as its aim the comprehension of the sentence-meaning as it truly is, none of these can serve as a common cause [for truth] when known, because they cannot be apprehended at the outset.

However, among those factors intended to convey the speaker's intention— namely, the knowledge produced by reasoning (*nyāya*), the context (*prakaraṇa*), and so forth— one or another of these is subsumed under the property of being pervaded by the intention;

likewise, there is the ascertainment of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and proximity (*satti*), because in the absence of these, or when there is doubt regarding them, verbal cognition (*śābdajñāna*) does not arise.

And the cause here is merely the knowledge of semantic competency (*yogyatā*), because even when there is doubt, error, or valid cognition regarding it, the knowledge of the sentence-meaning still arises. Likewise, the co-occurrence of case-endings and so forth, as well as simultaneous utterance, are the causes for verbal cognition in general. Even when multiple meanings are presented in a word with multiple senses or a pun (*śliṣṭa*), the comprehension of the connection (*anvaya*) occurs by taking up only one meaning due to the force of context (*prakaraṇa*) and other factors. Furthermore, figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) does not arise from the failure of the intended meaning (*tātparya-anupapatti*), but rather solely from the failure of syntactic connection (*anvaya-anupapatti*). For example, in the case of [the command] "enter," which is understood through context to produce the act of eating, the connection with a staff is impossible; thus, *lakṣaṇā* occurs.

In the case of a word that does not abandon its own primary meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*), the agency of movement is understood for both the one with the umbrella and the other simply through the context by the phrase "they go. This [agency] cannot be construed with the mere person with the umbrella alone. Furthermore, the word "cooks" (*pacati*) does not convey a meaning when joined with "kalāya" (a type of pea) as uttered by another, because there is no syntactic co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*).

Even in your view, that [context] serves to apprehend the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), for it is established by linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that words uttered together convey a meaning collectively.

Others, however, maintain that while there is a requirement for the apprehension of *tātparya* (speaker’s intention) regarding the word-meaning—both in cases of multiple meanings (*nānārtha*) and in cases of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—this is for the sake of ensuring a restricted presentation, since such a presentation does not occur without it; this requirement does not apply to the sentence-meaning.
For even when that [intention] is unknown, people understand through context and other means that the word *saindhava* refers to a horse or that the word *kāka* refers to a destroyer;
thus, in other cases, the presentation of the correlate for syntactic connection occurs without the apprehension of *tātparya*, and so there is no dependence upon it.

In reality, however, the purport (*tātparya*) of a word consists in its being directed toward the cognition of the relation between the meanings of other words; and this [purport] is ascertained in the Veda through logical reasoning (*nyāya*), while in common worldly usage it is ascertained through logical reasoning, context (*prakaraṇa*), and so forth.

For this very reason, verbal cognition does not have an indefinite cause. Furthermore, that cognition of the relation between the meanings of other words is precisely the cognition of the sentence-meaning; thus, the apprehension of its purport occurs by way of its general character, and not specifically.

And since that [purport] is inexplicable without producing the experience of the relation between the word-meanings themselves and the meaning of other words, the words, acting in concert, produce it.
For this very reason, there is a determining factor (*vinigamanā*) regarding multiple meanings;

the impossibility of that [multiple meanings] is itself the seed of *lakṣaṇā* (indication), and precisely because of its absence, there is no cognition of the connection with black gram (*kalāya*) when the word *pacati* is recalled. Thus it is established that verbal testimony is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, since it does not produce knowledge of a relation in cases such as those lacking expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), expectancy and the like are its auxiliary factors (*sahakārī*).
In the *Tattvacintāmaṇi*, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) concerning the theory of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) regarding words: Now, what is this expectancy?
First of all, there is no necessary concomitance (*avinābhāva*),
because it is absent in cases such as "the lotus is blue.

Furthermore, in the case of "there is a buffalo on the riverbank where the water is clear," since the river is necessarily concomitant with water, it would follow that the term "riverbank" (*kaccha*) would require a complement [to specify its relation to the water].

Nor is it the desire to know the meanings of words recalled by the words uttered in proximity [to one another], because even one who has no such desire understands the meaning of a sentence; and furthermore, because in the case of "One should sacrifice with the Viśvajit" (*viśvajitā yajeta*) and "The door" (*dvāram*), there is an expectancy for an eligible person (*adhikārī*)—even though not a word-meaning—and for the act of closing (*pidhāna*), which is brought to mind [by context].

Moreover, even on the view that [the expectancy] is supplied by the postulation of a word (*śabdakalpanā*), in the sequence "Pot, objectness, bringing, effort" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam ānayanam kṛtiḥ*), there would result an expectancy for the bringing and so forth, even though they have not been specifically desired to be known.
Now, as for the fitness for inquiry and that inquiry itself: they occur when there is ignorance regarding a particular [object];
and fitness, on the part of the listener, is the prior non-existence of the comprehension of the relation produced by the utterance of that [word].

In the sentence "There is pure water in the riverbank" (*vimalaṃ jalaṃ nadyāḥ kacche mahiṣaḥ*), by virtue of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), there is sometimes an apprehension of the relation [of the water] with the riverbank; yet, even though the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of that [relation] exists, because of the utterance of those words to the listener according to that intention, there is no apprehension of the relation of the riverbank with the river as qualified by water— thus, there is no prior non-existence of that [relation].
If it is argued that the same applies even to the case of "the pot, the objectness, the bringing," we say no.

This is because, in a sentence that lacks expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*), the prior non-existence of the comprehension of a relation produced by the utterance of those words is refuted by both proof and disproof.

Furthermore, consider a case where one person, without having heard the words "pure water," understands through a mistake regarding the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) that the sentence is intended to convey the connection of the river with its banks.

Another person, having heard the word as a whole, determines that its purpose is to convey the connection with the water of the river; in that case, since both [the speaker and the hearer] understand the relation produced by that utterance, the word "of the river" would be expectant of both.
Furthermore, since the absence of the effect is pervaded by the absence of other causes, the absence of the effect follows from that alone—what need is there for expectancy?

And thus, even fitness (*yogyatā*) and proximity (*āsatti*) are not causes, because in the case of what is unfit or non-proximate, there is an absence of the cognition of a relation produced by the utterance of those words, due to the absence of its prior negation (*prāgabhāva*).
Nor, in this way, is the absence of sublation (*bādhābhāva*) a cause even in inference and the like;
for the absence of the effect follows simply from the absence of the prior negation, and a prior negation is a cause only of its own specific effect.

In the case of sound (*śabda*), there would be no "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇya*) [of the definition], nor would there be the elevation or depreciation of the "arising" and "aroused" expectations (*utthita-utthāpyākāṅkṣā*), because those do not exist in the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Alternatively, *ākāṅkṣā* may be defined as: the state of not having produced a cognition of the connection between the intended meaning (*tātparya-viṣaya-anvaya-bodha*), while possessing the capacity to generate a presentation of word-meanings (*padārthopasthiti*) that is conducive to the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) the manner in which the object to be made known (*jñāpya*) connects with something other than itself. For example, in the sentence "Bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), when "the jar" (*ghaṭam*) is uttered, one wonders: "Does he bring it, or does he see it? [and thus an expectation arises].
When it is said "he brings," a desire to know arises as to whether he brings a jar or something else.
In the case of the analysis "the jar is the object, bringing is the action, and [bringing] is the effort," there is no connection by way of identity because of incompatibility;
nor does the cognition of the relation "the bringing of the jar" arise, because the jar is not presented from the word "jar" as having the status of a related entity.

If it is argued that the word *rājñaḥ* (of the king) does not require [the word] *puruṣam* (the man) because it has already produced a cognition of its syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with its son, then indeed the presentation of the meanings of the noun, case-ending, verbal root, and verb-ending—namely, the pot, the objecthood, the bringing, and the effort—in their own forms would not be conducive to the desire for knowledge regarding the mode of their mutual connection; consequently, there would be no expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) in that regard.
Thus, even in the case of "pot, objecthood, bringing, effort," there would arise a cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya-bodha*) just as there is in the case of "bring the pot" (*ghaṭam ānaya*).
For in that case, there is no presentation of the individual word-meanings as being distinct from one another;
since all three are remembered equally,

the word *rājñaḥ* (of the king) does not first connect with *puruṣeṇa* (with the man), but rather with *putreṇa* (with the son), and for that very reason, even subsequently, it remains incapable of producing a cognitive apprehension of syntactic connection (*anvaya*).
The established doctrine regarding the theory of expectancy for words is now stated.

The non-termination of expression (*abhidhānāparyavasāna*) is expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). That which, in the absence of another, does not possess the capacity to cause the experience of the connection of its own meaning [with that other], has non-termination with respect to that [other].

For instance, among nouns, case-endings, verbal roots, finite verbs, actions, and words denoting grammatical factors (*kāraka*), there is no generation of the experience of a mutual connection of their respective meanings in the absence of one another.

According to the view of others (*paramata*), in cases such as "the blue pot exists" (*nīlaghaṭo 'sti*) or "bring the blue pot" (*nīlaṃ ghaṭam ānaya*), there is no cognition of a mutual connection between the meanings of the nouns and the grammatical factors.

Because the case-meaning conjoined with the qualifier cannot be related [to the qualified], there is no relation by way of "the qualification of the qualified" (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭya*); rather, it is a collective [relation] (*samāja*).

For us, however, on the strength of the experience of non-difference between the blue and the jar, non-difference itself is the relation; the specific case-ending is for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*).

Alternatively, on the strength of the experience of non-difference between two words having the same case-ending, the case-ending conjoined with the qualifier has non-difference as its meaning; therefore, those two words possess the capacity to bring about the experience of the qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).

Not without one another; for in the case of the word "door," without supplying an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), there is no cognition of the connection with its own meaning due to the absence of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*). Similarly, in the case of "One should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," there is no cognition of the intended meaning that prompts action—namely, "This task is mine"—without [the knowledge of] those entitled to perform it (*adhikārin*); therefore, there is an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) for them.

Alternatively, since the agent is obtained for the qualified person (adhikārin) through implication just as it is for the agent, its connection is not verbal but inferential; this is because, on the view that figurative (gauṇa) and secondary (lākṣaṇika) meanings are not themselves expressive, what is presented by them lacks expressiveness without another word, just like a supplied (adhyāhṛta) term. In cases such as "the pot, the objectness, the bringing, the effort," there is no cognition of connection through identity due to incompatibility; furthermore, the knowledge of the nature of each respective word-meaning as the intended object from those respective words [requires] another word.
Even in the absence [of such a relation],

as in the case of "he brings the jar," although there may be an intention for such a connection through error, there is no connection by way of the relation between action and its factors (kriyā-kāraka-bhāva).

For in the cognition of the connection [between meanings], only those specific words— the noun, the case-ending, the verbal root, the verb-ending, the word for the action, and the word for the factor— are capable [of producing that cognition].
However, other words do not convey that meaning;

for from words such as *agniḥ* (fire), *karaṇatvam* (instrumentality), *odanaḥ* (rice), *karmatā* (objecthood), *pākaḥ* (cooking), *kṛtiḥ* (effort), and *iṣṭasādhanatā* (being a means to what is desired), there is no comprehension of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*), just as there is none in the case of *agninā odanaṃ paceta*. Indeed, the sentence "the effort directed toward cooking rice, which has fire as its instrument, is a means to what is desired" is a complete utterance (*vākya*), not a single word (*pada*).

For this very reason, in the expression "dvāram" (the door), there is the ellipsis of the word "pidhehi" (close); for even if the meaning of the verbal action is presented from another source, there would be a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthyam*) due to the absence of syntactic connection with the case-role (*kāraka*), which is inherent by its very nature.
Furthermore, even that which is not proximate becomes capable of producing a cognition of syntactic connection through the state of proximity or through the illusion of proximity.

In the case of "He sprinkles with fire" (*vahninā siñcati*), although there is the capacity for the cognition of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) between the words denoting the action and the instrument, the cognition of incompatibility (*ayogyatājñāna*) acts as an obstacle—just as a jewel [neutralizes] fire that is otherwise capable of burning.
For this very reason, when the obstacle is absent due to an error regarding compatibility (*yogyatābhrama*), the cognition of the syntactic relation arises even from such a sentence.
Indeed, that which is incapable by its own nature, or that whose capability is merely superimposed, neither burns nor cooks.
In the present case, however, there is knowledge of the individual meanings of the words, and not even a delusion regarding their syntactic connection (*anvaya*).
Even without the word *puruṣa*, the expression *rājñā* possesses the capacity to convey its own meaning in connection with *putreṇa*; thus, there is no expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) for that [word].

Alternatively, at the stage when the recollection of the three [words] has occurred but the cognition of the syntactic connection has not yet been produced, there is no cognition of the connection because there is no intention (*tātparya*) regarding the connection with *puruṣa*; the same applies subsequently as well.
Nor should it be said that the understanding of the syntactic relation (anvaya-bodha) occurs through the son alone because of his having arisen [in the father's mind] as an object of desire; for,
by virtue of the speaker's intention (tātparya), the understanding of the syntactic relation occurs first in the person [the father] himself.

For this very reason, some maintain that expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) consists in the state of not having produced an understanding of the intended connection, while still possessing the capacity for such an understanding of connection.

Even when an understanding of connection has already been produced by a stem and its suffix, there remains an expectancy between the words for the action and its factors (*kāraka*), just as there is between sentences that form a single syntactic unity (*vākyaikavākyatā*). The Neo-Naiyāyikas (*navya*), however, hold that expectancy is either the presentation of word-meanings (*padārthopasthiti*) brought about by specific words—such as "pot," "objectness" (*karmatva*), "bringing," and "effort"—or the presentation of word-meanings not brought about by words arranged in such a way [as a complete sentence], such as "pot, objectness, bringing, effort."

Proximity (*āsatti*) is a factor for the cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya*); therefore, due to the absence of proximity, there is no cognition of connection from such words. You yourself must necessarily admit that the presentation of word-meanings (*padārthopasthiti*) is a cause of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).

Furthermore, after a cognition of one connection has been produced, there is no cognition of another connection because of a lack of speaker-intent (*tātparya*); thus, expectancy does not possess the status of a [direct] cause, but rather serves merely as a specifier (*paricāyaka*) of its own producer, namely the presentation [of meanings].
The Pūrvapakṣa on the Theory of Semantic Competence (*yogyatā*) in the *Tattvacintāmaṇi* (Bibliotheca Indica 98, IV,1, p. 245).
Now, what is this "fitness" (yogyatā)?
It cannot be the observation of positive concomitance (anvaya) with similar instances,
because similarity in any sense whatsoever is not a definitive differentiator.

It cannot be the possession of a similarity with the delimitor of the word-meaning, because such similarity is absent in cases like "The newborn drinks milk," and because the sentence-meaning is something not previously known (*apūrva*).
Nor can it be the possession of a property pervaded by the relation between the word-meanings expressed in proximity,
for that would entail that the sentence-meaning is inferable (*anumeya*).
Nor should it be argued that, in reality, a property that is pervaded by a relation is not useful for knowing that object, and therefore the relation is not inferable;
for this would entail the impossibility of verbal error arising from an error regarding semantic competency (*yogyatā*).

For this very reason, the following view is refuted: that semantic competency is simply the absence of a certainty regarding the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), existing as a real entity (*svarūpasattī*) and serving as the cause, because when there is a certainty of the absence of that property in that locus, a verbal cognition having that [property] as its qualifier does not arise.

Nor is it the absence of a property that is pervaded by the absence of a relation between the meanings of the words uttered together; for in cases such as "the knowable is denotable," the absence of a relation is unestablished and thus cannot be defined. Furthermore, even when the absence of a jar in a house has been cognized, the cognition of the relation [of existence] does not arise from the sentence "the jar exists" even if its [existence] is thereby ascertained.
Nor is it the absence of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, that which constitutes a sublation exists even in what is unfit [for such sublation];
nor is there an absence of a sublation of the relevant connection, because of the contradiction regarding whether the counter-positive (pratiyogin) is established or unestablished.

Nor is there an absence of subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) for something established elsewhere regarding the connection with the subject at hand, because the connection with the subject is cognized first, and because that [connection] exists even in what is unfit [for it].
(Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p. 256)
If it is argued that there is also a sublation (bādhaka) in that case, then [we reply]: the absence of a sublation of the relevant connection is what is required, and that is unestablished;
for this very reason, no sublation can even be determined in that instance.

Nor is there an absence of being the object of a valid cognition of the non-existence of connection with other word-meanings in a word-meaning that lacks a [corresponding] word, because such a thing is unestablished in the case of a purely positive (kevalānvayin) [property].
By this, the view that "that for which no means of valid cognition apprehending a relation exists is fit [to be so]" is refuted.
Nor is there an absence of a valid cognition of the non-existence of the connection with the object to be understood,

because the counter-positive is unestablished and the connection with the object to be understood has not been previously cognized; furthermore, it has already been stated that actual existence in its own nature (svarūpasattva) is of no utility [for establishing validity].

Furthermore, because the existence of that [absence] cannot be determined in what is unfit; moreover, because the absence of one's own subverting cognition exists even in the unfit, while the mere absence of any subverting cognition cannot be known even in the fit— since another person's cognition is itself unfit—
and because this reason is not a cause existing merely by its own nature (*svarūpasan*).

If it is argued that a verbal error is impossible when there is the expectation of the absence of a subverting cognition regarding one's own [object], because of a misconception of semantic competency (*yogyatā*), and that the mere absence of a subverting cognition must be inferred by means of the possession of a form that necessitates the connection—[we reply: No.

This is because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of water used for sprinkling, where even though it possesses fluidity (the form necessitating connection), a subverting cognition exists; furthermore, it would follow that this [absence of subversion] itself constitutes semantic competency, since it is what is depended upon (*upajīvya*).
Nor should it be said that this is exactly so;

for even when a sentence lacks the properties that cause expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sattī*), and syntactic connection (*anvaya*), no understanding of the connection arises if there is a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pramā*) regarding an untrustworthy speaker.
If it is argued that the absence of a subverting cognition is the cause [of such understanding], then that very absence must necessarily be what constitutes semantic competency (*yogyatā*).
The established doctrine regarding the theory of competency (*yogyatā*) is stated as follows: competency is the absence of any subverting cognition (*bādhakapramā*).

It is the absence of being the qualificand of a cognition that [erroneously] apprehends the state of being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in another term-entity within the relation to other term-entities.

Alternatively, in the case of "the knowable is denotable," the state of being the qualificand of a cognition that [erroneously] apprehends the state of being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in "knowability" is well-known in the case of "cowness"; its absence [in "denotability"] exists in the relation to "denotability.

In reality, however, semantic competency (*yogyatā*) is the state of being devoid of a property that delimits the counter-positiveness of an absolute non-existence residing in another term-entity within the relation to other term-entities; this is because of parsimony (*lāghava*) and because it is easier to cognize.

Nor should it be argued that there is no comprehension of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) from the scriptural statement teaching the impurity of that [human head], because it is sublated by the inference of its purity;
for the scripture is more powerful, being of a nature that the inference depends upon (*upajīvya*), and thus by that very scripture, the inference is sublated.

If it is argued that the validity of a word as a means of knowledge depends on its possessing expectancy and proximity (*ākāṅkṣā-sattimat*), and not on compatibility (*yogyatā*) as well—since the absence of sublation (*bādhābhāva*), which is included therein, is a cause for all valid cognition—[we reply]: No.
For when there is sublation, a defect in the means of knowledge must necessarily be asserted;

otherwise, sublation would be impossible regarding the object of a valid means of knowledge. Just as in inference, sublation leads to the destruction of pervasion (*vyāpti*) by way of postulating a limiting condition (*upādhi*).

If it is argued that because there is no room for sublation in the case of the unconditioned (nirupādhi), this [existence] does not serve as a motivator when existing in its own nature (*svarūpasat*), since that would entail the consequence of the total elimination of verbal illusion (*śābdabhāsa*);
and furthermore, that determination of it does not occur due to the absence of a means—[we reply: No.
Because the cause [of verbal cognition] is merely the knowledge of semantic competency (*yogyatā*), which is common to doubt, error, and valid cognition;

because the absence of the obstructing factor—the knowledge of non-competency—is present everywhere; and because, in some cases, even the ascertainment of that [non-competency] occurs when competency is not perceived, as in the case: "There is no jar here.
(Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p. 286)
The prima facie view regarding proximity (*āsatti*) is as follows: proximity is the presentation of the correlates of syntactic connection without intervention;
and since that [presentation] is recollection (*smṛti*) and not direct experience (*anubhava*), there is no circularity (*anyonyāśraya*).

Now, it may be argued: "Since simultaneous occurrence is impossible for successive recollections of word-meanings—which are produced by successive cognitions of words possessing various qualifiers such as object, agent, instrument, locus, action, and so forth—because it is illogical for successive items that perish very rapidly to coexist, how then can there be a comprehension of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) of those word-meanings? For a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) is necessarily brought about by the cognition of its qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*). [This objection is raised to set up the following response.]

From the convergence of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the individual experience of each word through hearing, there occurs simultaneously the recollection of all those words; then, when the recollection of the meanings of all those words occurs simultaneously, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) arises.
Nor should it be argued that a latent impression regarding one object cannot produce a recollection of another;

for, due to the otherwise inexplicable nature of the sentence-meaning and by virtue of the resulting effect, it is postulated that the latent impressions assist one another to produce that single recollection.

Just as the individual phonemes, having no other recourse, lead to the recollection of the word, so too it has been said: "Whatever is expected, whatever is semantically appropriate, and whatever is present— by each of these being construed with its own meaning, the word-meanings themselves are understood [as syntactically connected]."
Nor should it be argued that there would be no statement of a subsequent positive concomitance (*anvaya*) because of the absence of a separate operation [after the first];

for even so, since no reason was offered for the first instance of non-concomitance (*ananvaya*), one might say that this deficiency in causal conditions (*sāmagrīvaikalya*) belongs to the latter and not to the former.

Let it be so for now; nevertheless, regarding the experience of the sentence-meaning as constituted by the final set of word-meanings, the aforementioned explanation must be accepted, as there is no other way.
On this point, they say:

proximity (*sannidhi*) is not necessarily produced by words alone to be the cause of the cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya*), for we observe that in cases such as "the door," the connection is understood even through [words] like "closing" which are merely supplied (*adhyāhṛta*).
Nor is it the case that the word "close" (*pidhehi*) itself is what is supplied.
Because it is useless;
because the object alone is useful as the counter-correlate of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*); because it is necessary;
and because presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) has as its object that which accounts for the fact to be explained (*upapādaka*).
And it is not the mere word that is the probans, but rather its meaning;
for the recollection of a word occurring by chance is otherwise accounted for through its association with a meaning that must necessarily be postulated.

Otherwise, one would have to assume a restrictive rule that only an object already indicated by the word itself can trigger the cognition of its syntactic connection (*anvaya*). If it is argued that since words are directed toward the connection of their own primary meanings, the word "door" (*dvāram*) does not trigger the cognition of a connection with "closing" (*pidhāna*), and therefore a word must necessarily be supplied to bring about that cognition—[we reply]: no, because such [secondary] indications (*lakṣaṇā*) are inconsistent, and because even for you, the agent is connected through what is merely implied (*ākṣipta*).
Now, if it is argued that, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the word *pidhehi* is assumed to denote merely the coexistence with the word *dvāra*,
and that there is no lack of a determining factor (*vinigamaka*) when multiple words expressive of "closing" are presented—
since the recollection of a specific word occurs due to the relative strength of their latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)— we say: no.

Since it is well-established that words have as their primary purpose their own meaning as connected with a counter-correlate possessing expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, one should supply the missing word (*arthādhyāhāra*) on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*).
Nor should it be argued that because the heard words have already achieved their purpose, they cannot have any intentionality (*tātparya*) toward a supplied word;
for [the supplied word] is introduced precisely because the connection of the heard meanings is otherwise untenable.
[This is] because of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*).

If it is asked, "How then, in the case of 'He cooks this,' is there a syntactic connection with everything merely mentioned together, since even *kalāya* (a type of pea) and so forth are remembered [as being present]?"—we say: No. Understand that it is due to the restriction by intention; for that which a word aims at is indeed the meaning of that word.

Otherwise, even for you, there would be a cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the word *kalāpa* brought to mind by the force of destiny (i.e., memory) in such sentences as "This Devadatta [is] rice," because the agent is not denoted due to the absence of an expressed verb; and thus, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would have to occur. If this is argued, we say no: for even by the supplied word *pacati*, the agent is not denoted.

If it is argued that the number of the agent is expressed [by the suffix], we say no; for then the third case ending would also result in expressions such as *devadattasya pākaḥ* ("the cooking of Devadatta").
If it is argued that the determination [of the case] is based on the intended meaning (*tātparya*), then the same applies here as well.

If it is argued that in cases such as "Close the door," there is a causal function [of the word *pidhāna*] by virtue of its being a word that presents the act of closing (*pidhāna*) upon the experience of the word *pidhāna*, we say no.

This is because the causal function consists in being a word that presents the correlate for the syntactic connection (*anvaya*), and not in being every word that presents that correlate, due to the resulting complexity (*gaurava*).
The same applies to the cognition of the connection with the act of closing.

Otherwise, there would be no comprehension of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) for metaphorical (*gauṇa*) and indicative (*lākṣaṇika*) expressions, because those two do not possess the capacity to produce such an experience (*ananubhāvakatva*).
The doctrine of the theory of proximity (*āsattivāda*) is stated:
the action is that which is presented by the verbal root (*kriyāpada*).

Furthermore, a *kāraka* presented by a *kāraka*-term requires mutual expectancy with another *kāraka*, not merely its presentation; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a syntactic cognition occurring even in cases such as "the door [is] the object, close it" (*dvāraṃ karmatā pidhehi*) or "the door, the closing, the effort" (*dvāraṃ pidhānaṃ kṛtiḥ*), because the presentation of the action and the object is equal in those instances as well, just as in the case of supplying an elided action or object.

If it is argued that there is no mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) between words presented by such [ungrammatical] forms, then [we reply]: in the case of expectancy, what is the determining factor is being presented by specific words, not mere presentation;
if it is further argued that because of ungrammaticality (*asādhutva*) regarding a specific meaning, there is no comprehension of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) here, we say: no.

Since the word "dvāram" (door) is also incorrect without the word "pidhehi" (shut), and since correctness (*sādhutva*) is equally applicable when connected with that meaning, and since the knowledge of correctness is not a causal factor in the cognition of syntactic relation (*anvaya-bodha*)— both because it involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) and because syntactic cognition occurs even from corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*)— it cannot be claimed here that there is merely a failure to grasp the non-connection (*asaṃsarga-agraha*), for there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) to the contrary.
