Therefore, a verbal form conveys a syntactic connection with a nominal form denoting a *kāraka*, and a nominal form denoting a *kāraka* conveys a syntactic connection with a verbal form; however, it is not the case that one is unintelligible without the other.

For there is no occurrence of the accusative case when there is a connection with the meaning of a verbal form, since otherwise the accusative would undesirably follow even in a construction such as "ghaṭa ānayanaṃ kṛtiḥ" (the pot, bringing, effort).
And likewise, in the case of "puṣpebhyaḥ" (from flowers), the dative case is untenable without the ellipsis of the word *spṛhayati* (desires).

If the dative occurs in connection with the meaning of the word *spṛhayati*, then it would also occur in the expression "puṣpam icchati" (desires flowers), because the words *spṛhayati* and *icchati* have the same meaning.

Now, if the ellipsis of the words *pidhehi* (shut) or *spṛhayati* in the case of "puṣpebhyaḥ" is accepted merely for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), and not for the sake of understanding the syntactic relation (*anvaya*), this is because that relation is established simply through the cognition of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the relation.
In that case, since a case-inflection for a *kāraka* cannot occur without connection to a verb (*kriyāpada*),

and a verb capable of syntactic connection with it cannot occur without connection to a word denoting a *kāraka*, it is necessary for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) to supply a verb in the case of an isolated *kāraka* word, and to supply a *kāraka* word in the case of an isolated verb; thus, the mental representation (*upasthiti*) produced by such [supplied words] is conducive to the comprehension of the syntactic relation (*anvayabodha*).

Therefore, since the mutual connection between an action and its factors occurs only between those very action and factors presented by the words [themselves], there is indeed a verbal ellipsis (*śabdādhyāhāra*). However, regarding the implication of the agent (*kartṛākṣepa*), we shall explain it later.
(Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p.
319) The Doctrine of Intentional Meaning (*tātparyavāda*):

The validity of verbal testimony depends upon intention (*tātparya*). In this context, "being intent upon that" (*tatparatva*) does not mean "having that as its probandum," because neither the individual word-meanings nor their mutual relations are established by the words themselves.
If it is argued that "being intent upon" (tatparatva) consists in having as its objective the engagement with or withdrawal from the domain [of action],

and that this— whether in the case of a future object directly, or in the case of a statement of praise or censure regarding a past fact— is the capacity to generate engagement with or withdrawal from the indicated subject through the medium of conveying a praiseworthy or censurable meaning (i.e.,
figurative indication), we say: no.

If [it is argued that] being intent on that (*tatparatva*) consists in producing a cognition of that [object] and then inducing activity toward it, and inducing activity toward it consists in being intent on that, there is a circularity (*parasparāśraya*).

Furthermore, even though a word used in its secondary sense (*lākṣaṇika*) does not produce a direct experience, it is intent on the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*); and since poetry and the like ultimately terminate in being intent merely on the description of their own nature, they too would be intent on that.

Now, if being intent on that means "producing a cognition of that," then even sentences of praise or censure are indeed intent on that, because they are causes for the cognition of their own objects as praiseworthy or censurable.

If it is argued that this knowledge is called "intentional" (*tatpara*) because it produces engagement (*pravṛtti*) and disengagement (*nivṛtti*) regarding its own object—such that everyone proceeds toward what is praised and turns away from what is censured—we say no. This is because figurative (*gauṇa*) and indirect (*lākṣaṇika*) expressions lack the capacity to produce direct experience; furthermore, to define intentionality as the production of such a cognition would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
If it is argued that intentionality consists in the capacity to produce that [cognition], [we reply...]

In that case, upon a single utterance, there would be a focus on multiple meanings in the case of multiple meanings, and a focus on the primary meaning in the case of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because the capacity [for such meanings] exists.

Nor can it be the state of being what is conveyed by that [utterance], because without *tātparya* (intentional focus), it is not so; thus, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

This is because sentences of praise or censure do not bring about activity or other such responses, and because that which is used figuratively (lākṣaṇika) does not [itself] effect such communication.
If it is argued that the word "Ganges" (gaṅgā), while denoting the bank—which is invariably concomitant with its own primary meaning—is actually directed toward that [bank], we say no.

In the case of the sentence "The platforms are shouting," there is an intention (tātparya) toward the men even in the absence of that [shouting] [on the part of the platforms]; thus, a word like "Ganges" could be directed toward fish and so forth, and yet directed toward the bank in its primary sense, since the state of invariable concomitance remains unchanged.

If it is argued that [the secondary sense arises] only when there is an obstacle to the primary sense, then there would be no such thing as "primary meaning," nor would there be the sense of the absence of going in the phrase "Go, you are going. It is replied:
Having that as its purpose (*tatprayojanakatva*) means being directed toward it (*tatparatva*), and its object (*tadartha*) consists of cognition, engagement, and disengagement.
Furthermore, "being a purpose" (*prayojanatva*) does not mean "being that which is to be accomplished" (*sādhyatva*), because that would involve mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
Nor does it mean "being the object of the speaker's desire."
For that which is the object of someone's desire, there arises a state of being intent upon that very thing.
If it is argued that the restriction of the desire is determined by the fact that it is to be accomplished for that purpose, we say no;

because in the case of "here is smoke," since the probandum (*sādhya*) is manifold due to the distinction between what is produced and what is made known, there would follow a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), as it is impossible to restrict [the meaning] by means of a person's desire.
However, "being directed toward that" (tatparatva) consists in being the object of the speaker's intention;

whatever word is employed by a speaker with a particular intention, that word is directed toward that [object]. And since that intention has as its object the understanding, engagement, or withdrawal of the person to be informed, [the word] possesses "being directed toward that."

"From a word with multiple meanings (*śliṣṭa*), which possesses a single verb connected to several word-meanings, and from a word that is both primary (*mukhya*) and secondary (*lākṣaṇika*), there arises through repetition (*āvṛtti*) a cognition of the various word-meanings sequentially, but not simultaneously;

for it is a rule that what is uttered once has a single intended meaning, and thus in a single utterance there is no intention toward multiple meanings—so say all the Tantric authorities in unison. We, however, say this:"
Indeed, there is a single utterance when there is a desire for the cognition of multiple word-meanings, because it is impossible to restrict human intention.

Furthermore, if that utterance were not intended to convey multiple meanings, then repetition would also not occur, since one assumes repetition only to fulfill the requirement of *tātparya* (purport); otherwise, such repetition would result even in the case of an utterance intended to convey only a single meaning.
For this very reason, when the utterance of that [word] is directed toward both meanings, there is no assumption of repetition; therefore, when multiple meanings are presented simultaneously,

a simultaneous cognition of the connection with multiple [meanings] occurs because the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is equal, and because it is impossible to restrict [the process] such that the cognition of the connection of one occurs first and not that of the other, given the knowledge of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) and so forth.

Now, if it is argued that the utterance of the word *akṣa*, which is the subject of dispute, brings about the experience of only one object as the domain of a single power in a single utterance— because it possesses multiple meanings, like a word with multiple meanings that is restricted to one [specific] referent— the answer is no.

This is because the argument is sublated by the existence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for the experience of multiple meanings, and because the secret of the causal complex constitutes a limiting condition (*upādhi*).

Therefore, when it is said, "Bring the two [objects] that cannot be brought," if—due to a difference in context or other factors—the cognition of the intended meaning (*tātparya-pramā*) is distinct or there is an error (*bhrama*), then for the two persons being addressed, there is simultaneously a comprehension of multiple meanings without repetition; however, in that case, it is not as if only one [meaning] were intended.

Likewise, in the sentence "Bring the jar or the cloth," if the act of bringing pertains to both, there is a simultaneous cognitive connection (*anvaya-bodha*) and no repetition. Sentence-splitting (*vākya-bheda*), moreover, arises from a difference in meaning, not from a difference in cognition.

In the case of the sentence "The water and the cowherd station reside in the Gaṅgā," when the intention (*tātparya*) of the word *gaṅgā* is grasped simultaneously as referring to both the current and the bank, there arises at one and the same time the comprehension of the connection between both the water and the cowherd station, since they are present together in that single location.
Nor does this entail the occurrence of two simultaneous word-functions (*vṛtti*), for such a result is accepted.

The function [of a word] follows from the intended meaning (tātparya), but the intended meaning does not follow from the function; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the abolition of figurative (gauṇa) and metaphorical (lākṣaṇika) functions, since those two are postulated as functions only insofar as they serve to fulfill the intended meaning.

If both the primary (mukhya) and the secondary (lākṣaṇika) meanings were intended as the sole referent, there would be a contradiction between two simultaneous functions (*vṛtti*). If, on the other hand, both were intended to convey multiple connections, the contradiction between the two functions would constitute a formal flaw (*doṣa*), resulting in the status of a mere technical rule (*paribhāṣā*). In such cases, because the connection with the primary meaning occurs first due to its speed, the subsequent connection with the secondary meaning follows immediately thereafter.
In that case, there is indeed no repetition; therefore, when the intended meaning (tātparya) is grasped simultaneously, there is no repetition.

However, where there is multiplicity of meanings and the sequence of comprehension of the syntactic connection (anvaya-bodha) occurs through a succession of graspings of the intended meaning, there is repetition, because the first utterance has already reached its completion.

And thus, since this [principle] is established in common worldly usage, it applies to the Veda as well; "this is the intended meaning"—by this very fact, the Veda would possess authorship by a person (pauruṣeyatva).
(Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p.

340) Here, the Mīmāṃsakas argue that just as utterance in the Veda is dependent because it is preceded by [another] utterance, so too is intention (*tātparya*) dependent because it is necessarily preceded by [another] intention; however, there is no first intention for anything whatsoever, because of its beginninglessness (*anāditva*). For each subsequent utterance depends upon the preceding one, being occasioned by the desire to communicate the meaning of the sentence of the prior [utterance].
For that very intentionality (*tatparatva*)—which is common to both worldly usage and the Veda—is simply the utterance [of a word] by virtue of that speaker’s intention;
and as for whether that intention is independent or dependent, there is no distinction whatsoever.
Furthermore, it is established for both disputants that the Veda is so called because its determination is based on the logic refined by the beginningless Mīmāṃsā.

Therefore, in accordance with its intended meaning (*tātparya*), the Veda is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*). Now, one might object: "How can there be knowledge of the sentence-meaning from the Veda when it is uttered without knowledge of the [word-]meanings, since there is no utterance [of the Veda] by desire [for a specific result] without such knowledge?
Furthermore, because the utterance differs for each person. If this is argued:

In that case, one might argue that from the *Bhārata* being recited, there would likewise be no cognition of its meaning; for although Vyāsa uttered it with the intention that such a meaning be understood, since the recited version belongs to the same class [as the original], one could have a cognition of the meaning of the recited *Bhārata* even without knowing the meaning [of the original].

If this is so, then the same applies to the Veda as well, because the determining factor is belonging to the same class as that which possesses the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Otherwise, you too would not have a cognition of the meaning from the Veda being recited, since it was not composed by God.
If it is argued that the Veda is of human origin because it consists of sentences, like the Mahābhārata and other such works, [we ask]:
what is the Veda?
For, due to the absence of a common defining characteristic (*anugata-dharma*), it has diverse meanings across its various branches (*śākhā*).
For instance, the Veda is not the subject of the application of the term "Veda" in its primary sense, because it does not denote its own primary meaning; nor is it the collection of branches (śākhā),
because that collection is itself defined by the Veda, and because a collection, lacking the capacity to convey meaning, cannot be established as a sentence (vākya).
Nor can it be the statement "one desiring heaven" and so forth, because the Smṛtis, the Mahābhārata, and other such texts would likewise [be invalid].
(Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p. 344)
Nor is it a statement whose author is doubtful, because both disputants have certainty regarding it.
If it is argued that doubt arises in the mind of the neutral arbiter because the disputant's inference and [the opponent's counter-inference] are equal in strength;

In that case, there would be a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): first, doubt regarding that [word] arises from two inferences, and only after the inquiry of a neutral person who is in doubt does the inference occur.

Nor can it be the subject of dispute (*vivādādhyāsita*), because without a common property (*anugatadharma*), even the dispute itself would not exist, and because such [words] are present in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts as well.
Nor is "Veda-ness" a universal (*jāti*), because common usage follows the form of the Vedas even for those who are not great authorities;
furthermore, there would be the consequence of *saṅkara* (overlapping) with universals residing in words that lead to the inference of being uttered by Devadatta and so forth.
Moreover, "being of human origin" (*pauruṣeyatva*) is neither the state of being produced by a cognition of its meaning, nor the state of originating from a cognition of its utterance.
There is no proof by means of being produced by both the teacher and the cognition thereof, because that would result in proving what is already established;
nor is there beginninglessness of the utterance itself, since each individual utterance is indeed beginningless.
Nor is it the case that they were composed by an independent person,
because that is absent in the Veda and the Mahābhārata as they are currently being recited.
If it is argued that [the Purāṇas] are of the same class as those composed by an independent person, [we reply:]...
In that case, how could it be that the *Bhārata* being recited belongs to Vyāsa and not to me?

Furthermore, if independence (*svātantrya*) pertains to a specific instance of utterance, then it would belong to me as well; and if it pertains to the general category of utterance, then it would belong to Vyāsa as well.

Moreover, if what is to be proven (*sādhya*) is the quality of belonging to the same class as works composed by an independent person, then the property of being a sentence (*vākyatva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the primordial *Bhārata* and the *Smṛti*.

If it is argued that the probandum— that "something of that same class was composed by an independent person"— is not specified in detail, and that one merely asserts "there exists a living being somewhere," [we reply:
no,
because this is contradicted by the case of the *Mahābhārata* as it is currently being recited.

If it is argued that "human authorship" (*pauruṣeyatva*) consists in the state of having words connected [into a sentence] with a view toward a meaning, by virtue of being directed toward that meaning—and that this is the primary requirement—therefore even a verse uttered silently by a silent sage (*maunīśloka*) is human-authored; we say: no.
For this would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*), since even a silent sage possesses a teacher who knows the meaning.

Otherwise, there would be a deviation from the rule due to the Vedas and the *Mahābhārata*, which are recited in other ways. For this very reason, the following argument is refuted: "The quality of being a Veda (*vedatva*) has as its locus a composition by an independent person, because it is a property residing in sentences, just like the quality of being the *Mahābhārata*. For "being composed by an independent person" means uttering [a work] with the desire to communicate a true cognition regarding the meaning of the sentence; and thus...
By such a teacher, the argument commits the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
By this, the claim that "having an author" is the probandum—on the grounds that the distinction between being a speaker and being a repeater is established by common worldly experience—is refuted.

Furthermore, defining "human origin" (*pauruṣeyatva*) as the utterance of a word independently of any prior utterance of the same kind is untenable, because it is contradicted in the case of the Veda as it is currently recited, and because it would lead to a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the *Bhārata*.

It is said: Vedahood (*vedatva*) consists in being a word that produces knowledge of the meaning of a sentence generated by words, while having as its object a thing that is not the object of any means of valid cognition other than verbal testimony and the means of cognition dependent upon it; this is because the cognition of the Lord is ungenerated, and even though the subject matter of the Veda may be the object of inference and so forth, inference and the like are themselves dependent upon the Veda.

Although the *Smṛtis* and portions such as the *Mahābhārata* share the same meaning as the Veda, they are nonetheless human compositions because they are produced by cognitions generated by words, having been composed after perceiving the meaning of the Veda.
Being "human composition" (*pauruṣeyatva*) consists in belonging to the class of those utterances that are produced without depending on a prior utterance of the same kind.
Even in the case of the *Ādibhārata*, there is no deviation [from the definition] because it belongs to that same class.

Alternatively, "Vedic-ness" (vedatva) resides in utterances produced independently of other utterances of its own kind, because it is a property residing in a sentence that serves as a delimiting factor for validity (*prāmāṇya*), just like "smṛti-ness.
Or else: the Vedas are produced by a true cognition whose object is the meaning of a sentence not generated by [another] word, because they are authoritative words, like the *Bhārata*.

Furthermore, there is no sublation (*bādha*) when the Veda is being recited, nor is there any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the *Mahābhārata* or the *Smṛtis* of Manu and others, because those were produced by two types of agents (the author and the reciter). Alternatively, the probandum (*sādhya*) may be "belonging to the same class as that which is produced by such [authorial] knowledge.
For you as well, the conventional designation of the Veda as "not of human origin" (*apauruṣeya*) exists precisely because of the absence of this [human authorship].

Now, it might be argued: "This [reason] is not decisive; for what is essential for the validity of a word is simply its being preceded by a true cognition whose object is the sentence-meaning, and not also the fact that such a cognition is not produced by the word itself, since the latter involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*)."

Otherwise, even the Veda would lack authority for you because it possesses two authors, since such is observed in the world; and thus, since its purport is understood through the logic established by beginningless Mīmāṃsā, there is a beginningless succession wherein the study and comprehension of the meaning of the Veda by each successive student proceeds from the Veda recited by each preceding teacher— so what need is there for an independent person?
Because that purpose is established from the very fact of dependence [on others];
furthermore, since the intended object of the proposition—that the prior time was not devoid of the Veda—is unestablished, there is no proof of what is already established in part.
Likewise: "Vedic study at a prior time was preceded by study under a teacher, because it is study, like contemporary study."
Nor is there any deviation [from the rule] in the case of studying the Veda inferred from its script, because the script itself is preceded by study;
nor, for that reason, would the study of the Mahābhārata and similar texts be of the same nature.
Because it is stated that its authorship was by Vyāsa and others specifically in the *Bhārata* and other such works. To this it is replied:
its authority would be dependent upon the authority of the Vedas; thus, there is the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).

Nor should it be argued that the validity of a subsequent Veda does not depend on the validity of a preceding Veda because they are distinct individual instances, and thus there is no self-referential circularity (*ātmāśraya*);
for in that case, the validity of each preceding one would likewise depend on the validity of its own predecessor, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If it is argued that this is not a fault because [the Veda] is beginningless, we say no; for there is an absence of any other foundational means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which would result in a mere succession of the blind.
If it is argued that the Veda itself is inherently valid and serves as the foundation for everything in the Veda, we say no.

Since all [means of knowledge] depend on other Vedas and thus lack intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), for this very reason, in the case of the transition from custom (*ācāra*) to tradition (*smṛti*) and from tradition back to custom, there is an assumption of a Vedic basis due to the fear of an "infinite regress of the blind" (*andhaparamparā*), because of the absence of a foundational authority that is independent of any further source of trust. Even if the validity of the beginningless stream of the Vedas is established through the acceptance by great persons (*mahājana*) since time immemorial, there remains a lack of confidence because of the absence of a foundational authority independent of anything else to sustain that [validity].
Otherwise, if memory and conduct were also determined to be authoritative in this way, there would be no need to postulate that they are rooted in a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, it is precisely because the Veda is rooted in the direct perception of the Lord—which is independent of any other seed of confidence—that its authority is ascertained through the acceptance of the great multitude of people.
By this, inference (*anumāna*) is also refuted.

Because, in the absence of a foundational perception (*mūlabhūtapratyakṣa*), the authority of the Veda would be untenable; thus, there is a sublation (*bādha*) when the non-existence of the probandum is established.
If it is argued that there is a subverting argument (*bādhaka*)—namely, "the Veda is not of human origin because its author is not remembered"—we say no.
Because from the time of Kapila, Kaṇāda, and Gautama, along with their disciples, until the present day, the remembrance of the Veda’s having an author is observed;
nor is there an impossibility of such remembrance due to a lack of a foundational experience,
since that experience is established precisely through the inference of its being of human origin.
If it is argued that non-remembrance itself is the subverting factor in that case, we say no; for if this were so, there would be a mutual dependence between non-remembrance and non-experience.
Even if there is no recollection of its author at the time of its initial appearance, the scripture is still a source of valid experience.

This is because we hear of an author in such passages as, "From him, as he performed austerity, the four Vedas were born; the Ṛg-verses and Sāman-chants were produced," and because of the traditional recollection of authors such as, "In every Manvantara, this Śruti is ordained differently. Since there is no subverting evidence against its being of human origin, it is impossible to claim that it is merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).
"This Blessed One, the Veda, is self-existent; it was sung by You in the past.
From Śiva down to the sages, they are its rememberers, not its creators"—this statement from the *Mahābhāgavata Purāṇa* has a different intended meaning because it contradicts the Śruti.
Furthermore, authoritative scripture does not concern itself solely with what is to be accomplished (*kārya*).

Because the recollection of an author is everywhere intended for a purpose other than an injunction, and because the explanatory passage (arthavāda) concerning having an author is subordinate to the injunction "One should meditate upon Īśvara"— just like the explanatory passages concerning heaven and hell—
and because the validity of statements regarding established facts will be proven later;
nor should it be said that, on these grounds, bliss would also [be attributed] to Īśvara.
If it is argued that there is no confidence in the Veda because it contradicts other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and because a person is prone to error, negligence, and the like;
we say: no. For since the person is established by the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject as being eternally omniscient, there is an absence of defects in him.
(Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p.

375) The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) for the doctrine of the eternity of sound: "But even so, the inference of [the Veda's] being of human origin is not probative, because its authority is established simply by its being eternal and faultless. [Reply: No.
Because the phonemes (*varṇa*) are impermanent, their aggregate is all the more impermanent.
Nor is this unproven; for sound, which consists of phonemes, is impermanent because it is produced while being inherent [in something], just like a jar.
Nor is there a failure to establish the reason (*hetvasiddhi*),
because there is the cognition that "the letter *ga* which has arisen exists as a clamor arising in the marketplace.
Nor is its apprehension merely the apprehension of what was previously unapprehended due to the absence of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*).
This is because of the cognition "the letter *ga* has arisen";
nor is this [cognition] merely adventitious, for it is experienced even when the arising of any other [letter] is not perceived.
Nor is there a superimposition of what is being remembered,
because there is no sublation;
otherwise, even the production of a jar would not be established.

As for the claim that the sequence is apprehended by the auditory organ alone— because of the uncontradicted after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) "I hear the word" following the operation of the ear, and because it cannot be grasped by any organ other than the ear— and that this sequence consists in the property of being the counter-positive of a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) existing at the time of the letter's manifestation, such that the letter's possession of prior non-existence as its counter-positive (i.e., its state of having an origin) is perceived directly: [This is the position to be refuted.]
That is not so;

for "immediacy" (ānantarya) consists in one cognition being the object of the cognition immediately following it, and their sequence (ānupūrvī) is grasped by the mind alone, just as in the case of the cognitions of a jar and a cloth.
And that [sequence], brought forward [by the mind], becomes an object of the auditory organ.

But surely this [position] is refuted by the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this is that very same letter *ga*"; thus, each individual manifestation of the letter *ga* and so forth is one and the same.

Even though eternity is not the object of recognition, nevertheless, since there is no possibility of any other sound—which is considered its destroyer—intervening, recognition grasps the letter *ga* as persisting for that duration; thus, "it is stable for that length of time."

The question "Who will destroy it later? results in nothing other than permanence, as it implies a state that exceeds the rapid perishability asserted by the opponent. Furthermore, even if there is a difference in the individual phoneme *ga*, recognition occurs on the basis of belonging to the same class;
for if that were the case, there would be a cognition of similarity to that class, rather than the cognition "this is that very same one."

Now, [the opponent might argue that] this [perception] is not a valid means of knowledge because its object is superimposed with contradictory properties such as high-pitchedness (*tāratva*) and low-pitchedness (*mandatva*).
However, neither the inherent nature nor the contradiction of these qualities—high-pitchedness and so forth—is unestablished;

for their existence is proven by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which cannot be explained otherwise, in the form: "The *ga*-sound that is low-pitched is different from the high-pitched one, and the high-pitched one is different from the low-pitched."
For there is no means of valid cognition other than direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) to establish that coldness and fluidity are the inherent natures of water.

Now, if it were the case that whatever appears as belonging to something must be a property of that very thing, then it would follow—without distinction—that in cases such as "a red cloth" or "a red crystal," the same would apply. But this is not so;

for while it is established that redness and the like are properties of other things (the dye), and it is established that crystals and the like possess properties incompatible with them, [the attribution of redness to the crystal] is an error due to sublation, since it conforms to the presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*) and so forth.
Furthermore, in this case, there is no presentation of pitch and so forth as properties belonging to something else;
nor do the phonemes such as *ga* possess properties contradictory to them;
nor is there any conformity to another entity that possesses pitch and other such properties.
Nor should it be said that the properties of air itself, such as length and so forth, necessarily appear as residing in the letter *ga* and others;
for since the skin has no operation when touch is not being grasped, those [properties] cannot be grasped by the skin. Nor can they be grasped by the ear.
Alternatively, [the pitch and other qualities] do not have air as their substrate alone, because they do not apprehend the specific properties of air, just like the eye;
or, pitch and so forth are not properties of air, because they are audible, like the letter *ka* and others;
or, air does not possess properties that are apprehended by the sense of hearing alone, because it is corporeal, like a cloth.

For this very reason, qualities such as high-pitchedness (*tāratva*) are neither properties of the air nor properties of the sound (*dhvani*), because a property of the air is not perceived within the sound. Nor should it be argued that the word, being of the nature of sound, resides only in space (*nabhovṛtti*), for if that were so, its properties such as high-pitchedness would be perceived by hearing; however, in the cognition "this letter *ga* is high-pitched," the sounds themselves do not manifest.
And because of the absence of its cause;
furthermore, there is no manifestation of the universal (jāti) without the individual (vyakti), since that [universal] is to be cognized by the same cognition as the individual.
Nor can it be argued that there is a superimposition of pitch and so forth upon what is being remembered,
because there is no subverting evidence and because it would follow that pitch and so forth could not be perceived at all for the first time.
This is not so.

Highness and other such qualities are not universals (jāti) belonging to the letter *ga* and so forth, because that would entail the fallacy of their commingling (*saṅkara*) with the universal of *ga*-ness (*gatva*) and the rest.
Nor is highness itself manifold,
for that would entail the absence of a unified cognition (*anugata-pratyaya*) corresponding to the high *ga*.

Nor can there be a unifying factor (*anugama*) for various instances of "highness" (*tāratva*) by way of being a genus residing in sound that serves as the delimiting condition for the obstruction of the direct perception of its own class;
for even when such [a genus] is not cognized, there arises a unifying cognition of "highness.
Furthermore, "highness" and "lowness" (*mandatva*) are not genera residing in sound, because they are relative (having counter-correlates).

Nor is there a contradiction between high-pitchedness (*tāratva*) and low-pitchedness (*mandatva*), because through the difference in time and the difference in speakers, one perceives their identity, thinking: "That very same *ga*-sound which was high-pitched is now low-pitched. If it is argued that there is a perception of difference—namely, "This is high-pitched, not higher; this is lower than the high"—we say no.

Because, while the substratum (*dharmin*) appears without distinction, the cognition of the distinction between qualified substrata has as its object the distinction between the properties (*dharma*);
it is like the cognition regarding a single jar: "This is red now, not dark.
Nor is there a distinction between those two [sounds] due to the suppression of the dull *ga*-sound by the intense *ga*-sound, for that very same thing cannot be its own suppressor.
It must be said that this is because there is a contradiction between the apprehension and non-apprehension of that very same [letter] by that very same [perceiver] at that very same time;
for, due to the strength of the air manifesting the high pitch (*tāratva*), the air manifesting the low pitch (*mandatva*) is overwhelmed, and thus the low pitch is not apprehended.
Alternatively, let the *ga*-sounds in the forms of high and low pitch and so forth be indeed distinct, since there is no sublation of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of them.

Therefore, properties such as high pitch (*tāratva*) and so forth, which belong to air itself, appear as if they were properties of sound, just as the properties of a mirror appear [superimposed] upon pleasure and the like.

And the perception of these [properties] occurs either by means of the skin-sense organ (*tvag-indriya*) located in the ear-cavity (*karṇa-śaṣkulī*), preceded by the perception of touch— since you yourself accept the increase and decrease of the winds that produce high and low pitches, as well as the manifestation of touch— or else by the auditory sense organ (*śrotra*) alone.

The fact that the eye and other [senses] do not grasp air or its qualities is due to their incapacity (*ayogyatva*), which serves as the limiting condition (*upādhi*); otherwise, the ear would not grasp its own quality, since such is observed to be the case with the sense organs.
Furthermore, one could also argue: "The eye does not grasp color belonging to earth, because it is a sense organ not composed of earth, like the tongue," and so forth.
Now, if a capable [sense] perceives its own quality or the quality of another by virtue of its capacity,
and that capacity is determined by the presence of the result, then the same applies to the auditory organ in the perception of the qualities of air.

Furthermore, there is no non-perception of air in the case of the statement "the *tāra* [note] is the letter *ga*," because even though it is not perceived as air, it is perceived precisely through its quality of being *tāra* (high-pitched), just as in the case of an iron ball, where even though it is not perceived as fire, there is the perception that it is "red."
If it is asked: "But by what means is there the superimposition that 'this *ga*-sound is high-pitched' when air and sound are perceived respectively by the skin and the ear?"—we say no;
for the linguistic usage of "conjunction" arises from the non-apprehension of the non-conjunction between two things that are actually perceivable by two different sense organs.

Or rather, let it be as stated: there is a superimposition upon the sound—brought forward by the organ of touch—by means of the ear, or else the apprehension of the quality of being high-pitched (*tāratva*) occurs by the ear alone.

Furthermore, the property of having an origin (*utpattimattva*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), because that [origin] is sublated by recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) in the form: "This *ga*-sound is one previously heard.

If it is argued that recognition itself is sublated by that [perception of difference], and that the cognition of non-difference regarding the *ga*-sound is merely conditioned by the adventitious factor (*aupadhika*) of the universal *gatva*, we say no;
for the universal *gatva* is unestablished. Indeed, it is only when difference is manifest that a cognition of non-difference takes recourse in a universal.
Furthermore, there is no perception of a difference between [instances of] the letter *ga*;
nor are "high-pitchedness" (*tāratva*) and "low-pitchedness" (*mandatva*) causes for such difference, because of the recognition that "that which was high-pitched is now low-pitched.
If it is argued that this is possible even if the letter *ga* were non-eternal, [we reply: no.
In that case, even if [sound] were eternal, it is possible for the ear-cavity to function as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) because it produces qualities of air conveyed by the sense of touch;
nor is there a non-perception of the air, since it is perceived precisely through its being produced, just as a *japā* flower is perceived in a crystal through its redness. 51
Or rather, let it be that, given its non-perception previously and its perception [now], there is a superimposition of the production of memory through similarity onto what has arisen.
Nor should it be argued that in this way, production would not be established even for things like a jar;

for in the case of a jar being experienced immediately after the activity of a potter, its non-identity with the jar experienced prior to that activity does not appear, but rather its very difference. Thus, in that case, there is existence following prior non-existence.

Regarding the letter *ga*: immediately after its production, because there is a cognition of non-difference from the *ga* experienced prior to the operation of the throat, palate, and so forth—and because there is a cognition of non-difference from the *ga* experienced previously—it is merely a manifester, like a lamp. If it is argued that sound is produced because, while possessing intensity (*utkarṣa*), it also possesses diminution (*apakarṣa*), just like sweetness, and therefore it is impermanent; [we reply: no.

Because the properties of highness (*tāratva*) and lowness (*mandatva*), which constitute excellence (*utkarṣa*) and deficiency (*apakarṣa*), are not established in the letter *ga* according to the previous reasoning—or even if they were established—due to the fear of a confusion of universals (*jātisaṅkara*), there would be a plurality of universals for excellence and deficiency that are subsumed under the universals of "taste" (*rasatva*) and "sound" (*śabdatva*), and thus these would lack commonality between taste and sound. For this very reason, excellence is a universal that delimits the capacity to obstruct the direct perception of its own kind, while deficiency is a universal that delimits the objective domain of the direct perception that is so obstructed; thus, it is common [to both].
The reason has been refuted,
because the properties such as high-pitchedness (*tāratva*) and so forth are not established as being the universal (*jāti*) of the phoneme *ga*.

Furthermore, the property of being produced by a preceding quality (*pūrvaguṇatattva*)— which pervades the probandum as delimited by the probans— and the property of not being audible (*aśrautratva*) function as extraneous conditions (*upādhi*), and the reason is also inconclusive (*aprayojaka*).
For increase and decrease are not dependent solely on causes, since they each exist individually in the dimension of the infinitely large and the atom;
nor is the coexistence of both in a single locus brought about by causes.
Because each one is individually a single unit, even in the case of two [sounds], it would be so.

This might be argued: since immediately following the operation of the auditory organ, there is the cognition, "The *ga*-sound previously heard no longer exists; it has perished; it was a clamor," the impermanence of sound is indeed perceived directly (*pratyakṣa*) by means of the inference that it possesses the quality of being produced, because it is a perishable entity.

For the perceptibility of destruction, as in the case of the destruction of a jar, consists in its being an absence whose counter-positive is perceptible; however, the perceptibility of the locus (samavāyin) and the counter-positive is not the determining factor for the perception of destruction, because otherwise it would follow that the absence of a quality (*dharma*) is perceptible.
Furthermore, this is because the absences of odor and taste are perceived even when their locus and counter-positive are not grasped by that particular sense organ.
Nor can it be both, because of the lack of gravity [in such a position] and because it would lead to the absurdity of the destruction of the conjunction with the remembered jar being perceptible.
Nor should it be argued that if the fitness of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) were the governing factor, then the destruction of the touch of air would also be perceptible;
for that [destruction], being produced by the destruction of its substrate, lacks contact with the sense organ that could apprehend it.
Furthermore, for that whose existence is not perceived in a certain place, its absence is therefore not perceptible;
for example, the absence of earth-nature (*pṛthivītva*) in a water-atom is not perceptible, whereas the absence of color (*rūpa*) in air is perceptible.
And it is the same in the case of sound: if it were present there and in conjunction [with the conditions], it would follow that it would be perceived.
If it is argued that there is no cognition of an absence without a locus, we say no;
for there is the cognition: "Now, here, the sound does not exist.
Therefore, an absence is determined in whatever locus—whether a place or a time—in which the counter-positive would otherwise be present.
For this very reason, it was stated that non-existence is determined by two positive entities;
and since the non-existence of sound is itself in direct sensory contact, there is no requirement for contact with its locus.
If it is argued that non-existence is not apprehended as a qualifier of the sense organ, we say no.
This is because unfitness (*ayogyatva*) serves as the limiting condition (*upādhi*).
Otherwise, since a quality (*guṇa*) is observed to be perceived through inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), sound would not be perceived through mere inherence (*samavāya*).
Do not say so.

For it is only in the case of an existing sound that there is mere non-perception due to the absence of a manifestor, but not its destruction; because when all the conditions for perceiving it—excluding those specific [obstructive factors]—are assembled, there is an absence of the "non-apprehension of what is capable" (yogyānupalabdhi), which consists in the non-perception of that [sound].
[The notion of destruction] is merely conditioned by the destruction of the touch of the air-currents that serve as the manifestor of the counter-positive (pratiyogin).
If it is asked what the decisive evidence (*vinigamaka*) is for the claim that air is not a producer but a manifester [of sound], we say: none.

For immediately after the cognition, "The *ga*-sound previously heard does not exist; it has perished due to the clamor," when one hears it again, there occurs a recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) such as, "This is the same *ga*-sound previously heard" or "This is that very same clamor.

However, after the cognition of the destruction of a jar, there is no recognition such as, "This is that very same jar. Therefore, in that case, by the cognition of its having perished, only its destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is established.

For this very reason, the hypothesis that the cognitions of highness, higher-highness, lowness, and lower-lowness are erroneous is rejected; for even when these [variations] exist, there is a recognition of non-difference.
This might be argued:

Sound is produced by effort; for [the removal of] that which does not manifest it must either remove an obstruction to the connection with the sense organ or bring about its proximity to the sense organ, just as the clearing away of a wall brings about the proximity of cloth and other objects.
Neither of these two is possible in the case of sound, because, being eternally inherent [in its substrate], there is no removal of an obstruction nor any bringing about of proximity.
Nor is it [manifested] through the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ.

It is observed that the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of a sense organ— such as its opening or the presence of light— produces a refinement conducive to the perception of all objects simultaneously with which the sense organ is capable of contact; in the same way, air too would impart to the ear a single refinement conducive to the perception of all sounds, and consequently, there would be the perception of all sounds at once.
As it has been said: "If the auditory organ were refined [to perceive one sound] once, it would manifest all sounds;
for the eye opened for a jar does not fail to perceive a cloth.

Now, based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), just as an effect is produced by its own specific cause, so too in the case of sound, there are specific manifestors (*vyañjaka*) for specific manifested objects (*vyaṅgya*). This is because, when they occupy the same location and are grasped by the same sense organ, they are delimited by a single [cognition].

It is like the singularity and dimension of a jar. Nor is there any deviation [from the rule] due to the singularity [of a jar], which is not manifested by the conjunctions of its parts—just as the blueness of a lotus is not manifested by the lamp that manifests the lotus-nature (utpalatva)—nor by the separateness residing in the jar, which is not manifested by that same lamp. This is because the conjunctions of the parts and the lotus-nature are respectively non-pervasive and pervasive, and because lotus-nature, having a wider extension, does not occur at the same delimiting point as the other properties.
Plurality and distinctness are manifested by that which manifests [them];

for this very reason, there is no deviation [of the rule] in cases such as "the crane is blue" (*nīlā balākā*), where color and dimension [are involved], or in cases involving the number and dimension of a bamboo pole half-buried in the ground.
Not so;

for the [phonetic] colors (*varṇas*) are manifested by specific manifestors because they are not perceptible by the same sense organ as their substratum, just like odor— this being [an argument] that appears to be countered at first sight.

In reality, however, once non-difference is established by the force of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) which is not otherwise accounted for, the argument proving that [sound] is manifested by specific manifestors lacks strength; furthermore, the notions that sound produces sound, that sound destroys sound, and the postulation of its production according to the analogy of waves and ripples, are mere mental constructs. This is because sound neither produces nor destroys itself, just like the final or the first sound in a series.
By this, the argument "because it possesses a universal and is perceptible by the external sense organs of persons such as ourselves" is also refuted.
Because recognition (pratyabhijñā) sublates [the contrary], and because properties such as "sound-ness" (śabdatva) and "g-ness" (gatva) are unestablished;
therefore, sound is eternal, because it is a unique quality of space (vyoma), like its dimension,
and because it is perceivable by the auditory organ, like sound-ness.
Because it is a quality residing in a single locus that does not have co-inherence with any other specific quality, like the dimension of time (*kālaparimāṇa*);
because it is a specific quality of an eternal element other than earth, being non-produced by heat and eternally inherent in a single [locus], like the color of a water-atom;
and because it is a quality of the non-self and the all-pervading that does not exist distributively, like the dimension of time.
And the subverting argument against the contrary position is precisely recognition;
this is the established tenet of the doctrine of the non-eternality of sound.
To this it is replied:
the individual manifestations of the letter *ga* and so forth are not one and the same;

for among the *ga*s produced by parrots, starlings, and humans, and further distinguished by whether they are produced by females, males, or specific individuals, there is a manifestation of difference in their essential nature (*svarūpa*) due to a very clear distinction, just like the sweetness of sugarcane, milk, and so on.
Nor is this perception of difference merely adventitious (aupādhika);

for the fact of being born from a woman or a man is not an adventitious condition (upādhi) based on experience in the way that "the young woman is red with saffron" is experienced by one who knows saffron;
because even for one who does not know the distinction between female and male through sensory contact, there arises a cognition of the difference between the words [themselves].

For it is from this that they infer: "This is the sound of a parrot," "This is the sound of a woman," and so forth; otherwise, there would be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), since the cognition of difference would be known only if its origin were known, and from that [cognition], the inference of that [origin] would follow.

Nor is it reasonable to claim that this is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*)—like the length of a face [seen] in a sword due to the sword's positive and negative concomitance—because [the sounds] do not follow the presence or absence of a sword.
Because there is no conformity with anything else.

Or, if it is argued that it is simply the distinctness of the manifesting air itself that appears as residing in the *ga*-sounds of the parrot and others, and that the perception of the air occurs in that very form—[we reply:
no, because there is no subverting evidence against its residing in the *ga*-sound.
Nor does the recognition of non-difference constitute a sublation,
for there is no recognition such that "the very same word *śuka* is the very same word *strī*";
otherwise, due to the absence of any cognition of difference among them, there would be no inference of a specific speaker.

Nor is it the specific difference of the manifesting air itself that serves as the inferential mark for [distinguishing] Śuka and others, because that [difference] does not reside in the letter *ga*; for if it were superimposed there, the resulting inference would necessarily be erroneous.

Therefore, just as in the cases "the cow is black" or "the cow is white," when a difference is manifesting, the cognition of the recurring *ga* takes the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) as its objective support.
Likewise, although a difference appears among the *ga*-sounds of a parrot and others, the cognition "this is a *ga*-sound" and "this too is a *ga*-sound" takes the universal *gatva* as its object;
thus, both recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and the manifestation of difference are logically accounted for.

Furthermore, if *gatva* and the like were not a universal (*jāti*), then there would be no cognition of a "tumultuous noise" (*kolāhala*). For instance, when many people simultaneously utter various phonemes in a city or similar place, a person standing at a distance does not perceive the distinct divisions of the phonemes such as *ga* and so forth.
Only a tumultuous noise is heard; however, the perception of phonemes within that sound, which consists merely of resonance, is impossible,
because the striking of a drum or other means that manifest it are absent.

Nor are those very [air-currents] that manifest the phonemes (varṇa) the ones that manifest the sound (dhvani), because it would follow that the sound would be heard even when the phoneme is being heard in close proximity.
Nor is it the case that by the same air-currents which manifest the phonemes, only the sound is manifested at a distance.

Just as there is no capacity for the manifestor of a cow to manifest the cow itself— as in the case of the syllables manifesting the word *go*— so too there is no capacity for the manifestor of the phonemes (*varṇa*) to manifest the sound (*dhvani*), because the conch-shell or other such sources capable of producing it are absent.

Nor is it the case that "soundness" (*śabdatva*) alone is perceived there and not the "sound" (*śabda*), for a universal (*jāti*) cannot be perceived if its individual instance (*vyakti*) is not perceived.

Nor is it the case that the manifesting air itself is perceived as a "tumultuous noise" (*kolāhala*), because it is perceived as sound (*śabda*), and because if it were so, it would follow that such a perception would occur even when [the air] is in close proximity.
If it is argued that the cognition of a "tumultuous noise" arises because, even when the phonemes *ga* and so forth are apprehended, their mutual differences are not grasped, we say: no.

Because there is an absence of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) among them, and because in its absence there is an absence of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), [the universal must be accepted] since it is through the apprehension of its own nature that [the difference is grasped]. Furthermore, if there were no apprehension of the difference due to the absence of distinction among many *ga*-sounds in close proximity, it would follow that there would be the cognition of a "tumultuous noise" (*kolāhaladhī*). If the utterance of multiple phonemes were the cause of that [cognition], then it would follow that such a cognition would not occur even at a distance. Therefore, one must necessarily accept a genus-form (*jātirūpa*) such as *gatva* (the "ga-ness"), such that when it is not apprehended, even though the individual *ga*-sound is apprehended, there arise both the cognition and the designation of a "tumultuous noise."

Furthermore, there exists a certain specific universal (*jāti*) of sound that is perceivable by the auditory organ, by virtue of which its origin from a conch shell located in a specific direction—such as the east—is inferred;
for even though it is inexpressible, this universal exists just like the internal distinctions in the sweetness of sugarcane, milk, and so forth.
Otherwise, since the auditory organ lacks the capacity to grasp conch shells and other objects as qualified by spatial directions, there would be no cognition of them at all.

If it is argued that there are no specific universals (jāti-viśeṣa) in the *ga* sounds produced by a parrot and so forth—because, due to their being neither prior nor posterior, the relation of priority and posteriority is untenable—we reply:

in the *ga* sounds produced by a parrot and so forth, there exists a distinct universal subsumed under "ga-ness" (*katva*) and so forth; this universal is unique to each instance of the parrot-produced *ga* sound, as it either infers its origin from a parrot or accounts for the conventional usage thereof, since otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of confusion (*saṅkara*) with the universal "ga-ness" (*gatva*) and others.

The *gatva*s (the universal of "g-ness") are not manifold, because if they were not inclusive (*ananugata*), then inclusive linguistic usage (*anugatavyavahāra*) would be impossible. For this very reason, even the property of high pitch (*tāratva*)—which is subsumed under *gatva* and the like—is manifold, whereas *gatva* itself is not; furthermore, even when that [high pitch] is ascertained, there may still be doubt regarding *gatva*. This is because inclusive linguistic usage is possible with respect to the various high pitches through their inclusion by means of the inclusive delimiter of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka*).
Because linguistic usage cannot be established without knowledge of that [distinction].
If it is argued that "highness" (*tāratva*) and "lowness" (*mandatva*) are not universals (*jāti*) because they possess counter-correlates (*sapratiyogikatva*), we say no; for highness—

The specific universals (jāti-viśeṣa) such as "louder-ness" and so forth, which consist of excellence and the like, are perceived only when their substratum is perceived; they do not depend upon a point of comparison for that excellence.

Just as [qualities] such as "sweeter-ness" produce the conventional usage of excellence in dependence upon other tastes, so too does the conventional usage of "louder-ness" and so forth occur in dependence upon "softer" sounds and the like.
However, an excellence (*utkarṣa*) distinct from the universal (*jāti*) and the form (*rūpa*) is simply impossible in the case of the letter *ga*; this is not so for the universal *gatva*.

For the existence of that [excellence] is established by the force of the cognition of difference—which cannot be explained otherwise—and by the force of the inference of a specific speaker; thus, one must accept a plurality of those [universals] subsumed under *gatva* and *katva*.

Even for you, if [the excellence] resides in the air, it must be stated that the manifesting airs of the *ka*-sounds and *ga*-sounds of a parrot and so forth are of different classes (*vijātīya*), and likewise [for other sounds].

Furthermore, if the nature of the air manifesting the letter *ka* were pervaded by the nature of the air manifesting the phoneme *śuka*, then that [nature] would not exist in the air manifesting the phoneme *ga* of *śuka*;

if, on the other hand, it were the pervader, then all airs manifesting *ka* would necessarily be airs manifesting the phoneme *śuka*. Therefore, even though they reside in the air, their plurality is indispensable.

Now, suppose one argues: "Let there be a distinction between the *ga*-phonemes of women, men, and so forth; nevertheless, as many as there are speakers, the phonemes must be infinite and eternal because of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)."
Even though there is the perception of production and destruction, there is the recognition that "this is that very same letter *ga*";
for indeed, even immediately following that, there is the manifestation of production and destruction.
And there is no sublater other than one or the other—namely, either the perception of production or the recognition of non-difference—to set aside the other.

Nor is there any determining factor (*vinigamaka*) between these two whereby one might be the sublated and the other the sublator, such that their contradiction could be resolved by attributing error to only one of them.

Or how else could recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)— having entered a state of peril by disregarding the mutual obstruction established elsewhere between the cognitions of difference and non-difference— be subject to the consequence that even when one of the two exists first, the other would arise?
It is not possible to establish the permanence of sound through such means.
But surely, [if that is so], how is impermanence established even by such properties as having an origin? Indeed, it is so.
Thus,
there must necessarily be a difference in the objects of both the cognition of origination and so forth and recognition;
for if they had the same object, the other would not arise immediately after the first due to contradiction.
And thus, while difference appears, the object of recognition is the identity of the genus (*sajātīyatva*), not the non-difference of the individual.

Nor should it be said that in this case one would have "it belongs to that genus" rather than "this is that," for even in the cognition of belonging to that genus, we observe the form "this is that," as in: "This is that very same verse," "This is that very same medicine," or "That which was prepared by many still exists, being prepared by me every day," and so forth.
Sequence is certainly not merely the phonemes themselves, because it differs in cases such as *jarā*, *rājā*, *nadī*, and *dīna*;

rather, it is the utterance [of a phoneme] immediately after [another], or the cognition [of a phoneme] immediately after [another]. And since that sequence is manifold, the verse containing it is likewise manifold.
Furthermore, when non-difference is being manifested, it is not the case that the cognition of arising and so forth regarding one thing apprehends the arising and so forth of another;
for this would entail the consequence that the cognition of [the quality] residing in the letter *ga* is erroneous. Nor is such a consequence acceptable.

Since, when non-difference appears, there can be no arising of the delusion that it possesses contradictory properties, and since both [the appearance and the cognition] are equally real due to the absence of any determining factor (vinigamaka),
how then can non-difference be its object?

Where there is no initial manifestation of difference, for that very reason, because one is ignorant of the existence of difference, such [recognition] is in some cases erroneous; therefore, where there is a cognition of difference that is not sublated by any sublater other than itself, recognition does not occur at all, or if it does occur, it takes as its object merely the belonging to that same class (*tajjātīyatva*), and is not erroneous.
Because error does not arise when a specific distinction is perceived.

Furthermore, just as the recognition "this is that same *gurjarī* melody," despite the perception of the arising and destruction of sounds such as those from a conch-shell and the association with contradictory properties such as high pitch (*tāratva*), has as its object merely belonging to that same class (*tajjātīyatva*)—
so too is the recognition of phonemes (*varṇa*).

Otherwise, even the *dhvanis* (articulatory sounds) would have to be eternal, because the cognitions of their production, destruction, and degrees of intensity (*tāratva*) would be merely adventitious (*aupādhika*) by virtue of the force of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Nor is it possible for the *dhvanis*, which appear as having varying intensities, to be adventitious adjuncts (*upādhi*) in relation to the phonemes (*varṇas*).
But it should not be argued that phonemes do not exist in sounds (dhvanis) because of the absence of the impact of the throat, palate, and so forth that produces them;
for even at the time of the utterance of a phoneme, there is likewise an absence of those [impacts] that produce the *gurjarīkā* and other such [sounds].

Therefore, since the cognition of production, destruction, degrees of pitch (*tāratva*), and so forth, as well as the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), are equal in both cases, both must be either eternal or non-eternal.

Nor is it the case that both [the word and its manifestation] are eternal, because—according to the reasoning already stated—the recognition has as its object the identity of the class (*tajjātīyatva*) of the word.

Furthermore, if the word were merely manifested, then just as a jar is not perceived in the absence of external light, the word would likewise not be perceived in the absence of a manifestor; consequently, there would be doubt regarding its existence.
However, there is no certainty at this point that sound does not exist here; therefore, the phoneme (varṇa) is neither eternal nor non-eternal, because it possesses existence while being produced,
because it possesses a genus while being perceptible by the external sense organs of persons such as ourselves,
or because it is a quality directly perceived by persons such as ourselves.
In the view that the self is perceived as a unity, [the reason is] because it is a specific quality perceived [by the self],
because it is a specific quality perceived as inhering in a pervasive [substance],
and because it is a quality perceived as non-self.
Because it is non-pervasive in its occurrence,
whereas the knowledge of God is not so,
due to the absence of a cause that would produce it [in such a manner].

Because it possesses the quality that is the cause for the establishment of external sense organs; because it possesses the quality of being perceptible by the elements; or because it possesses a genus (jāti) which is the basis for the application of terms such as "superior" and "inferior," and so forth.

Even though there is a multiplicity of universals (jāti) pervaded by "tastiness" (*rasatva*) and so forth, the status of being such a ground for application (*pravṛttinimittatva*) is common to them all. Furthermore, in this case, "being inherent in that which possesses touch" (*sparśavatsamavetatva*) cannot be an adventitious condition (*upādhi*) that pervades the probandum—whether the probandum is delimited by the probans or not—because, when sound consisting of phonemes is everywhere taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), it does not pervade the probandum in the case of eternal sounds (*dhvani*) which are qualities of space (*ākāśaguṇa*); moreover, the term "possessing touch" excludes only the subject itself, and thus constitutes the fallacy of *pakṣetaratva* (being other than the subject).

And when even the phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves are not eternal, what need is there to speak of words (*pada*), which consist of a collection of phonemes qualified by a sequence dependent upon the speaker's intention?
How much less so for a sentence (*vākya*), which consists of a collection of such words, and how much less so for the Veda, which is a collection of such sentences?

If it is argued that, although there is the doctrine of being obscured and then re-obscured, we nevertheless maintain that "eternality" consists simply in the non-interruption of the stream due to its dependence on a succession of dependent persons, we say no; for we observe the disappearance of Vedic branches (śākhās) inferred from [the existence of] Smṛtis and traditional practices.

It might be argued as follows: "The Smṛti under dispute, which conveys a new meaning, is rooted in the Veda because it is a Smṛti accepted by great persons without censure, just like a Smṛti whose root is directly perceived Veda;

and its being rooted in the Veda consists in its being produced by an experience generated by the Veda. This is known through inference, since the Veda is the cause of the Smṛti only when it is itself known [as the source], just as a weaver is the cause of a cloth even though he is separated from it by the intervention of his knowledge and other factors."
But there is no lack of causal relationship,
because the composition of the Smṛti occurs precisely when the Veda exists and is recollected; furthermore,
the status of the Smṛti as a recollection of the meaning of the Veda is established by common consensus.

And the meaning of the *smṛti* is already present through the *smṛti* itself. Furthermore, when inferring the Veda as the source that conveys the meaning of the *smṛti*, the Veda is not merely repetitive (*anuvādaka*), because the meaning of the Veda—which is the very object of the *smṛti*—serves as its content. This is because a qualified cognition is possible when something brought forward by another cognition functions as a qualifier, just as cooking is [the qualifier] in the case of the mental perception of the act of cooking.

In the case of the cognition of a name and its bearer, when there is a lack of knowledge regarding the name or when that knowledge is not as it truly is, this occurs during the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), just as in the case of the object of an error;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of confusing the erroneous cognition with the cognizer of that error. However, the meaning of a word is not the object of inference, because since it is unestablished (*asiddha*), it lacks the capacity to produce [cognition], and because it does not pervade memory.
Furthermore, that Veda is indeed always inferable, for it is possible to compose a Smṛti only after one has determined its meaning through inference alone.

If it is argued that something which has not been recited since beginningless saṃsāra cannot be a Veda—whether by way of its origin, its manifestation, or by intention like the poetry of a silent sage—because a mere sequence of phonemes devoid of order is meaningless, and because there is no inference of a specific [authorial] intent when there are multiple utterances that produce knowledge, we say: no. For a Veda, once known as a communicator of the meaning of a Smṛti, serves to cause the experience of that very meaning of the Smṛti.
For a fixed sequence of words is not the cause of verbal cognition,
because of the occurrence of deviation.

Even though there is a fixed sequence of specific phonemes for a word, a particular word possessing that specific sequence of phonemes cannot be the cause [of the cognition of its meaning], because this would lead to inconsistency (vyabhicāra) in the case of each individual pair such as *hasta* and *kara*. Rather, it is the word known as the non-deviating indicator of its meaning that is the cause; this is due to parsimony (*lāghava*) and its necessity.
It is precisely for the sake of knowing that it indicates that meaning that, in certain cases, specific sequences of phonemes and accents are employed.

For this very reason, even when there is a doubt regarding the letter *sa* in the case of elision of phonemes—as in the command "bring *kuśa*"—or when there is a doubt between *hasta* and *kara* in either writing or pronunciation, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning still occurs.
Now, one might object: "The nature of a sentence consists in possessing a sequence of words;
yet here, there is no sequence of words."

If it is argued that [the sentence] does not exist because it is not being uttered—since utterance is dependent [on the parts]—or because it is simultaneously inferred—since it is dependent on the cognition [of the parts]—we reply:

no, for being composed of sequential words is not what constitutes "sentencehood," as this is absent in cases such as *gaurava* (the word *gauḥ* and the word *aravaḥ*). Rather, it is the state of being a word directed toward a qualified meaning; and that indeed exists here as well.
If it is argued that what is not being uttered lacks both the status of a sentence and the capacity to convey meaning, we say no;
for even those [sounds] inferred from written signs possess the status of a sentence and convey meaning,
and memory is equivalent to written signs.
Furthermore, it is not the case that a sentence is produced merely by being uttered;
for if it were so, there would be the consequence of a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) in the sentence "utter a sentence" (*vākyam uccāraya*).

Moreover, an unuttered verse from the *Mauṇiśloka* would not be a sentence, and if sententiality were to exist only at the time of utterance, the sentence would be non-existent [at other times], since the words are not being uttered simultaneously.
Furthermore, that which has been uttered, is being uttered, or will be uttered does not constitute a sentence,
because each individual [part] lacks that status within the aggregate.
Therefore, the cognition of a specific object arises only from that which is known as the indicator of that specific object.
For this very reason, there is an inference of fire from smoke based on the cognition [arising] from the word "there is a mark of fire";
however, from a word known merely as an indicator of its own meaning, there would be only the cognition of that isolated meaning, and not the cognition of a relation (*saṃsarga*).

Even when there is the cognition, "The pot is the object, bringing is the productive operation (bhāvanā), and [the suffix] is its indicator," there is no comprehension of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) as there is from the sentence "Bring the pot.

Thus, the cause of the cognition of the sentence-meaning is the knowledge of a specific word possessing an inflection or the like that presents the objecthood (*karmatva*) and so forth as the mode of the relation, as well as the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors aroused by it; therefore, in cases such as "Bring the *kuśa* grass" where there is doubt regarding whether the word is *hasta* or *kara*, the experience of the sentence-meaning arises solely from the knowledge of the inflection and so forth, and not merely from the status of being an indicator in their absence.
Not so;

for it is not as specific words possessing particular case-endings and so forth that they serve as causes for the cognition of the sentence-meaning, because there would be a lack of uniformity (ananugama).

However, the cognitive presentation of word-meanings that does not arise from words incompatible with the syntactic relation—such as in "the pot" (*ghaṭaḥ*) or "objecthood" (*karmatvam*)—is likewise present here.

In reality, the causal complex for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning following the presentation of word-meanings from various words is exactly the same; it is indeed distinct [from ordinary cognition] when the sentence-meaning is experienced through the Veda known by inference, because that which is known merely as a signifier of a remembered meaning functions as the cause of the experience of that remembered meaning, according to the means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*).
Because it is established in that very same way;
for [the Veda] is like your God, being a creator despite being bodiless.

Precisely for this reason, because it brings about the experience of the meaning of a sentence—whether that sentence be indivisible or divisible—by being composed of specific features such as phonemes, words, and inflections, [it does not require a creator].

The sentence-meaning stands in the place of the word-meaning for that [cognition]; in this regard, a collection of phonemes is a *pada* (word) and a collection of *padas* is a *vākya* (sentence), and the apprehension of these occurs there as well, because its status as a valid word is established merely by its being a word of authority (*pramāṇa-śabda*). Otherwise, in cases such as "that which causes experience" (*anubhāvaka*) without an established cause, if that were not established, there would be the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*); if it were established, there would be contradiction (*bādha*). Therefore, having overcome all these inconsistencies even without that [cause], [the sentence-meaning is established].
Because the fact that [the Veda] causes that experience is established by the very means of cognition that apprehends its subject;
for this very reason, in some cases, having understood the meaning of the Vedic injunctions and prohibitions as they are inferred through praise and blame, one engages in activity or desists from it.

Otherwise, since injunctions and prohibitions exist in various forms, it would be impossible to infer the specific word—such as those with particular case-endings—and consequently, no understanding of the meaning could arise from them.

If it is argued that, nevertheless, just as after the inference of the speaker’s knowledge, the meaning of the sentence is established through an inference based on an inference (anumitānumāna), and thus the Veda—like an ordinary worldly sentence—would be merely reiterative (anuvādaka), we say: no.

This is because [the Veda] lacks the causal totality (sāmagrī) required for such an inference, since it is known by the very means of cognition that apprehends its subject (dharmigrāhakapramāṇa) as being a communicator of the object of Smṛti;
furthermore, inference is delayed by its dependence on the cognition of pervasion (vyāpti) and other factors.

Nor is there any delay on the part of the Veda due to its dependence upon the knowledge of semantic competency (*yogyatā*) and so forth; for it is established by the means of cognition that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakamāna*) that the Veda is a communicator independent of such factors, or because it is inferred as qualified by semantic competency and the like.

Thus, having inferred the obligatoriness of the practice of auspicious rites (*maṅgalācāra*) through its being the unobjectionable conduct of the learned (*avigītaśiṣṭācāra*), one concludes that this obligatoriness is taught by the Veda.
