[The opponent argues: "Because it is a duty according to the non-worldly, unobjectionable conduct of the learned (*alaukikāvigītaśiṣṭācārakartavyatātva*), there is a cognition of its being a duty derived from the Veda inferred as the indicator of that [conduct]; from that, activity [arises]. [The author replies: But surely, that conduct has its duty-status indicated by the Veda because it is such conduct; thus, the cognition of its duty-status arises from the Veda inferred [from that conduct]. However, there is no inference of a Veda in the form "one should perform auspicious rites" (*maṅgalam ācaret*) from the mere knowledge of its duty-status derived from an inferred Veda lacking [specific] case-endings and so forth, because there is no such pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Therefore, infer the necessity of performing that [action] from the inference of the Veda which makes it known;
for even when there is first a cognition of the necessity of performance, the inference of the Veda follows by way of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
Nor does the inference of the perceptible Veda follow from that [cognition of necessity] alone.
If [the Veda] were directly perceptible, its destruction would be impossible, as in the case of other recensions (*śākhā*).
As for the claim that a sentence of the form "the Aṣṭakā rites should be performed" or "the Aṣṭakā rites must be done" is to be inferred because of its presence [in memory], [that is not so].

And thus, regarding that very same meaning, there must be a separate inference of a Veda for each individual person; for if [the Veda] were perceptible, its disappearance would be impossible, as is the case with other recensional branches (*śākhā*).

As for the statement that the *aṣṭakā* rites are to be performed—that is, that the *aṣṭakās* ought to be done—it is precisely such a sentence that is to be inferred, because it is what is present [in the mind].

In that very context, it is argued that there is no fault in inferring separate Vedas for each person regarding the same subject matter, or rather, when multiple words present a single meaning, one simply infers multiple sentences; however, this is not so, because when inferring the Veda from established practice (*ācāra*), there is no fixed rule as to whether one should infer "one should perform an auspicious rite" (*maṅgalam ācaret*) or some other such injunction.
Furthermore, the postulation of multiple Vedic texts would contradict one's own experience;
since it is not necessary for the *Manusmṛti* to have multiple verses as its source, how could a modern person infer such a multiplicity?

Nor should it be argued that the Veda which conveys the meaning of a Smṛti must necessarily be inferred as being similar to that Smṛti, because the Smṛti is invariably present [in the mind] at the time of inference.

Since the recollection of that [Vedic] meaning also possesses various forms, it is logical that—just as the Veda has the status of "Veda" even when not being recited at dawn and other times—it possesses the status of "word" (*śabda*) by virtue of being capable of being apprehended by the sense of hearing, and the status of "sentence" (*vākya*) because it conveys a meaning. Furthermore, when [the Veda] is inferred through tradition and practice, it conveys its meaning; thus, from each preceding inferred Veda, the subsequent tradition and practice arise.
The [tradition] is not a blind succession (*andhaparamparā*), because—like the apprehension of the power of word-meanings—it is rooted in its own intrinsic means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, the Veda is eternally inferable, but it is not subject to annihilation. To this it is replied:

since the Smṛtis and customary practices (*ācāra*) are established through the comprehension of meaning from an interrupted Veda, there is no need to postulate another complete collection [of Vedas]. For this very reason, there is no realization of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), because we accept that the Veda is inferred from the Smṛtis and customary practices.
And now, activity [toward Smṛti] proceeds by inferring its duty from the object of the Smṛti and from established custom;
yet it should not be asked, "What is the use of the Veda in this case?

For they are equal, and because of their inseparable connection, the postulation of that [Vedic basis] is equal as well. Thus, precisely through the inference that Smṛti and custom are rooted in an experience produced by the Veda, the fact that they are rooted in a directly perceived Veda is established by the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
Otherwise, since it would lack the capacity to produce cognition, its status as a source (mūla) would be untenable.

Therefore, the Veda inferred from tradition (smṛti) and custom (ācāra) is both directly perceived and a subject of study, because it possesses the nature of the Veda, just like that which is commonly accepted;
otherwise, there would be the fault of unnecessary complexity (gaurava) in postulating a different causal complex.

If it is objected: "How can one engage in activity or desist from it by understanding the meaning from a prescriptive or prohibitive statement that is merely constructed through explanatory passages (arthavāda) consisting of praise or censure?
For in such cases, inference of the specific details of phonemes, words, case-endings, injunctive suffixes, and word-order is not possible due to fallibility," we reply: No.
From the sentences of praise and censure, it is the object itself that is postulated as the cause for engagement and withdrawal,
due to parsimony;
not, however, the prescriptive or prohibitive sentence, because of its complexity and the aforementioned defects.

Furthermore, in cases such as "He crosses over death," where the meaning is understood from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) itself, there is not even the possibility of [independent] postulation (*kalpanā*).

If it is argued that, since it is a subject of study, its loss is impossible—just as with other recensions (*śākhā*)—because it would be maintained by many intelligent individuals endowed with spiritual power, we say no.

For one individual lacks the capacity to study all recensions; thus, just as it might be lost by one person, it could likewise be lost by others. Consequently, there is no evidence for a rule that what has not been studied by one person must necessarily remain a subject of study for another.
Although there are indeed those such as Vyāsa who know the thousands of branches of the Veda, nevertheless, the loss of a branch occurs precisely through the absence of its study.

If it is argued that, upon the loss of a branch, because of the fear of losing the phonemes, words, and sentences, one would be unable to determine the meaning of sentences or their practical application even from the directly perceived Veda, and thus the entire Vedic practice itself would perish— this is not so.

Since that which is merely being heard is embraced by the great [tradition] of those who have mastered the *mahājapa*, and since it is practiced by the learned (*śiṣṭas*) precisely with the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) taught by that alone, there is certainty regarding its meaning.
Nor does the suspicion that the procedure might be taught by a lost branch lead to a lack of confidence even in a single rite;
for it is not currently the case that that rite must be completed by drawing the procedure from various different branches.

For there exist Smṛtis composed by the sages—who, fearing a lack of confidence due to the sequential occurrence [of various rites], intended to provide knowledge of the entire procedure (itikartavyatā) taught in various Vedic branches (śākhā)—and these have been accepted by the great multitude; thus, there is no lack of confidence. Otherwise, since a single person cannot comprehend all the branches, there would be no certainty regarding the purpose from a single branch due to doubt concerning the procedure taught in other branches.

As for the claim that, although words beginning with case-endings and their collections are perceived, there is nonetheless some [portion] that is Veda, yet there is no certainty that "this collection is Veda"— whereby the object would be eternally inferable,
or else "Veda-ness" itself would be inferable therein— that is incorrect;
for among those great persons who are experts in the Veda, there is a certainty regarding the absence of Veda-status in any sentence other than the perceptible Veda.

For this very reason, "Veda-ness" (vedatva) cannot be inferred there, because it would be contradicted and because the specific subject (pakṣa) is not known. Furthermore, "Veda-ness" as the capacity to produce the knowledge of dharma cannot be inferred, because that capacity is directly perceived. Nor can it be the state of being an object of Vedic study, because that is absent [in the case of the Purāṇas]. Nor can it be a universal (jāti), because such a thing is not admitted.

It might be argued as follows: if it were established that tradition (*smṛti*) and customary practice (*ācāra*) are rooted in the Veda, then disputes regarding their interruption and so forth would arise; however, that very point remains unproven.

For indeed, Smṛti, which possesses the same meaning as the Veda and is accepted by the great multitude of people, serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*) for inferring a Vedic text that causes the experience of the meaning of that Smṛti immediately after the Smṛti's own meaning has been established. Thus, because it is primary and because it must be relied upon to establish the probandum (*sādhya*), let the knowledge of the sentence-meaning regarding *apūrva* and so forth belong to Smṛti alone; what is the use of the Veda? For its meaning is already established through Smṛti itself, since even *apūrva* is cognizable solely through verbal testimony once it has been known from Smṛti.

Furthermore, it would result in the Smṛti being merely a restatement (anuvādakatā) by virtue of its being an indicator (jñāpakatvena); and since that [indicator] comes from another Smṛti, an endless stream of Smṛtis is necessarily required.
Otherwise, there could be no inference of the Veda even for the prior limit (pūrvanta) of the Manusmṛti.

Furthermore, all Smṛti is authoritative because it is produced by a valid cognition of the meaning of sentences generated by Smṛti, and because it is accepted by great persons; thus, it is not a blind tradition.
Moreover, Smṛti is directly perceived, and its source is direct perception, not inference—as is the case with the inferred Veda—because [Smṛti] does not itself produce an inferential experience.

As for the well-known status of Smṛti as having the Veda as its source, this is due to a delusion arising from its association with Smṛtis whose sources are directly perceived Vedas, just as in the case of a Smṛti based on greed or logic (which is not Vedic). For the scholars (tāntrikas), the notion that it is rooted in the Veda is produced by fallacious marks (liṅgābhāsa).
[The opponent] imagines:

"Now, just like the *smṛti* itself, the well-known fact that it is rooted in the Veda is also accepted by the great masses of people; and thus, this [fact of being rooted in the Veda] is based on the Veda, because it is a well-known fact accepted by the great masses of people as being rooted in the Veda, just like the well-known fact regarding a *smṛti* whose Vedic root is directly perceived."
If it is argued that the established status of the Vedas as the source of meaning is likewise [to be accepted],
otherwise the authority of both the Vedas and the Smṛtis would not exist due to the disregard shown to what is embraced by the great multitude of people— [we reply: no,
because there is a deviation in the case of the Smṛti concerning the "elephant-shaped sacrificial post" (yūpahasti) and so forth, even though such a thing is well-known [among some].

If it is argued that there is a discrepancy among the great masses regarding its establishment because [the object] can arise from greed and so forth even when [the text] is fabricated, and because of the conflicting opinions of investigators, we say no; for here too, since other sources are possible and because of the conflicting opinions, their discrepancy remains exactly as it is.

Therefore, since it is possible for the Smṛtis to be rooted in reasoning (nyāya), even though there is a well-known tradition that they are rooted in the Veda, they do not actually have the Veda as their source.
Nor can it be argued that the Smṛti has the Veda as its source simply because it is accepted by the great community of people on the grounds that "this is rooted in the Veda";
for it is impossible to know initially that "this is rooted in the Veda," and if such knowledge were already possible, what would be the use of inference?

Nor is the acceptance by great persons (mahājanaparigraha) based on the mode of being rooted in the Veda, because that is unestablished; for the performance of rituals and so forth is possible through the successive acceptance by later generations based on the prior acceptance by great persons such as Manu and others as Smṛtis.

Likewise, in the case of customs such as the Holākā, since the knowledge of its duty-to-be-performed is established by the very indicative marks (liṅga) within the Veda itself, what is the use of the Veda?
Because that meaning [of the Smṛti] is established through inference (*liṅga*) alone;

for we observe that the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), which concerns non-contradicted worldly matters, is rooted in the Veda. Furthermore, if one were to infer a Veda based on such conduct, then even the practice of eating and so forth would have to be rooted in the Veda by virtue of being the uncontradicted conduct of the learned.
However, since the cognition that those acts ought to be performed can arise even without a Veda, the Veda is not required for that purpose—and this point is the same here as well.
Because the practice and the inference of its duty are beginningless, and because practices are rooted in the inference of their duty, there is no "blind tradition" (andhaparamparā).

Nor is there such a tradition because each subsequent inference depends upon a preceding inference; rather, since all [inferences] possess both pervasion (vyāpti) and the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatā), they are all rooted in independent means of valid cognition (svatantra-pramāṇa).

Nor is it the case that the validity of everything depends upon the validity of something else, for if that were so, there would be no independence [of a means of knowledge], as this would apply to perception and other means as well.

By this, the following argument is refuted: "The practice under dispute is rooted in an independent means of valid cognition, because it is not contradicted and is practiced by great men, like practices rooted in direct perception or the Veda."

Because inference is an independent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the reason [for its validity] is established simply by its being rooted in another means of valid cognition; furthermore, independence is not a necessary factor due to its complexity (*gaurava*).
Nor does it lack the status of a means of valid cognition merely because it is dependent [on other factors], since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and other requisite conditions are present.
Nor does its being dependent [on other factors] negate its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth do exist;
otherwise, the independence (*nairapekṣya*) of a means of valid cognition would be rendered useless.
Nor can there be an inference [of the Veda] from the fact that established custom is known to be rooted in the Veda,
because that is unproven, because of deviation, and because it can be explained otherwise.
Nor is it the case that [custom is so established] simply because it is accepted by great men on the grounds of being rooted in the Veda.

For the acceptance of this [practice] by the great masses is not on the grounds that it is rooted in the Veda, because it is impossible to know its Vedic basis at the outset; or, if it were possible to know it, what would be the use of inference?
Nor is the acceptance of this practice by the great masses based on the knowledge that "this conduct is accepted by the great masses precisely because it is rooted in the Veda."

[The opponent argues: "Because of [the Veda's] authority and because it is not [otherwise] established; for the performance [of rituals] is logically possible due to the successive acceptance by later generations based precisely on the prior acceptance by great men [in the past].
Furthermore, since such Smṛti and custom are pervaded by being rooted in the Veda, the Veda is thereby established. [The author replies: No.
Because the impossibility of having another source constitutes a limiting condition (*upādhi*);
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even those Smṛtis rooted in greed or worldly logic would have the Veda as their source.
Or, let it be granted that Smṛti and practice are beginningless.
Nor should it be said that "from practice comes tradition (smṛti), and from tradition comes practice," resulting in a blind succession due to the absence of an underlying foundational authority;
for both tradition and practice possess the status of valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
Otherwise, one could not even infer the Veda from them.
It is said:

because memory and practice are interrupted at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), memory and practice at the beginning of creation must be rooted in the Veda composed by the eternally omniscient Lord.
Otherwise, in the absence of a foundation, there would follow the fallacy of a "blind tradition" (*andha-paramparā*).
Nor do Manu and the others possess the capacity to perceive supersensuous objects, because at that time there was no hearing of the means for such perception and so forth.
If it is argued that those very Manu and others were omniscient beings established in a previous creation, [we reply:]...
It is not so, because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that the very assumption [of such a source] is based on the fact that memory and practice must have a foundation in a valid means of knowledge, we say no;

for it is simpler to assume a single, eternal, and omniscient being than to assume a different [source] for each successive creation (*pratisarga*), which would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).
Furthermore, the Smṛtis themselves were not composed by Him,
because they are understood within the Smṛti tradition to have Manu and others as their authors, and because it is recorded in the Smṛtis themselves that the Smṛtis are rooted in the Veda.
Thus, since both Smṛti and custom are accepted by great men (mahājana), they also serve as evidence for the Lord's status as the source of the Veda.
For this very reason, there is also the traditional scripture (āgama) stating: "In every Manvantara, this Vedic revelation is ordained differently.

Thus, in the beginning, Smṛti and Ācāra were indeed rooted in direct perception (pratyakṣa); subsequently, however, due to the daily diminution of the power of longevity, health, strength, faith, comprehension, and retention over the course of time, and because of the interruption of their study leading to the disappearance of the Vedic branches (śākhā), [the authority of] Smṛti and Ācāra alone [remains].

Activity occurs after one has understood that something ought to be done. Now, if it is argued that while the Smṛtis may thus have the Veda as their source, practices such as performing auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) must originate from Īśvara himself—just like the traditions of writing and the potter’s craft—the answer is no. This is because those various practices involve many constituent operations and are therefore cumbersome; by contrast, it is simpler to postulate a scriptural injunction such as "one should perform an auspicious rite. Thus, [the practice] is derived from the Veda.
Furthermore, that [recourse to usage] is appropriate for the purpose of grasping the word-potency (*śakti*) of terms such as *maṅgala* (auspiciousness) and so forth.
For this very reason, where comprehension of another arises from mere speech, there is no reliance on usage by the investigators;
nor does that [speech] possess the status of Veda, because its being composed by God (*īśvara*) is subject to deviation in the case of that speech which serves to grasp word-potency.
"But such conduct must necessarily have its root in the Veda.
One might object: "This would be so if a dissolution (pralaya) actually existed; however, that dissolution does not exist because there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for it. We reply: No.

The prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of a jar, which does not recur in time or in the potsherds, has as its locus a substratum that is not the locus of any effect-substance, or else it resides in a locus of an effect that is not the locus of any effect-substance, because it is a non-existence, like the mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva) residing in space.
This is because it establishes a dissolution [of the world] by means of a formal argument (*vṛttapralayasādhanāt*).
In exactly the same way, one may take the destruction of a jar as the subject (*pakṣa*) and establish a future dissolution:

"Alternatively, a jar is the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of a destruction that resides in a locus of an effect which is not a locus of any other effect-substance, because it is an effect, like sound."

Alternatively, the property of being a product-substance (kāryadravyatva) resides in that which is the counter-positive of a destruction occurring in a locus of a product that does not reside in a product-substance; this is because it resides in all products, like the nature of sound (śabdatva).

Alternatively, all atoms existing at a single time are devoid of a continuous series of effects produced by their causal complex (samagrī), because they are initiators [of new aggregates], like the atoms initiating a vanished wind.
In every case, the probandum is understood as qualified by the delimiting condition of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka); thus, emptiness at a single time is established.

Nor is there a partial *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) regarding even the atoms of air by virtue of their being included in the subject (*pakṣa*), because the probandum obtainable through the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is not [already] perceived;
and, as in the case of an inference based on non-difference, there is no contradiction in the subject itself serving as the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Alternatively: atoms possess effects that do not subsist in the locus of an effect-substance, because they are eternal substances, like space;
or, this continuum of the earth possesses a destruction that does not subsist in the locus of the continuum of the earth, because it is an effect, like a jar;
or alternatively, actions other than this action are obstructed by the obstructor of this [action], because they are actions, like this action.
Nor is there any suspicion of deviation here,
because all things possess this very nature, and if they were otherwise, their essential nature (svabhāva) would be lost;
otherwise, even if a rule were established, it would lead to an infinite regress by requiring another rule for that rule.
Scripture also confirms this very point; enough of this digression.
The prima facie argument for the theory of injunction (*vidhivāda-pūrvapakṣa*):
Since the Veda’s status as the root of conduct arises from its being the generator of the knowledge that prompts action, the knowledge that prompts action is now defined.
In this regard, the knowledge of denotation (*abhidhā*), intention (*saṅkalpa*), unseen merit (*apūrva*), and mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) are not motivators,
because activity does not occur even when they are present, and activity does occur even when they are absent.
The teachers (*guravaḥ*) maintain that the knowledge of being a task to be accomplished (*kāryatvajñāna*) is the motivator.

For this reason, when the production of knowledge—which is something to be produced—is to occur, there is nothing further to be done beyond the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), because in its presence there is no other cause for a delay in the action.

Furthermore, the desire to act is a desire directed toward an action that is to be accomplished by an effort, characterized by the mode "to be accomplished by an effort," as evidenced by the experience: "I shall accomplish the cooking by means of an effort.

And that [desire] is produced by the cognition that [the object] is achievable by one's own effort, because it is a rule that desire is necessarily produced by a cognition whose object has that [achievement] as its own qualifier.
For this very reason, one engages in cooking that is achievable by one's own effort;

however, it is not the case that the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) is produced by the cognition of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*), because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of such a desire arising even for what cannot be achieved by one's own effort.
If it is argued that the cognition of something being unachievable by one's own effort is an inhibitor, we say no.
Because it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) to posit non-existence as the cause.

If it is argued that since non-existence is established for both parties, but the cognition of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatā*) is not, there is thus no occasion for the application of parsimony (*lāghava*), we say: no.

For where that [cognition] arises from verbal testimony or inference by chance, parsimony applies; because desire is invariably established by a cognition whose object is its own qualifier (*svaprakāraka-jñāna*).

Furthermore, because the knowledge that [the action] is achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatvajñāna*) is indispensable, and because a cognition functions as an obstacle only by subverting the cognition that produces [the action], just like the cognition of an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) which obstructs inference by way of subverting the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
(Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,2, p. 23)

Otherwise, since [an action] would not be accomplished by one's own effort, the cognition that it is a means to an undesirable end, that it is to be disregarded, or that it is fruitless would act as an obstacle; thus, one would have to assume that the mere cognition of the action itself is the motivator. If it is argued: "Since the suffix *san* denotes a desire whose object is the meaning of the verbal root, and for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), 'the desire to act' (*cikīrṣā*) is simply a desire directed toward the action; and this [desire] arises from the cognition of it being a means to a desired end, just as [the desire] for rain does," we say: no. Just as there is the thought "I shall accomplish [my goal] by means of fire," there is likewise the experience prior to the action of the thought "I shall accomplish [it] by means of an action. Since this desire cannot be dismissed due to its being denoted by the suffix *san* and because of the resulting complexity (*gaurava*), [your position is untenable].

Furthermore, in the expression "one who desires to cook" (*pākaṃ cikīrṣati*), it is experienced that cooking (*pāka*)— and not the act of doing (*kṛti*)— is primarily the object of the desire; moreover, the suffix *san* expresses a mode of the desire denoted by the verbal root,
because in the expression "one who desires to eat rice" (*odanaṃ bubhukṣate*), rice is experienced as the object of the desire by virtue of being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the eating.

Although a desire for action may arise toward an act—just as it does toward rain—because it is a means to a desired end, it is not the desire for action that motivates; rather, it is the desire for [the act] to be accomplished by one's own effort.

This is because we experience the object of knowledge, the object of the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), and the object of the action as being one and the same, as in the sequence: "one knows the jar," "one desires to make it," and "one makes it.
Now, if this desire were merely the wish to accomplish something by means of an effort, then that desire would not cease even when the intended cooking was already accomplished by other means.
If it is argued that one is not deterred from a specific means simply because the result can be achieved through it, since the attainment of the fruit depends on other optional means—
just as the desire for wealth is not eliminated by receiving it as a gift even when one has already obtained it through pleasure—
the answer is no; for the fact that the object of one's own [desire] is already accomplished, and the cessation of the desire for the fruit, are both contrary to the desire for the means.
Moreover, in that case, there is the establishedness (*siddhatva*) of both the cooking and the rice;
for when there is a desire for another [portion of] rice, the desire to cook (*pākacikīrṣā*) certainly arises.

On the contrary, because of its unestablishedness (*asiddhatva*), the desire for the action itself would not be interrupted, provided that the establishedness of the object of the effort (*kṛti*) and the interruption of the desire for the result are not mutually contradictory.

Furthermore, when wealth is acquired through pleasure, the desire for even more wealth is not severed, because that [greater wealth] has not been achieved and the desire for its fruit still exists; however, for one who seeks merely wealth, even when wealth is acquired through pleasure, there is no longing for it by way of acceptance,
because the mere wealth itself has already been achieved.
For the cessation of the desire for a general [object] occurs precisely through the establishment of some specific [instance] thereof;
otherwise, since it would be impossible to establish all of its own objects, that cessation would never occur.

In reality, however, when there is the cognition that "the action is a means to the desired" (iṣṭopāya) based on an effort (kṛti) conducive to action, the action possesses both the state of being achievable by effort (kṛtisādhyatva) and the state of being a means to the desired.

An action manifests [as an object of desire] solely through the door of activity, because it is the means to achieve what is desired; thus, from the cognition of that [means], just as there is a desire for activity, there arises a desire for the action itself by way of its being achievable through activity.
Therefore, in the case of the desire-to-act (*cikīrṣā*), there is a necessity regarding the mode [of the object] as being achievable through activity.

Consequently, the desire-to-act is the cause of activity by virtue of being a desire-to-act whose object is identical to that of the activity, and not by virtue of being a mere "desire for activity," because the latter would involve the fault of complexity due to having a different object.

Nevertheless, in whatever form something is a means to a desired end, there arises a desire for it in that very manner; just as there is a desire for rain because it is a means to a desired end in its capacity as rain upon one's own field, so too, since cooking is a means to a desired end by virtue of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatvena*), a desire for it arises in that same capacity of being achievable through effort.
If it is argued that when there is an action or an object of action, there is no desire for rain in the presence of a desire to act,
and thus one must postulate a distinct causal complex (*sāmagrī*), this might indeed be so.

If the rice-porridge’s status as a means to an end were established by its being achievable through effort, that would not be the case due to the fault of unnecessary complexity; rather, it is established by its nature as cooking,
though it is another matter that this [cooking] does not exist without effort.

If it is argued that the desire "I shall accomplish [this] by means of an action" (kṛtyā sādhayāmi) arises from the very cognition that [the object] is a means to a desired end—just as the desire "I shall accomplish [this] by means of fire" [arises from the cognition that fire is a means to a desired end]—then, just as the cognition that [fire] is achievable by means of fire is necessary there, so too here the cognition that [the object] is achievable by means of an action (kṛtisādhyatva-jñāna) is necessarily a cause.

Furthermore, the specific characteristic of an action is its dependence on the desire-to-act (cikīrṣā), which is established by experience; therefore, there is no inclination toward the movement of the five vital breaths (prāṇapañcaka-sañcāra), even though that is achievable by means of an action that is the source of life (jīvanayoni-kṛti).
Otherwise, one would also act toward that which is merely achievable through effort (*kṛti-sādhya*) even if it were not a means to a desired end (*iṣṭa-sādhanatā*).

Now, if being dependent on the desire to act (*cikīrṣā-dhīnatva*) is taken as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), then—since there is no property residing in the indicated object alone that avoids over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), and since mere effort (*kṛti-mātra*) would lead to over-extension—the specific instances of those respective efforts must be the objects indicated. And thus, because of the lack of a commonality among them, there would be a lack of commonality in the resulting activity (*pravṛtti*).

If desire-to-act (*cikīrṣā*) and activity (*pravṛtti*) were taken as qualifiers [of the object], there would be the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) and a lack of evidence regarding their being causes for the knowledge of desire-to-act.

Furthermore, if it is argued that the state of being "to-be-accomplished-by-effort" (*kṛtisādhyatā*) could not be known in the case of cooking and the like—because there is a contradiction between the state of being "to-be-accomplished-by-effort" and the state of being a "means already accomplished"—we say no.

For there exists a specific kind of effort, established by mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), which is excluded from the life-sustaining effort (*jīvanayoniprayatna*) and is characterized by desire-to-act; it is in this [effort] that the apprehension of the causality of desire-to-act occurs. And while for you this [effort] is of the nature of a universal (*jāti*), for me it is of the nature of a recurring causal adjunct (*upādhi*).
And thus, by means of the common factor of being dependent on the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), there is also a commonality among the specific acts of doing (*kṛti*) which are to be characterized;

just as, for example, specific instances of the act of milking that are excluded from buffaloes and the like are denoted by the word "cow" (*dhenū*) when characterized by the accidental property of cowness (*gotva*), but cowness itself is not [denoted].
The same applies to the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*).

Thus, since the cognition of specific volitions—distinguished from the effort that is the source of life (*jīvanayoni-yatna*)—as being "volition" (*kṛti*) is the cause, there is no lack of uniformity (*ananugama*).

Now, one might object: in the case of what is to be accomplished by volition (*kṛtisādhya*), volition cannot be a qualifier because it does not yet exist; or, if it were already present, there would be a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*), such that the volition exists when the cognition exists, and the cognition exists when the volition exists.
If it is argued that [the object] is not a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), we say no;

for in the case of knowledge, the object is indeed a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) by virtue of being its content, whereas in the case of what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it is a secondary characteristic by way of being a specifier. Otherwise, even in the case of "accomplishing what is desired" (*iṣṭasādhana*), "desired" would not be a qualifier because it is non-existent [at the time of the action], nor would it be a secondary characteristic because that would lead to over-extension.
Furthermore, what would be the status of the cognition of a logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth?

[Objection: In that case, there would also be a desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) regarding fatigue, since that too is to be accomplished by an effort (*kṛti*) dependent upon a desire to act. [Reply: To this they say:

Fatigue, however, is accomplished by actions such as eating, and is not accomplished by an effort directed toward it, because it is not something one desires to do (*acikīrṣitatvāt*). This is because an effort is a generator only with respect to its own object of desire (*cikīrṣā-viṣaya*), excluding the direct perception of its own cessation;
for it is not the case that it generates everything merely within the scope of what is desired through eating.
Some maintain that movement is not accomplished by an effort (kṛti) dependent on the desire to eat;
however, that is not so.

For even when an effort directed toward lifting a very heavy load—which cannot be accomplished by such effort—is undertaken through delusion, or when one's body is rendered motionless by shackles, although the actions of lifting or moving do not arise, fatigue is nonetheless experienced from the effort itself.
Because it is the cause;
however, this does not apply to the action produced by that [desire], as there is a deviation in the case of pleasure.
For pleasure is not the object of the desire-to-act (cikīrṣā) which is the cause of performance.
For effort (*kṛti*) is produced by the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) regarding a means, but not by the desire to act regarding pleasure itself.
Others maintain that being achievable through an effort produced by a desire to act does not apply to fatigue, because fatigue arises even from an effort born of aversion (*dveṣa*).
This is not correct.

Because the killing of an enemy is something to be accomplished by an effort produced by a desire to act (*cikīrṣā*)— since it serves as a means to achieve a desired end— and because aversion (*dveṣa*) does not produce effort,
the existence of aversion is established by the force of the experience "I hate the enemy.
As for the claim that fatigue is to be accomplished by an effort merely in its nature as an effort (*kṛtitva*), and not by an effort dependent on a desire to act (*cikīrṣādhīna-kṛtitva*).

If, even in the case of exertion that one does not wish to perform, causality were to consist in being produced by an effort (kṛti) dependent on a desire to act (cikīrṣā), then it would follow that only food which is desired to be eaten is accomplished through effort, and not undesired actions such as walking; for in that case, walking too would result in being produced by that [effort], just like the exertion.
However, eating and the like are produced from a specific effort dependent on a desire to act.
For that [effort] deviates from mere effort, because it does not arise from the effort of living (jīvanayoni-kṛti).
Alternatively, one might argue that fatigue is not produced by the effort of eating, but rather solely by the effort of the life-force (jīvanayoni-prayatna) arising continuously from it;
but that is not so.
For it is not the case that [exertion] produces fatigue by virtue of being an action (*kṛti*),
nor does fatigue arise solely from another action.

Even when the effort that is the source of life (*jīvanayoni-prayatna*) exists, one who does not perform tasks such as carrying a burden does not experience such fatigue; therefore, that [life-sustaining effort] does not produce exhaustion. Consequently, like eating and so forth, even specific instances of exhaustion must be produced by an effort directed toward eating and the like, for there is no other recourse.

If it is argued that the exhaustion inferred from perspiration and so on in a sleeping person is produced by that [life-sustaining effort], we say no, because perspiration and the like have causes other than exhaustion; otherwise, if they were caused by exhaustion, it would follow that exhaustion would persist even during waking hours, since perspiration persists then as well. This is not so, because [the effort in question] is qualified by being an effort dependent on one's own will (*svecchādhīna-kṛti*).

Furthermore, exertion (*śrama*) is necessarily achievable through an effort (*kṛti*) dependent on the desire of another, because there is an absence of desire for exertion due to its being a form of suffering; for this very reason, exertion is said to be "unavoidable" (*nāntarīyaka*) insofar as it is achievable through an effort produced by the desire of another.
However, being dependent on one's own desire to act (*svacikīrṣādhīnatva*) is not a qualification of the effort, because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Others, however, maintain that "being the object of desire" (*uddeśyatva*) is itself a distinct property residing in the action; and that which is to be accomplished by an action qualified by that [property] is not labor, because it is not something one desires to do, but rather something to be accomplished by mere effort.
For this very reason, people have the experience that "work is painful.

Thus, in the case of the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), for me (the proponent) a single factor is the motivator: being achievable through effort. But for you (the opponent), there are four factors: being achievable through effort, being a means to a desired end, being pleasure, and being the absence of pain.
But for me, the motivator of desire is the dyad consisting of my own state of happiness and the absence of suffering;
for there, desire arises because [happiness] is a means to rain, since being a means is not opposed to desire.
For you, however, it is a triad.

Regarding the consumption of poison, some maintain that although it is achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhya*), there is no desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) because it is a means to a powerful undesirable end; therefore, they claim that being produced by a desire to act is a necessary qualification for an action.

This is trivial, for if this were so, the consumption of poison would not even be achievable through effort, since such an effort—namely, that which originates from the will to live—would never arise; thus, the qualification is redundant.

It might be argued as follows: due to an error regarding the means of achieving a desired end, there exists in both the eating of poison and the worship of a shrine the state of being achievable through an effort produced by a desire to act, because the status of being a task (*kāryatva*) is necessitated by cognition; thus, even one who has already realized the truth [of the situation] might still engage in those acts out of a cognition that they are tasks, and likewise, even one who is satiated might engage in eating.

[Objection: But surely the experience of being achievable by one's own effort is likewise [required]; otherwise, if there were merely a recollection of its being a means to a desired end, one would act even toward eating poison.
And if it is argued that there is no Vedic statement to cause the knowledge of its being a means to a desired end, [we reply: No.

In reality, since the state of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) can be experienced there either by means of another inferential mark (*liṅga*) or through the word of a reliable person (*āptavākya*), and because it would follow that one would not act upon a fallacious mark (*liṅgābhāsa*) or a fallacious word (*śabdābhāsa*);
furthermore, for you who maintain that [action arises from] the non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgraha*), such experience of that [state] is absent— do not say this.

For it is the cognition of being an effect (kāryatājñāna), produced by the recollection of one's own qualifying attributes, that motivates action. To illustrate: in the case of an optional rite (*kāmya*), the desire for the result is the person's qualifying attribute; consequently, through the cognition that the sacrifice or cooking is a means to that desired end, one is motivated.
In the case of a mandatory rite (*nitya*), time, purity, and so forth are the person's qualifying attributes.

Thus, in the thought "At this juncture, I am one who performs the sandhyā-vandana achievable through my effort," there arises—during the time of the sandhyā—a cognition produced by the knowledge of one's own qualifying attributes such as purity.
As it has been said:
"And that specific effect, understood as a qualification of the person, is the cause of activity.

Furthermore, for one who has recognized a sublation, there is no cognition of something being a means to a desired end in the case of consuming poison or worshipping a shrine, just as in the state of delusion.

One might argue that one would act because of a cognition of being an effect produced by that [action], but for one who is satiated, there is an absence of the cognition of it being a means to a desired end due to the lack of desire; thus, such a cognition does not occur.

Others, however, maintain that a cognition of the action being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*) regarding fatigue can arise from the recollection of one's own continued life, and therefore "being distinct from mere living" is a qualification of the qualification of the subject itself;
but that is not correct.
Because in the case of exertion (*śrama*), there is an absence of being achievable through an action performed according to one's own will;
others maintain that the knowledge of "task-to-be-done-ness" (*kāryatā*)— which has "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) as its logical mark— is the motivator,
but that is not correct.
Because that [desire] does not exist in the case of what is eternal (*nitya*).

Now, one might object: let it be that "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), as excluded from the consumption of poison, is itself the qualifier in the objective case within the cognition of "being achievable through effort" (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*), since this is simpler than [the view that the action is] produced by a cognition of its own possession of a qualifier (*svaviśeṣaṇavattājñānajanyatva*).
Furthermore, the desire to act regarding a means is produced by the cognition that [the action] is a means to achieve a desired end, because it is a desire for a means, just like the desire for rain.
(Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,2, p. 81)
If it is argued that when there is a desire for enjoyment (*bhoga-cikīrṣā*), being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) is not the motivator because of the absence of that [desire], we say no;
for even in your view, since it lacks being produced by a cognition of its own qualifier (*svaviśeṣaṇadhī-janyatva*), it is not the motivator in that case either.
It is rather the motivator for the desire to act (*kṛti-hetu-cikīrṣā*).
And if it is argued that there is no such desire for enjoyment,
because the production of an action arises solely from the desire for the means [to it], then:
Regarding the claim that they are "equal," it is not so;
for because of the contradiction between being the probandum (sādhya) and being the probans (sādhana), it is impossible to know both as one and the same thing.

For that which is in an unestablished state possesses the nature of being an object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), because that nature is absent when it has reached the state of being established (*siddha*); and that which is in a state of being established possesses the nature of being a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), because an effect does not arise from that which remains in an unestablished state. Thus, upon the cognition of the unestablished and established states of cooking and the like, there occurs the apprehension of their being objects to be accomplished and their being means of accomplishment.
Furthermore, a single thing cannot be cognized at one and the same time by one person as both established and unestablished.
Nor should it be argued that there is no contradiction because the states of being the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) reside within the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of the entity];
for if both were based on the essential nature, then that very nature would have to be both eternally established and unestablished.
This is because, even if those two states are defined by different perspectives, their establishment and non-establishment remain unintelligible due to the lack of knowledge regarding them.
Therefore, the relation of both [the fuel and the fire] to the cooking is conditioned solely by the difference in time.

If it is argued that "it is understood that [the fuel] possesses the state of being the object-to-be-accomplished (*sādhyatva*) now, and the state of being the means-of-accomplishment (*sādhanatva*) later," we say no.

Now, because the two subsequent categories [of substance and quality] are diverse, there is no commonality (*anugama*), and thus pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot be grasped; consequently, it is impossible for a word to convey [the relation] in that way, and it would also involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).
Furthermore, desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) does not arise from the cognition "this is an established means to the desired end," for no one desires to act toward what is already established.

Furthermore, because there is no cognition that "it is established prior to the action by means of the action," and because cooking and the like are means [to an end] due to their being desired as things to be accomplished by action (*kṛtisādhyatva*), it is not the case that their status as a means is itself something to be accomplished;
for cooking does not become a means for obtaining boiled rice simply by virtue of its being to be accomplished by action.

Thus it has been said: therefore, that which is distinct from what has already been done and what is currently being done—namely, "the state of being achievable through effort" (*kṛtisādhyatva*) characterized by a future existence immediately following the effort—is the motivator of the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*). And such [a state] is indeed incompatible with being a means (*sādhanatva*). Furthermore, since being a means is a property belonging solely to what is already established, the cognition of being a means is contrary to desire;
for it has been stated that no one desires what is already established.
By this, the claim that the cognition of something as a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*)—such as rain—is established as the cause of desire for that means, is refuted.
How then does desire arise for rain and the like, which are not inherently pleasant?
Understand it thus: it arises from the cognition of the desired object to be accomplished by them (*tatsādhyeṣṭajñāna*).

Others, however, maintain that there exists a distinct property (*dharmāntara*), denoted by the term "human goal" (*puruṣārtha*), which is a common feature underlying the absence of pleasure and pain as well as the desire for their means; for a common effect must be governed by a common cause.
It is this very [property] that serves as the motivator for the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) regarding suffering and its causes.

Nor should it be argued that being the opposite of suffering itself constitutes such [a contradiction], because a contradiction characterized by the rule of non-coexistence is impossible; furthermore,
the relationship of the slain and the slayer lacks co-location at a single moment, and [the property of] being the cause of destruction is common to effort and other factors as well.
That is not so;
for even when that [pleasure itself] is unknown, desire arises from the cognition of "pleasurability" (*sukhatva*).
Indeed, once "pleasurability" is known, one does not fail to desire it merely because of the lack of knowledge regarding some other property (*dharmāntara*).
If that were the case, it would follow that the inherent purpose [of the action] is lost;
for that alone is the inherent purpose which, once understood, is desired as residing in itself.
Furthermore, even the postulation of a recurring property must apply to the cause.
And pleasure and so forth are not the cause of desire because they are future;
rather, it is the cognition of them [that causes desire].
If it is argued that, in the case of the cognition of pleasure and so forth, that [cognition] itself, being existent by its own nature (*svarūpasat*), may be the motivator of desire, we say no.

For just as the status of being an object (*uddeśyatva*) arises in the cognitions of pleasure and so forth—either because they are one of two alternatives or according to the logic of the grass, the fire-stick, and the gem (*tṛṇāraṇimaṇinyāya*)—in the same way, let desire itself arise.
Furthermore, the state of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) exists in its own nature at a subsequent moment when the effort is present, but not without the effort.

And this [status of being an object] is common to both security (*kṣema*) and that which is to be accomplished through effort (*kṛtisādhya*). Furthermore, the state of being accomplished through effort does not exist prior to the effort itself.

Now, one might object: "Once the effort has perished, even though the substratum (*dharmin*) still exists, it is no longer something to be accomplished; thus, how can there be a connection for those desiring [the result] with the *apūrva* as the object to be accomplished, since, due to its momentariness, it is equivalent to a mere action (*kriyā*)? To this we say: No.

The pervasion (vyāpti) is that where there is the state of being a means to what is desired (kāmyasādhanatva), there is the cognition of it as something to be done (kāryatā), because the cognition of "to-be-done-ness" is the motivator; it is not the case that the state of being a means to what is desired is qualified by "to-be-done-ness. If it is objected: "But in the case of cooking and the like, the knowledge that it is achievable through effort (kṛtisādhyatājñāna) cannot be established through perception; for if the knowledge of 'to-be-done-ness' arises after the cooking has occurred following the effort, then there is a circular dependency (anyonyāśraya)—namely, that the effort exists when that knowledge exists. Furthermore, since desire to act (cikīrṣā) and effort are impossible regarding something that transcends being achievable through effort," We reply: No.

The knowledge that cooking is achievable through one's own effort arises from the following inference: "Cooking is achievable by my action, because, while being non-existent without my action, it is a means to what I desire; or, while not being dependent on fate and the like, it is a means to what I desire," just like my own meal. This is based on the pervasion (*vyāpti*): whatever is a means to what someone desires, and which cannot occur at a given time without that person's action, is at that time achievable through that person's action.

Because for that which is not established [as a means], there is an absence of being a desired means (*iṣṭasādhanatva*); furthermore, "not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence" (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*) is a qualification of the probans (*liṅga*). Therefore, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of eating food mixed with honey and poison; nor is there deviation when [the action] has passed beyond being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*), because even in that general sense, it is achievable through effort.

Furthermore, in the past state, because there was an absence of the desire for cooked rice, there was an absence of its being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). For this very reason, one whose body is emaciated by the heat of summer does not engage in plunging into a lake when it rains, even if there is a possibility of obtaining water from the cloud; for he perceives that the connection with water—which is the means to the desired alleviation of his torment—is already accomplished even without his own effort.

Because, in the absence of a [valid] logical mark (*liṅga*), there is an absence of the cognition that [an action] is to be accomplished by one's own effort. And when one reflects that "it is not possible without my effort," then one engages in the activity.

Some [maintain] that for one whose sole desired object is the cessation of distress, there is no reflection on bathing in the river as being a means to achieve that desired end, because that [cessation of distress] could also occur from rain that has already arrived.

Therefore, its status as a means for alleviating heat does not consist in its being connected with water, because that [quality] exists even when one merely plunges into a lake; otherwise, rain too would not be a means for it, since that [alleviation] could be accomplished by plunging into a lake as well. Furthermore, being a means to an effect (*kāryasādhanatva*) is not a mark (*liṅga*) for being achievable through volitional effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*), because—just as in the case of cooking and so forth—one has no knowledge of the state of being achievable through effort prior to the activity directed toward rice and the like.
(From *Bibliotheca Indica* 98, IV,2, p. 111):
But in that case, let the cognition of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) itself be the motivator, because it is both primary and necessary.
Nor can the cognition of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) be so on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*).

If it is argued that [desire] does not arise because there is no means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the simultaneous presentation of the two [factors] at the time of the inference of "being achievable through effort" (*kṛtisādhyatā*), and because the inference obstructs the causal complex for activity (*pravṛtti*), we say: no.

For when the cognition of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) does not manifest "being achievable through effort," that [mark] is not a cause for a desire-to-act (*cikīrṣā*) whose qualifier is that [property].
For this very reason, even the cognition of another inferential mark is not what prompts action.

Now, it might be argued that neither the cooking already performed nor that currently being performed can be the subject (pakṣa), because their being achievable through effort is contradicted; nor can the future cooking be the subject, because there is no proof for a future cooking, which would result in the fallacy of an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi).

If it is argued that "the state of being cooked (pākatva) exists as a future function because it is a generality (sāmānya), like cowness (gotva)—this is the proof"—we say no; for since there is a lack of proof, that [future existence] is unestablished even in the case of cowness.
If it is argued that "mere cooking (pākamātra) is the subject (pakṣa)," we say no.

If "being an act of cooking" (*pākatva*) is intended in the sense of the individual substance (*mātra*), then there is sublation (*bādha*) and the unestablished nature of the logical mark (*liṅgāsiddhi*).

If, on the other hand, it refers to all acts of cooking, then there is sublation regarding its established portion and the unestablished nature of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) regarding its future portion.

Nor can it be maintained that the present and indifferent act of cooking is the subject (*pakṣa*), and that the fact of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) is not sublated with respect to the universal "act of cooking" (*pākasāmānya*).

If it is argued: "A thing that is already established cannot be the subject (*pakṣa*) of an inference, whereas that which is not yet established can; thus, since an inference has an established object as its domain, there would be a contradiction [if the desire to act were directed toward an unestablished object]. Alternatively, if they have different domains, then desire, activity, and so forth would not arise with respect to an established object. Rather, it is from the cognition of being achievable by effort—common to both what has been done and what is being done—that the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) and the effort itself arise regarding an unestablished object. In that case, since the kind of "being achievable through effort" (*kṛtisādhyatva*) that serves as the qualifier in the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) does not exist in that [initial] cognition, the desire to act would arise from a cognition having a different qualifier altogether.
And thus, let the cognition of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) alone be the cause of activity, because it occurs first.

As for the claim that activity toward a remembered cooking arises from the non-apprehension of the non-connection between it and "being achievable through effort," and that this non-apprehension of non-connection results from the apprehension of its being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*): [this is incorrect].

That is not so; for since the cooking remembered [in the past] is already established, the inference is sublated by the apprehension that there is no connection with "being a task to be accomplished" (*kāryatva*) in that case.
If it is argued that the established nature of the remembered cooking is not apprehended at that time, [we reply:]...
In that case, if one perceives the remembered cooking as already accomplished, a person desiring rice would not engage in the act of cooking;

for if there is a perception of accomplishment regarding that cooking and so forth, there can be no perception of its non-connection [with the desired result]. This is equally true [for your position].

Furthermore, since there is no perception of the non-connection of the remembered cooking with "being a task to be done" (kāryatva), and because there is no perception of the non-existence of such a connection, one's engagement would be inconsistent [with the actual state of affairs].
Furthermore, in this way, from the knowledge of the accomplishment [of cooking], there would arise desire and activity toward a cooking that is unaccomplished and unknown.
To this we reply:

the state of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) with respect to cooking is established; since it is sublated in the case of what is already accomplished, it is established by taking up the future cooking.

Since it is established in inference that the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the property delimiting the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka-dharma*) of the probandum is proven by the logical mark (*liṅga*),
just as even when a specific fire is sublated, fire in general is not sublated and thus an unestablished fire is nonetheless proven,

so too, even when the state of being achievable through volitional effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) is sublated in a specific cooking act, the cooking act in general is not sublated; therefore, [the unestablished] is proven.
Taking the cooked [rice] as an example, that [inference] succeeds;
for there is no distinction between the proof of two things—such as the subject (*pakṣa*) and the probandum (*sādhya*)—that are themselves unestablished.
Therefore, when something unestablished is established in one case, and something already established is established in another.
Furthermore, since that which is unestablished cannot be established by itself, inference is thus threefold.
Otherwise, even in the case of cooking and the like—which are to be accomplished through effort—how could their being "to be accomplished through effort" (kṛtisādhyatva) be understood?

Moreover, for you as well, how could desire arise toward rain and such things from the mere cognition of them as means to a desired end, given that "established-ness" (siddhatva) is contrary to desire and because it is impossible to know what is yet to come?

For this very reason, by refuting the possibility of [desire] having as its object either what is already established or what is not yet established, one does not desire even the fruit arising from the cognition of pleasure and so forth; thus, there is no "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) even in the case of rain and the like.

Nor does desire for rain and so forth arise from the cognition of a desired thing to be accomplished by rain and so forth, because that would entail the dilemma of whether such desire has as its object rain and its fruit—both of which must be either already established or not yet established.

Now, through the cognitive proximity of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇapratyāsatti*), a cognition arises regarding both realized and unrealized rain and its results, in their capacity as "rain" and so forth, and as "pleasure" and so forth. By means of that [cognition], having abandoned the realized [object] which is opposed [to desire], a desire for the unrealized object is produced.

Furthermore, if there were no general characteristic [proximity], then desire would be produced for an object known as realized in whatever form its status as a means to the desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) was apprehended.

If it is argued that, based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), such knowledge is determined to be the generator of such a desire, and thus even in the case of a desire for pleasure there is a single [instance], then for me as well, from the knowledge that cooking is achievable through effort (*kṛti-sādhyatā-jñāna*)—delimited by the nature of cooking (*pākatva*)—there arises a desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) regarding a future [act]; and whether that knowledge has all future cooking as its object or only proximate cooking as its object is another matter.

As for the first activity of an infant, since they have not yet grasped the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) and so forth, it arises from the awakening of impressions (*saṃskāra*) from a previous birth stimulated by the unseen force of life (*jīvana-adṛṣṭa*), specifically from the memory "sucking the breast is my duty" (*stanapānaṃ kāryam*); according to you as well, it arises from the memory of its being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭa-sādhanatā-smaraṇa*).
In this regard, the process of engagement occurs because there is no other possible resort; nor can there be an objection regarding another birth,
since the stream of births is beginningless and, being rooted in perception and inference, it is not a blind tradition.
In reality, however, a child experiencing pain due to a parched throat remembers pleasure because of its opposition [to that pain];

consequently, from the cognition of "pleasure-ness," there arises a recollection of the state of being an effect of the pleasure-function by way of being a function of pleasure, because of its internal proximity, and not a recollection that "the drinking of breast-milk is a means to a desired end."

Because it is an external factor due to its being a pleasant state, even the suckling at the breast is an object [of desire] by virtue of being an effect that brings about pleasure; therefore, activity toward suckling arises simply from the cognition of it as an effect (*kāryatva*), since at that time the conditions for the cognition of it as a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*) are absent. Thus, since the cognition of it as an effect is established as the motivator for the first instance of activity, that alone is posited as the instigator of activity in subsequent cases as well, owing to parsimony (*kalptatvāt*). However, the Neo-Naiyāyikas (*navīnas*) maintain that the cognition "this is achievable by my effort" (*mamedaṃ kṛtisādhyaṃ*) is not the motivator, because perception and inference are impossible regarding a future object.
However, a person engages in an action after reflecting upon himself as being like that person for whom the action was seen to be achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhya*).

For instance, one who desires rice, who knows it to be a means to that end, and who possesses the necessary implements such as rice, engages in cooking because of the knowledge: "Cooking is achievable through effort, and I am also like that [person].

Thus, regarding the cooking performed by another, both the knowledge that it is achievable through effort and the knowledge that oneself possesses the specific qualifications that make cooking achievable through effort are the motivators for engagement.
Since activity elsewhere also proceeds in this very same way, there is indeed beginninglessness.

For this very reason, one who has experienced sublation does not engage in bowing to a shrine (*caityavandana*) or in consuming poison; for that which is to be accomplished by an effort (*kṛtisādhya*) belongs to one who possesses the cognition that it is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*).
And one who has experienced sublation does not possess the cognition that it is a means to a desired end in those cases.

Thus, even for one who possesses the desire for satisfaction, eating is something to be accomplished through effort; yet, once satisfied, he does not perceive within himself the state of possessing the desire for satisfaction, and therefore does not engage in eating. However, the most recent [scholars] maintain that in the phrase "of such a person" (*yādṛśasya*) and so forth, the qualification for that action is "non-condemnedness" (*avigītatva*). One who has experienced sublation, however, understands poison-eating and temple-worship precisely as being actions to be accomplished through effort that are condemned; thus, he does not engage in them.
Furthermore, the object of activity is known in a general sense as being unconnected with time, such as "cooking" and the like;
and by the power of the inclination to act (*pravṛtti*), the future cooking is established.
Moreover, the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) has as its object that which is not connected with time, and it does not have the form "I shall accomplish this future task by means of my effort."
The established doctrine of the theory of injunction (*vidhivāda*) is stated here as follows.

In the cognition that something is achievable through effort—which excludes acts such as consuming poison—it is the status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) that serves as the delimiting factor by way of its object, due to parsimony;
it is not, however, the state of being produced by the recollection of one’s own possession of a qualifying attribute, because that would involve complexity.
Nor is there a contradiction between the states of being an end to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and being a means (*sādhana*) in their respective established and unestablished conditions.
Because there is no contradiction between those two when they are not qualified;
for we experience that "ripening" (pāka) is unestablished when it is the probandum (sādhya), and established when it is the means of proof (sādhana).
At that time, being a probandum is indeed contradictory to being a means of proof, because by that very fact it is necessarily rejected, due to the rule of non-coexistence (sahānavasthāna).
But it is not [the negation] of being a means at another time or of being a means [in general],
because those two are not rejected;
for even if there is being a means at another time, being a means still exists, since the absence of a particular would entail the absence of the universal.
Thus, at that time, "establishedness" is the contradictory of "unestablishedness," because it necessarily excludes that very [state of being unestablished],
but not merely "establishedness" in general;
for otherwise, it would follow that even other things would be subject to the absence of establishedness therein.
Furthermore, when two things that are unqualified stand in contradiction, only one of them can exist in an action such as cooking; even if there is a difference in time, both cannot coexist.
Moreover, at that time, the knowledge that something is a means to a desired end while being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhya*) is not what motivates action.

For this very reason, in the injunction "One should sacrifice with the Vājapeya," since the sacrifice exists in a state of being already accomplished (*siddha*) as the instrument (*karaṇa*), the Vājapeya cannot be the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Because these two states are contradictory at one and the same time, the term "Vājapeya" functions as a name for the ritual (*karmanāmadheya*).
However, there is no contradiction between the instrument being established and its being that which is to be accomplished, because both exist within the very nature of yoga.
Now, it might be argued that the cognition of these two contradictory factors in a single locus occurs by means of a distinction in their limiting conditions (*avacchedabheda*).

If it is argued that there is no single cognition of both "being achievable through effort" (*kṛtisādhyatva*) and "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) in one and the same object because their times differ, and likewise because of the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*), we say: no,
for it has already been stated that there is no contradiction between being an effect and being a means.

Thus, although being established and not being established consist respectively of existence and non-existence, there is no contradiction, because they are established by cognition as residing in a single substratum.

Therefore, just as in the case of conjunction and its absence, it is only in a specific manner that a contradiction between two things is perceived such that they do not reside in a single substratum;
it is not the case that this is so even in another form.

Moreover, if there were a contradiction between the state of being the probandum (*sādhyatva*) and the state of being the probans (*sādhanatva*), then even for you, the fact of being an effect (*kāryatva*) would not be inferred from the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) or from the state of being a means to what is to be accomplished (*kāryasādhanatva*). This is because, due to the contradiction between the reason (*hetu*) and the probandum (*sādhya*), there would be an absence of co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), resulting in the non-establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*);

furthermore, if either the probandum or the probans were present in the subject (*pakṣa*), it would entail the occurrence of either sublation (*bādha*) or the unestablished nature of the reason (*asiddhi*).

Nor should it be said: "Now, 'being achievable by my effort' is the probandum (*sādhya*), while later 'being a means to my desired end' is the reason (*hetu*); the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is that whatever is not dependent on fate and the like, and which is not a means to my desired end at a later time, is achievable by my effort at the present time; thus, by taking into account the difference in time, there is the comprehension of both the state of being a probandum and the state of being a reason."
Now, because there is a difference between the two subsequent objects and because there is no persisting form [to serve as a universal], pervasion cannot be grasped;

consequently, according to the logic of cooking (pākanyāya), even in other cases, the status of being a means to an end (sādhanatva) and the status of being an end to be accomplished (sādhyatva) would not be perceived within their respective specific times.

Or, if they were so perceived, then for me too, let the cognition that "this is a means to a desired object" at a future time, while being something to be accomplished by my effort at the present time, be the motivator of action.
Nor can the fact that cooking is achievable through effort be inferred on the grounds that it is an intended object of accomplishment;

for since an intended object such as cooking does not arise while it is in an unaccomplished state, one must first cognize the cooking’s state of being accomplished (*siddhatva*) in order to cognize that the intended object is to be accomplished by it, and then cognize its state of being unaccomplished (*asiddhatva*) in order to cognize that it is achievable through effort.
Thus, even in this case, the contradiction between the states of being accomplished and unaccomplished is unavoidable.
Moreover, how could there be a desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) toward pleasure in the absence of a cognition of its being an effect produced by a cognition of its own specific qualifier?

For that [desire] does not arise from the mere cognition of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a desire to act even toward such things as eating poison for one who has already experienced its harmful effects.

Now, regarding the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), when its cause—the cognition of pleasure (*sukhatva*)—has as its object both the production of that [pleasure] and its being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*), then there is a desire to act toward the pleasure; otherwise, there is merely a desire. Thus, these two alone are the causes of the desire to act. If that is so, then let the cause of the desire to act toward pleasure and its means simply be the cognition of its being achievable through effort—which appears in the cognition that is the cause of the [initial] desire—since this is simpler (*lāghava*).
This is because, just like the cognition of pleasure-ness (*sukhatva*), the cognition of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) is also a cause of desire.

For this very reason, when there is the cognition that cooking is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*), the fact of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) is its object; thus, a desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) arises therein, but not in the case of the cognition of rain and so forth, because that [cognition] does not have that [effort-achievability] as its object and is therefore merely a desire.
This is because it is determined that the cause of desire—the cognition [of an object]—generates a desire to act only when it has the fact of being achievable through effort as its object;
otherwise, a desire to act would not arise in that case.

In reality, however, the desire for a means (*upāya-cikīrṣā*) is produced by the cognition that [the object] is a means to achieve what is desired (*iṣṭa-sādhanatā-jñāna*), because it is a desire for a means, like the desire for rain.
Nor can it be argued that this [cognition] is not the motivator (*aprayojakatva*), as might be the case with the desire for enjoyment (*bhoga-cikīrṣā*), which could exist even without it;

for the desire for a means follows the presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [cognition], whereas no desire arises for rain in itself because it is not inherently desirable (*asundara*). Since a common factor can be established as the motivator for a general desire for a means, there is no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against this.
And because it is impossible [to explain] without [the concept of] renunciation (*tyāga*).

Nor is the nature of desire for a means (*upāyecchātva*) or the nature of desire (*icchātva*) itself the determinant (*prayojaka*) for being produced by that [desire], provided that there is a difference in the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*).
