If it is argued that— just as in the case of the injunction "one who raises a weapon against a Brāhmaṇa should be punished with a hundred [blows]," where the understanding that the attempt to kill a Brāhmaṇa is the cause for the punishment of a hundred leads one to postulate an unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) or demerit (durita)— the same should apply here as well— the answer is no. This is because, according to the grammatical rule *liṅ ca hetuhetumator* ("the optative suffix is used to express the relation between cause and effect"),

the optative suffix in the words "should raise a weapon" (*avaguret*) and "should punish" (*yātayet*) conveys a necessary sequence between the raising of the weapon and the hundredfold punishment, just as direct perception conveys the sequence between experience and memory.

And since both [the action] as a means and as a means-to-a-means involve an intervening element, they are remote constructions, like a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). Here, however, the optative suffix (*liṅ*), as taught by the rules of injunction, expresses the state of being an effect.

Furthermore, according to the rule that one who desires [a result] understands only that which is known to be a direct means to that desired end as something to be performed, it is not possible for one who desires [a result] to be connected with the mere action.

Nor is there a deviation [in the rule] regarding one who desires satisfaction, because such a person engages in cooking out of a desire for rice; the desire for satisfaction is merely instrumental to that desire for rice, not direct. Otherwise, there would be no engagement with the means of a means.
It is the status of being a means to what is desired (*kāmyasādhanatva*) that motivates action.

If it is argued that this is for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), we say no; for it would follow that one who desires food would engage in cooking even when rice is already prepared, since there is no difference in its being a means to the meal by way of the rice. However, if a qualification is added—namely, that where cooking is the immediate means, it is not something desired, and where something is desired, cooking is not the immediate means—then there is no engagement [in cooking].

But surely, it cannot be that cooking is a means to eating by way of cooked rice, because the medium itself is not something to be accomplished; and if one were to identify it as such by way of another instance of cooked rice, why would one not also be prompted toward cooking when there is an unmediated qualification?

If you argue that this is because, when another instance of cooked rice serves as the medium, cooking is a direct means [to eating], we say no, because the specific qualification is irrelevant to cooking being a means to eating.

Because "mere rice" (*odanamātra*) serves as the means (*dvāra*), and because there is no dispute regarding its being the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), [the two cases] are not equivalent; for when a specific kind of rice is already established, the desire for rice in general ceases to exist. Now, one might object: "Since rice is already established, just as there is no desire for it, for that very reason it cannot serve as the means either; rather, it is by taking another rice that is not yet established [as the object] that [the means-status is maintained]."

If it is argued that, since its [the cooking's] non-establishment is taken as a basis, even desire could then be the means (dvāra), we say no. For the fact that cooking has one particular as its means does not contradict its having another particular as its means, because it is impossible for all particulars to be the means simultaneously in a single instance; rather, this occurs when one particular is established.

However, that desire for the mere [general] is not severed; for the cessation of the desire for the general cannot occur through the accomplishment of all particular instances, because since the accomplishment of all particulars is impossible, it would follow that the desire could never be severed.

Alternatively, when a desire perceives something other than the desired object—which is known not to be a direct means—as something to be performed, it does so only by interposing that which is an immediate means to the desired object.

Alternatively, since desire [regarding] something other than the desired object first understands that which is the immediate means to the desired object as being what ought to be done, and only subsequently [understands] that [the sacrifice] is the immediate means by way of that [first object], the initial cognition of the sacrifice as something to be performed by one desiring the result is indeed struck down by [logical] incompatibility.
(Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,2, p. 339)

On the other hand, the following arguments are set forth: (1) The optative suffix (*liṅ*) conveys the state of being a task (*kāryatā*) as connected with the action mentioned in its immediate proximity (*samabhivyāhṛta-kriyā*), because it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-liṅga*) for such a task, just like a logical mark (*laukika-liṅga*) [in inference]. (2) The state of being a task presented by the optative suffix is connected with the action mentioned in its immediate proximity, because it is a state of being a task presented by the optative suffix, just like the state of being a task in the expression "one should cook" (*pacet*).
(3) Alternatively, the sacrifice (*yāga*) is connected with the state of being a task, because the apūrva must be postulated through the understanding that the sacrifice is a task to be performed.

In that regard, in the first [position], it is understood—not established—that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) conveys the fact that the action is something to be performed as connected with the sacrifice;
yet this is not possible without the cognition of semantic competency (*yogyatā*), as has already been stated.

For it is not the case that a word expresses a related meaning merely by the requirement for the validity of its inference, even in the absence of semantic competency and so forth; otherwise, there would be a deviation in the case of "one should not perform the last two," and it would follow that the Veda is merely repetitive (*anuvādaka*).
(From *Bibliotheca Indica* 98, IV,2, p.

342) But surely there is a lack of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) regarding the *apūrva*. For instance, the apprehension of its denotative power (*śakti*) must occur through the presence of a word whose meaning is already well-established—namely, the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*)—since this co-occurrence would otherwise be inexplicable.

However, the *apūrva* is not present prior to the verbal cognition, as there is a lack of evidence for it; moreover, if it were present, its very nature as "unprecedented" (*apūrvatva*) would be contradicted, and it would follow that it could not be the expressed meaning of a word.

Nor can there be the presentation of that [object] by means of a logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, because if that were to function after the acquisition of linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*), it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

Nor can there be the apprehension of the word’s expressive power (*śakti*) with respect to that [object] as characterized by being an effect (*kāryatva*), for a characterizing feature (*upalakṣaṇa*)—whether it be a memory or an inference—is impossible if the relationship has not been grasped.
Not so!

Since the potency is grasped as "being an effect" (kāryatva) with respect to the object (dharmin), that which is qualified by being an effect is already presented; therefore, at the stage of denoting the related meaning, there arises the experience:

"the effect has sacrifice as its object. Due to the incompatibility of this with one who desires heaven, objects such as jars are set aside, and by virtue of compatibility, it culminates in the *apūrva* (unseen potential) which is distinct from ordinary actions and has sacrifice as its object; however, the potency is not grasped specifically as "being an *apūrva*."

Nor is there an experience that the effect is something unprecedented (*apūrva*); rather, through the power of auxiliary factors, there arises a cognition of a general relation, which leads to the attainment of a cognition of the specific [relation], just as in your own view, the specific agent is established.

If it is argued: "Is the apprehension of the word's capacity (*śakti*) for objects such as a jar based on their being effects, or is it based on the *apūrva*, or both? It cannot be the first, because the apprehension of a capacity for one thing is useless for the comprehension of another. Nor can it be the last two, because [the *apūrva*] is not present beforehand. We reply: No, for in whatever form a verbal cognition is produced by a word, it is in that very form [that the capacity is apprehended].

The apprehension of the word’s expressive power (*śaktigraha*) and the recollection of the word-meaning (*padārthasmaraṇa*) are the causes of verbal cognition (*śābdānubhava*). Indeed, the apprehension of the power and the recollection of the meaning as "knowable-ness" (*prameyatva*) are not the causes of a verbal cognition [of a pot] as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*).

And thus, there is the apprehension of the power in the form "the optative suffix (*liṅ*) has its power with respect to the effect (*kārya*) such as a pot"; from that, there is the recollection "it is an effect"; and then, by virtue of semantic competency (*yogyatā*) and other factors—

Leaving aside those effects which consist of abundant substances, qualities, and actions, the experience that "the effect has sacrifice as its object" takes the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) as its substrate;
and because of its suitability, it attains permanence.
For this very reason, since it is the object of the mere experience of the meaning of the sentence, it is called *apūrva*.

Nor should it be argued that the cognition of syntactic relation (*anvaya*) is produced by a word with respect to remembered objects solely through the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, and that what is not previously [known] cannot be within the scope of memory.

This is because, based on parsimony (*lāghava*) and necessity, we determine the causal relationship between the apprehension of word-potency (*śaktigraha*), the recollection of the object-meaning (*padārthasmṛti*), and verbal experience (*śābdānubhava*) merely by virtue of their having the same cognitive mode (*samānaprakārakatā*); it is not the case that in every instance, only those things standing in a relation of syntactic connection (*anvayapratiyogin*) are presented [to consciousness] by mere co-occurrence.

Because of the [absurd] consequence that from the word "cow" one would experience the cognition of an unprecedented cow due to [mere] respect [for the term], and because in every case of a cognition of a qualified object as qualified (viśiṣṭa-vaiśiṣṭya-bodha), it must be exactly so; otherwise, since the fire on the mountain has not been apprehended as a pervader, how could there be its connection in an inference?

[Objection: But surely, by means of the cognitive proximity known as *sāmānyalakṣaṇā*, all individual instances become objects in the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and in the apprehension of word-meaning (*śakti*).

If it is asked, "How else could there be an inference from that [smoke] if the pervasion of mountain-smoke were not grasped?"—we say no. Let the cause for inference be either the grasping of the pervasion in its specific form, or the grasping of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) by way of being the pervaded (*vyāpyatva*) in that same form; what is the use of such [mountain-specificity]? Moreover, if that [pervasion] exists, it exists for me as well; if it does not exist, it does not exist for me either.

Furthermore, in your view, since that [apūrva] exists, there is all the more the problem of denoting something unprecedented (*apūrva-vācyatā*). For even the *apūrva* is the object of the apprehension of word-potency (*śakti-graha*) and the object of the recollection of word-meaning (*padārtha-smṛti*) by way of its form as an "effect" (*kāryatva*).

Nor does this entail a loss of its "unprecedented" nature; for specific features such as being the object of a sacrifice (*yāga-viṣayatva*) do not present themselves in the effect without an inferential mark (*liṅga*), just as the manifestation of "being on a mountain" (*parvatīyatva*) in fire does not occur without inference. Now, if the potency of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) resides in the effect through a property common to actions, and since action is unsuitable [as the primary meaning], then the suitable *apūrva* is obtained. If that is so—

There is no obtaining of either a permanent prohibition (*nitya-niṣedha*) or a transcendental result (*apūrva*). For in those cases, the action cannot be abandoned due to its inherent unsuitability, because no fruit is heard [in the scripture], and there is no basis for postulating one. Furthermore, by the maxim that "the meaning of a scripture established in one place is the same elsewhere," the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in those instances must also be the *apūrva* itself.

Thus, the apprehension of the word's power (śaktigraha) does not occur with respect to something unprecedented (apūrva) as such; rather, it occurs with respect to a substratum (dharmin) qualified by being an effect (kāryatva), and action (kriyā) is indeed of that same nature.

Nor can it be argued that because the connection of action with the effect is otherwise untenable, the term must terminate in the unprecedented, for non-difference (abheda) also constitutes a form of connection. This is not so.

For in worldly instances such as "one should cook" (paceta), the expressive power (śakti) is not postulated with respect to the substratum (dharmin) that is the effect; rather, it is postulated with respect to the mere state of being an effect (kāryatva) in the form of volitional activity (kṛti), which cannot be obtained through any other means. This is because the substratum—such as the act of cooking—is capable of being presented by the verbal root itself, and because the fact that an action is an effect is obtainable through the theory of "expression through relation" (anvitābhidhāna).
Consequently, in the case of the Veda, the expressive power must be postulated with respect to the substratum, and that [power] is established only by the exclusion of [the possibility of] an action.

For it is not possible to postulate a potency (śakti) in a substratum that is already fit for being connected with the state of being an effect of an action; therefore, after the exclusion of action due to its unfitness, the potency must be postulated as something distinct from that [action].
Nor should it be argued that "the mere state of being an effect is simpler than an effect distinct from action, and therefore action itself can also be the potency.

This is because we do not say that the potency exists by virtue of being an effect distinct from action, but rather that once action has been excluded due to its unfitness, [the potency is postulated].

At the time of postulating a power (śakti) in a substratum (dharmin), that power resides in what is distinct from the action; however, the action itself does not enter into the apprehension of that power.
For that which is postulated because of an inconsistency caused by something else cannot itself be the object of that [postulation].

Thus, even when postulating a power on the basis of being an effect (kāryatva), it is postulated only with respect to an effect distinct from that [action]; consequently, that same [effect] is what is fit for connection with worship and so forth, whether it be eternal or prohibited.

The *liṅ* suffix denotes [the object] itself, and not merely its status as something to be accomplished (*kāryatva*), because there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) regarding the substratum (*dharmin*) and because it would entail the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

However, in the apprehension of the denotative power (*śakti*) of the word *liṅ*, objects such as a jar are neither excluded nor prioritized, for in either case there is unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

At the stage of the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*), such an object does not enter [into the denotation] due to its lack of syntactic fitness (*yogyatā*) for connection; furthermore, the optative suffix (*vidhipratyaya*) is not applied to it, because the suffix used alone is ungrammatical (*asādhutva*).

Furthermore, in instances where a verbal root is uttered alongside a noun stem (*dhātu-samabhivyāhāra-sthala*), there is a rule that it generates a comprehension of the syntactic connection with that [noun's] meaning; therefore, [the word *kārya*] does not convey objects such as jars.
For this very reason, they say that the condition for its usage is either non-usage itself or "novelty" (*apūrvatva*).

Now, "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) cannot be the ground for application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*) by virtue of residing in unexpressed things like jars; rather, it is [the ground for application] by virtue of residing in jars and so forth that are expressed.

If it is argued that "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is not the basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), because that status belongs only to what is understood [by the word], and otherwise "knowability" (*prameyatva*) itself might as well be such a basis—[we reply: no, for whatever is the mode (*prakāra*) of the cognition produced by the word is precisely what constitutes the basis for application there, since the word's expressive power (*śakti*) is determined by its result; it is not simply that which subsists in what is understood, as this would lead to over-extension (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the dewlap and other such features.
And "knowability" (*prameyatva*) is not such [a cause], because it does not prompt that cognition.
For this very reason, in common worldly usage, the suffix *liṅ* is used figuratively for a substratum distinct from the action; whereas in the Veda, a specific power is postulated.

Furthermore, it is impossible for worldly people to have an intention (*tātparya*) regarding the *apūrva*, since it has never been previously apprehended by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), even though the power is common to the action.

In the world, in the expression "the ladle alone should cook" (*loke lakṣaṇaiva paceta*), it is the status of being an effect (*kāryatā*) that is understood regarding cooking; in that case, the *liṅ* suffix has its primary intention (*tātparya*) on the state of being an effect, because of parsimony (*lāghava*).

It does not intend the substratum (*dharmin*), since the action is already obtainable from the verbal root (*dhātu*). As they say: "The function [of a word] arises from the intention, but the intention does not arise from the function. Thus, due to the instrumentality and singularity of the third case (*tṛtīyā*), the effect is [established].

Furthermore, "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) cannot function independently; rather, it must be qualified [by its locus]. And since the qualifier is necessarily distinct from that which is qualified, there is *lakṣaṇā* (indication) regarding "being an effect. Nor should it be argued: "Even when the substratum (*dharmin*) qualified by being an effect is presented, let the connection with 'being an effect' apply directly to the action itself, abandoning the substratum; what is the use of *lakṣaṇā*? For a property presented as residing in one substratum has no requirement for another substratum. Therefore, for the sake of presenting "being an effect" as an independent entity, [the indication is necessary].

Since there is an expectancy for another property (*dharmyantara*), there is *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) for the purpose of presenting [the potsherd] as having an independent function; just as in the case of the statement "he roasts the husks with the *puroḍāśa*-potsherd," the potsherd—which is presented as being connected to that [cake] by virtue of its being intended for the *puroḍāśa*—has no expectancy for the scattering of husks (*upavāpa*).
Therefore, there is *adhiṣṭhāna-lakṣaṇā* (indication of the substrate) for the purpose of presenting the potsherd as having an independent function.

Nor is there any contradiction with linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*). For it is not the case that in common worldly usage the capacity (*śakti*) [of the suffix] is determined to denote the state of being an effect of an action, such that a contradiction would arise; rather, it is the state of being an effect in general, since the action is already obtained from the verbal root (*dhātu*). Nor does the presence of a capacity for one substratum (*dharmī*) entail the destruction of that [capacity]. Therefore, there is no contradiction, because it is grasped that suffixes convey their own meaning as connected with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), and the meaning of the suffix is indeed the *apūrva*.

Or, let it be that in common worldly usage the optative suffix (*liṅ*) has the power to denote being the object of an action; nevertheless, even without abandoning that [power], there is a different power for another substratum in the Veda according to the principle of multiple meanings (*nānārtha*), because otherwise the connection with "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) would be impossible. Others, however, hold that in expressions such as *paceta* ("he should cook"), the verb root itself denotes the cooking as the object to be accomplished, while the optative suffix merely indicates the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) regarding that.

However, it is not possible for [the word] to be invariably restricted to that very [meaning] because of its usage; furthermore, the fact that a general term has a particular as its referent cannot be sustained by any other mode of operation (*vṛtti*).

For this very reason, there is no power of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth to denote the present tense and such, since this can be grasped through worldly usage, and thus there is no contradiction with linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*).

This [position] is incorrect, because if the optative were powerless regarding the state of being an action to be accomplished (*kāryatva*), the cognition of that state of being an action to be accomplished could not arise from the word "cooks" (*pacati*), due to the contradiction of two modes of operation occurring simultaneously.
Nor can [the words] be non-abandoning of their own meanings (*ajahatsvārthā*), because that which is common to both [meanings] is not presented; this is the direction of the argument.

Alternatively, the word-potency (*śakti*) of words resides in the cognition [itself], because that is what is to be denoted (*śakyatva*). And thus, upon a single utterance of the word *liṅ* (the optative suffix), by virtue of semantic competency (*yogyatā*) and other factors, a single cognition in the form of an experience is produced, having as its object a task (*kārya*) concerning a sacrifice that generates lasting heaven, and whose object is distinct from abundant substances, qualities, and actions.

Nor should it be argued that, since the apprehension of word-potency (*śaktigraha*) occurs for each individual cognition as if they were distinct meanings, there would be an experience of each object individually rather than of the objects collectively.

This is not so, because at the time of the apprehension of potency, the qualification "in a single utterance" (*ekatroccāraṇa*) is present by virtue of its power, and thus such collective experience is possible; whereas in the case of multiple meanings, that qualification is not included in the apprehension of potency due to the lack of evidence and because of the resulting complexity (*gaurava*).

If it is further objected that even so, these [cognitions] would be a mere "cognition with a composite object" (*samūhālambana*) and not a cognition of mutual qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*), we say no; for a single cognition whose scope consists of a property (*dharma*) and a substratum (*dharmī*) that stand in need of one another (*sākāṅkṣa*) is precisely what constitutes a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*). Nor...
And there would be no distinction from a cognition that takes a collection as its object,

because that [cognition] has as its object that which is free from expectancy. Or rather, let there be a potency (śakti) residing in the stability, the capacity to produce heaven, and the state of being an effect— [properties] which are present and whose non-connection [with one another] has not yet been grasped— even though their mutual non-connection remains ungrasped.
Because it possesses a disposition identical to that of a specific cognition, by the aforementioned reasoning, a single cognition having that very object is produced by the word *liṅ*.
In this same manner, the apprehension of the denotative power (*śaktigraha*) occurs for words such as *svarga* regarding extraordinary objects.

[Objection: Granted that the apprehension of the denotative power occurs in the manner described, nevertheless, when there is the experience of an effect (*kārya*) concerning the sacrifice from the word *liṅ*, the *apūrva* (unseen potency) is obtained.

When one reflects upon the supporting factor— that the connection with "one desiring heaven" (svargakāma) is possible— the postulation of the word *liṅ*’s power to denote the task to be accomplished (*kārya*) arises from the otherwise inexplicability of its co-occurrence with the well-known term "one desiring heaven.
Indeed, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) cannot occur without first reflecting upon that supporting factor.

If it is argued that the *apūrva* (unseen potency), which resides within the explanatory body [of the causal complex], is not known prior to the postulation of the capacity, then is it the case that the very specific feature which serves as the explanatory factor—
established by the force of the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*)— is what constitutes the cause for the postulation in *arthāpatti*? If that were so,
then [the object] would be postulated based on what was previously grasped alone.
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of the elimination of all conceptual construction (*kalpanocchedāpatti*).

Therefore, just as the understanding of a specific [cause] arises from a conceptual construction when there is an established logical reason (*upapādakatarke*) based on the comprehension of the connection between food in general and corpulence,
or just as a specific [meaning] is denoted by the force of the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with a word that denotes a particular instance of a general capacity, so it is here as well.

Since the acquisition of a specific action is possible even when [the word] denotes action in general, the postulation of a [linguistic] capacity (*śakti*) occurs through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), based on the recognition of the supporting factor as inferred. Furthermore, the action denoted has sacrifice (*yāga*) as its object, and not a jar (*ghaṭa*) or the like, because the latter lacks the property of having an object.
And "object-ness" (*viṣayatva*)—as in the case of knowledge and a jar—is either a relation of essential nature (*svabhāvasambandha*) or a state of being defined by the definition of that [object].
Is it the state of being cognizable by that specific cognition, or is it the state of having an exclusion as its means of accomplishment?

For indeed, the *apūrvas* (unseen potencies) produced by sacrifice, gift, and oblation each possess the quality of being produced by that alone, through the exclusion of other means of accomplishment that would otherwise have a similar form.
As it has been said: "The word *vi-* signifies distinction (*viśeṣa*), and the root *si-* denotes binding."
It binds [the mind] specifically; therefore, the *viṣaya* (object) is the regulator.

Now, it may be argued: "In whatever form the apprehension of capacity (*śaktigraha*) occurs, in that same form, when the object is presented through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) from the word *liṅ*—which has the capacity for what is to be done (*kāryatva*)—the attainment of the *apūrva* (unprecedented potency) shall occur by virtue of semantic fitness (*yogyatā*) and other factors. For indeed, the recollection of what is to be done (*kāryasmaraṇa*) is useful for the theory of denotation through connection (*anvitābhidhāna*), but not the recollection of the *apūrva*."

And as for whether that [cognition] occurs through the word or through the word-meaning, there is no distinction whatsoever; and if it is argued that the effect (kārya) is indeed understood as being related to the capacity for what is to be accomplished, we say no, because an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is figurative (*lākṣaṇika*) and thus does not bring about the experience of the *apūrva*.

Nor should it be said that a word such as *yajati* (he sacrifices), which has the power to denote its own meaning as connected with another, brings about the experience of the *apūrva* by taking up that other [element].

For the capacity of words consists merely in their connection with their own meanings as qualified by others, and not in anything else, due to the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*) and because [other meanings] are obtainable through other words. Furthermore, in the case of *lakṣaṇā* (indication), a word brings about the experience of its own meaning which possesses a connection qualified by the bank; however, the bank itself is presented through mental impression (*saṃskāra*), because there is no *anvitābhidhāna* (expression of the related) with that which is not present.
Moreover, the unprecedented (*apūrva*) is not an object of mental impression.

Furthermore, by means of the word *yajati* (sacrifices), there would arise the experience that "the sacrifice is the object of the action [intended] by one desiring heaven," because in the case of *lakṣaṇā* (indication), a word produces an experience in which its indicated meaning is the qualifier and its own primary meaning is the qualificand.
Yet such a cognition is not what is required.

Nor is the connection of "one desiring heaven" understood through a mere action unqualified by the sacrifice; rather, it is understood with respect to a specific action whose object is the sacrifice. Therefore, for the sake of such a cognition, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) possesses a direct denotative power (*śakti*) toward the action.
Regarding this, the established doctrine concerning the theory of the unprecedented (*apūrva*) is stated as follows: (Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,2, p. 378) *apūrvavādasiddhāntaḥ atrocyate*.

The possession of a form that necessitates syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is not what constitutes semantic competency (*yogyatā*), because even in the case of an utterance by an unreliable person such as "sprinkle with milk," there is no comprehension of the connection despite the presence of the liquid nature of the substance—which is a factor necessitating the connection—since there exists a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pramā*). If it is argued that even when competency exists, there is no comprehension of the connection when a subverting cognition regarding it exists, then the absence of a subverting cognition must necessarily be regarded as a causal factor. Therefore, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), that [absence] alone is sufficient.

If it is argued that this very capacity is such that the same thing would be both fit and unfit, [we reply: this is true; just as in a particular state that same thing may be expectant or non-expectant, and proximate or not, so too, depending on the presence or absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pramā*), that very same thing is designated as fit or unfit for the cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya-bodha*). This is because we observe the linguistic usage of "fitness" and "unfitness" based on the presence or absence of a subverting cognition.

In the absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pramā*), even though there is the presence of semantic competency (*yogyatā*) and other factors, the comprehension of the syntactic connection (*anvaya-bodha*) in the sentence "He sprinkles with fire" does not occur because it is produced by a person characterized by the defect of untruthfulness (*apramā-doṣavat-puruṣa*).

Since the manifestation of a general property is necessarily concomitant with the manifestation of some particular instance, one might ask: "If the particular is not manifested, how can that [general] be manifested? This is not a valid objection.

In reality, while the particularity (*viśeṣa*) as the indirect means (*paramparāsādhana*) indeed appears, its status as an indirect means does not appear as a qualifying feature (*prakāra*). For if that [status] were to appear as a qualifying feature, it would require the cognition of the constituent elements of the indirect sequence as a cause. Just as in the command "Bring water with a jar," by virtue of semantic fitness (*yogyatā*), the jar appears as a jar (*ghaṭatva*)—and not as a non-leaky jar (*chidretaratva*)—so too, in the case of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), [the same applies].

Nor can it be *ajahatsvārthā* (not abandoning its own meaning), because that would entail the impossibility of the word "jar" being syntactically connected [to the sentence], due to the contradiction of two simultaneous functions, and because [the jar] is not presented in a form common to both [the primary and secondary meanings].
If it is argued that its presentation occurs through residual impression (*saṃskāra*),

one should not say that the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) would fail to be conveyed there, since there is a linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that case-endings convey their own meaning as related to the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*).
For the meaning of the base (prakṛtyartha) is indeed that which is conveyed by the base, in accordance with its connection to the indicated sense (lakṣya).
And that [meaning] occurs even in the case of the base due to the assistance of mental impressions (saṃskāra).
Nor is its presentation restricted because its excitants (udbodhaka) are not restricted.

If it is argued that this is due to conceptualization through the force of the result (*phala-bala*), we say no; for a word brings about the cognition of its own referent only through that which is presented by the word itself.

Nor should it be asked: "In this case, how can the state of being the substratum of sound (*śabdāśrayatva*), which is not denotable by the word 'space' (*ākāśa*) but is presented by latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), become an object of verbal experience (*śābdānubhava*)?

[The reason is that] there is a latent impression that generates the recollection of that which was grasped as having a certain power (*śakti*) with respect to something presented as possessing a specific property (*dharmavattva*) in a necessary manner.

Because of the restriction that it has those properties as its object, there is a restriction on its manifestation even in that aspect [of being a property] due solely to the factors that awaken it; thus, even though it is not denotable (*aśakya*), it appears from the word "space" (*ākāśa*).

Alternatively, let that too be denotable if there is a necessary presentation, since the co-occurrence [of the word with others] can be explained by its referring to the expressed meaning (*vācya*) and so forth.
However, in reality, there is no such necessary presentation at all.

Or, let it be granted that even from a word there arises non-conceptual [perception]; nevertheless, at the time of understanding the syntactic connection (*anvaya*), since there is no impossibility of connecting with other [factors], there would be no subsequent conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). If this is argued, then for you as well, after the cognition of the task to be accomplished (*kāryatā*), there would be no cognition of the means based on the material cause (*aupādānika-sādhanatā*), because the cognition of the impossibility [of the task otherwise] is the cause of the cognition of the material means.
Furthermore, in this way, there would be the total elimination of all conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), because conceptual construction is rooted in the impossibility of what is already perceived.

In reality, however, if the absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhakapramā*) constitutes "fitness" (*yogyatā*), then mere cognition—which is common to both doubt and certainty—is the sole determinant of that fitness. Consequently, only where there is a certainty regarding a subverting cognition is there an absence of the comprehension of the logical connection (*anvaya*); elsewhere, however, verbal comprehension arises from that mere cognition alone.

Thus, even in the case of a sacrifice (*yāga*), the cognition of the syntactic relation (*anvayabodha*) is not obstructed by a doubt regarding semantic competency (*yogyatā*), because a doubt concerning sublation (*bādha*) does not act as an obstacle;
otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the elimination of inference (*anumāna*) and other means of knowledge.

Even if the "unseen potency" (*apūrva*) were the denotation [of the verbal suffix], there would still be a mere doubt regarding semantic competency—namely, a doubt that the *apūrva* is the means to heaven—because of the *apūrva* itself.

First, because there is no certainty that [the action] is a means to heaven (*svarga*), and because the act of undertaking (*upādāna*) occurs subsequent to the expression of the related meaning (*anvitābhidhāna*), the connection with one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*) arises from the possibility of it being a means—based on the mere possibility of its being a means due to the absence of any proving or subverting evidence regarding the existence of an intermediate step (*dvāra*). This is the same [in both cases].
Furthermore, just as an action is not stable and thus unfit [to be a direct cause], so too...
Even the *apūrva* (unseen potency), though distinct, is not stable, because the action (*kṛti*) has perished.

Nor can the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*) reside in the mere *apūrva* as a substratum, because, being a part of a single word-meaning, it cannot serve as a correlate for syntactic connection (*anvaya*).

Others, however, maintain that fitness (*yogyatā*) consists in the absence of a form that contradicts the connection; for this very reason, when there is an error regarding it in the case of "sprinkle with fire," an erroneous connection occurs.

Furthermore, in the case of a sacrifice (*yāga*), the absence of any form that would contradict its causal connection [with the result] is easily established through non-perception of the capable (*yogyānupalabdhi*).
Nor should it be argued that perishability in an instant (*āśuvināśitva*) is contradictory to the production of a result occurring at a later time;

for since even experiences and the drinking of medicinal decoctions—which perish instantly—produce results occurring at a later time, such perishability must exist in the sacrifice as well, at least in some sense. Otherwise, the *apūrva* (unseen potency) would be rendered useless.

If it is argued that possessing the form which necessitates positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is simpler [than the negative], we say no; for even when that [form] is present, there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of what is spoken by an unreliable person.

Thus, some reflection (*pratisandhāna*) necessarily exists therein as an obstacle to positive concomitance, because at the very least, the cognition of the object of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramā*) itself constitutes such an obstacle.

The knowledge that something is a means to a desired end (*kāmyasādhanatvajñāna*) alone is the motivator, due to parsimony (*lāghava*). One who desires satisfaction from already-prepared rice proceeds toward eating, which is an easy means, and not toward cooking it, because cooking is a burdensome means; likewise, one seeking water proceeds toward what is already present. For this very reason, although the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices are heard in scripture to have heaven as their fruit, since they would otherwise incur invalidity—characterized by non-performance due to being burdensome means—a greater abundance of results is postulated [in the case of the *Kāmyeṣṭi*], namely, the production of effort that is not invariably connected to the arising of the desired object.
Or rather, it is an obstacle.

Furthermore, if there is a rule that a person desiring a result understands [an action] as something to be performed only when it is known as a means to that result mediated by desire, then [the action] would not have been understood as a task (kārya) even previously; for prior to the expression of the related meaning (anvitābhidhāna), there is no indicator of its being a means to the desired end, and because the act of undertaking (upādāna) occurs only after the expression of the related meaning.

For this very reason, the two alternatives beginning with "other than what is desired" (*kāmyāt*) and so forth are refuted, because in the cognition of something as a task (*kāryatā*) or in the resulting inclination to act, the sole cause is its being a means to what is desired (*kāmyasādhanatva*).

Furthermore, at the time of grasping the denotative power of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in the case of a jar or similar object as a task, there would be an exclusion of ritual action (*kriyā*) due to the incompatibility of connecting it with one who desires heaven; likewise, there would also be an exclusion of jars and the like due to the impossibility of connecting them with the sacrifice (*yāga*).

For a jar or such an object cannot possibly have the sacrifice as its objective domain; otherwise, even at the stage of "denotation through connection" (*anvitābhidhāna*), there would be no exclusion of them.

It might be argued as follows: since the connection with "one who desires heaven" (svargakāma) is otherwise untenable, the apprehension of the word's expressive power (*liṅ*) must occur in something capable of such a connection; and since that [capable thing] is a lasting result (*kārya*), it is logical that at the time of apprehending the expressive power, the action (*kriyā*) is excluded, but not a jar or the like. Furthermore, when the denotation of the related meaning occurs through the two words "one who desires heaven" and "liṅ"—with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) included—the exclusion of jars and so forth is due to their lack of fitness for connection with the sacrifice. [The author replies: Is the unfitness of the sacrifice for connection [with the result] then hidden by the hand at the time of apprehending the expressive power, such that...?
That [cognition] which excludes the jar and so forth would not be connected;

rather, since the suffix conveys the connection with the meaning of the base (prakṛti)—which is its own internal constituent—it conveys the connection with the other [meaning] only as it is conveying that [internal] connection. Thus, the impossibility of its [otherwise] connecting is what is perceived.

On the contrary, while the suffix conveys the connection with the meaning of the base—which is its own internal constituent—it possesses the capacity to convey the connection with the other [meaning].
The primary apprehension of word-meaning power (*śaktigraha*) occurs precisely through the recollection of the impossibility of [meaning] being connected otherwise;

for if, due to a human defect, this recollection does not occur, the apprehension of power would be a mere error, since objects such as jars and the like are impossible [to denote directly], and because it would follow that for a particular person, words like "jar" would have a previously unknown denotative function (*apūrvavācyatā*).

Furthermore, if the exclusion of jars and so forth were impossible because they are infinite in number, then that would be the case even at the stage of *anvitābhidhāna* (the theory that words denote meanings as already connected), since their exclusion is possible by way of their commonality as "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*), just as cooking and other actions are excluded by their commonality as "action-ness" (*kriyātva*).
And thus, when substances, qualities, and actions have been refuted as being abundant [in number], where could the apprehension of potency reside in a substratum that is an effect?
Nor should it be argued that even if specific instances are refuted, the generality of "effect" is not thereby refuted;
for a cognition of a generality is not possible without its particulars as its object.

By this, the view that the apprehension of word-potency (*śaktigraha*) occurs in the case of jars and the like through their having a common effect consisting of the *apūrva* is refuted. Furthermore, the view that the apprehension of potency occurs with respect to permanence, the status of being an effect, or the capacity to produce heaven—whether these be properties themselves or the cognitions thereof—among things whose relations [to the word] have not been grasped, is also refuted; for permanent entities such as jars have already been rejected, and an apprehension of potency regarding mere abstract properties (*dharma-mātra*) is useless in the present context.

Furthermore, regarding the apprehension of their expressive power (*śaktigraha*), does it occur with respect to them as a collective or individually? It cannot be the first, because initially the collective is not the object of a single cognition;

or, if it were an object, then since the qualified entity would already exist, its "novelty" (*apūrvatva*) would be contradicted, for a qualified entity is precisely that which consists of a property and a substratum that are both objects of a single cognition and stand in a relation of expectancy.
Nor can it be the second; for in that case, there would be three recollections from the word *liṅ* (the optative suffix) and one recollection of the sacrifice from the word *yaji*.

Furthermore, there is no simultaneity among those four [cognitions]. Nor is it logical that, even if the capacity [of each] is grasped individually, there should be a single recollection whose object is the aggregate, arising from the word expressing the *liṅ* (the optative suffix), because the aggregate was not previously experienced. Moreover, if the recollection were a single one whose object consists of both the property (*dharma*) and the locus (*dharmī*) in their state of expectancy, then the quality of being "unprecedented" (*apūrvatva*) would be lost; for the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) is constituted by, or necessarily determined by, precisely those two—the property and the locus—when they are presented within a single cognition in a state of mutual expectancy.

By this, the view that the apprehension of word-potency (*śaktigraha*) occurs in the case of words such as "heaven" (*svarga*) with respect to properties and property-bearers whose relation has not been previously grasped is refuted;
for [such a view] would be swallowed by the dilemma of whether the recollection has each [word-meaning] individually or their collection as its object.

Or, let there be an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the *liṅ* suffix in the sense of what is to be accomplished (*kārya*), just as in expressions such as "the platforms are shouting," where a particular person [on the platform] who was not previously perceived [as such] [is indicated].

Even so, [the object] is experienced because that which is indicated by a secondary meaning (lakṣaṇika) from another word is what brings about the experience; let it be thus even for the "unprecedented" (apūrva). Furthermore, let there be the cognition "sacrifice is the object of the task for one who desires heaven" following the verbal experience; subsequently, the cognition "there is a task whose object is the sacrifice" arises from the force of logical inconsistency (anupapatti).
For this very reason, after the verbal comprehension, activity proceeds primarily from the resulting comprehension (aupādānika-bodha).

Furthermore, even if the apūrva were the denoted meaning, one would not proceed to act after understanding from such injunctions as "one should not eat *kalañja*" an apūrva having the non-existence of eating *kalañja* as its object; for in the absence of that [apūrva], since the person has developed a notion of the duty to eat due to passion (*rāga*),
and because of the principle that "that which possesses a fruit is weightier than that which is fruitless," they would instead incline toward eating itself, which is the cause of pleasure.

If it is argued that [ritual action] would proceed even in the absence of that [result], and that the apūrva itself is the fruit because it is a negation [of the undesirable], we say no; for since the apūrva is distinct from both pleasure and the absence of pain, it is a mere "fruit" (phala) in name only, and because it does not produce [pleasure or the cessation of pain], it lacks the status of being either a primary or a secondary purpose (*prayojana*).
If it is argued that the apūrva is a purpose just like pleasure, we say no, because it is not understood as such in common worldly experience.
The status of heaven and liberation as *prayojana* (purposes) is due to their belonging to the same class as the pleasure and absence of pain understood from worldly experience;

even in the Veda, in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), it is the *apūrva*— the means to the desired end— which is designated by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) as a secondary purpose (*gauṇaprayojana*),

because it is impossible to convey that something is to be performed by one desiring a result without first knowing it to be a means to that desired result, and not because it is a primary purpose in itself.

In that case, because they lack capacity and are useless for initiating action— just as in the case of eating and so forth— it is sufficient to regard them as merely secondary purposes (gauṇaprayojana) based on the knowledge that they are means to desired ends as established by worldly convention, or based on the knowledge of their being what is to be done (kāryatā). Nor is the apūrva denoted by the optative suffix (liṅ) as an intrinsic purpose in the case of obligatory (nitya) and prohibitory (niṣedha) injunctions.

For in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), the *apūrva* is denoted as a "task to be accomplished" (*kārya*) that prompts action by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and so forth which apprehends the locus of the duty; therefore, even in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*) and the like, there is a cognition of the *apūrva* as a task to be accomplished, but not as an end in itself. If it is argued: "In the case of the obligatory, since no primary or secondary purpose is understood from either worldly experience or the Veda, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) itself must convey that the *apūrva* is an end in itself; for otherwise, its status as being aimed at inciting activity could not be maintained," we reply: No, because [being an end] consists in being the object of a desire that is unconditional (*nirupadhīcchā*).
For the fact that the *apūrva* is an end in itself must be established by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) as something already proven;
yet the *apūrva* has never been established anywhere as an object of such a desire.

Nor does the optative suffix generate a desire for the *apūrva* and then communicate it, because it lacks the capacity to do so, and because desire is produced by a different set of causal conditions.

For this reason also, in the case of both optional (*kāmya*) and obligatory (*nitya*) rites, the fact that the *apūrva* is the object of desire—that is, its status as the *prayojana* (purpose)—is not understood through the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth; for the desire for the *apūrva* does not exist prior to the verbal cognition [of the injunction]. Rather, it arises from the cognition of the *apūrva* as something to be accomplished (*kāryatā*). Now, in the case of the obligatory rite, the *apūrva* is denoted solely as something to be accomplished, and not as a purpose in itself; rather, it is [understood] through the optative suffix.

If it is argued that once the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is known, its status as an end-in-itself— its being the object of desire— is possible because the knowledge of the *apūrva*, like the knowledge of pleasure, spontaneously generates desire; and that consequently, from the knowledge of the *apūrva* as a means to a desired end, there arises an understanding of the *apūrva* as something to be accomplished (*kāryatā*) in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), leading to engagement in action— this is not so, because the knowledge of the *apūrva* has not been established as a cause of desire.

For in the case of optional rites (*kāmyāpūrva*), desire arises precisely from the knowledge that the act is a means to a desired end as established by worldly convention, and not from the knowledge of its being an *apūrva*.

If it is argued that for one who stands within the scope of the scripture (*śāstrastha*), the knowledge of duty (*kartavyatā*) born of the scripture is more powerful, [we reply: that is so when the subject matter possesses a fruit; however, this present case concerns a subject matter that is fruitless.

Furthermore, if it is held that one who is engaged in activity has the qualification (*adhikāra*) for the injunction of abstention (*nivṛtti-niyoga*), then at the time when one is engaged in eating, [the prohibition applies] to that very act.
If it is argued that the cognition of the scripture’s status as a cause for action arises first, and when a contrary effort is thereby produced, activity occurs due to passion;

and that because the scripture’s teaching regarding the status of cessation as the effect depends upon the very engagement caused by passion, the scripture must necessarily produce its own result—a contrary action—when it brings about that understanding, and thus the scripture possesses superior force: [we reply] no, because this applies only to the cognition of the status of cessation as the effect.

Furthermore, even regarding cessation, no effort would arise for one who might act as an obstacle, and there would be no means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*) indicating that cessation is the effect [of the action],

because volition (*kṛti*) is absent therein due to its fruitlessness. Now, since it is understood from a deprecatory explanatory passage (*nindārthavāda*) that the eating of *kalañja* is a means to achieve a powerful undesirable result, [one would refrain] from that eating.

If it is argued that [the person] does not engage [in action], even so, let him desist from eating *kalañja*; since there would be no purpose in engaging in its absence, what has happened to the engagement?
By this, engagement even in daily rites such as the *saṃdhyā-vandana*, which are means for accomplishing the eternal *apūrva*, is also refuted, because in the world, action is arduous.

In cases such as "one should cook," the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is known to have the power to denote a property consisting of being a task (*kāryatva*) and being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). In sentences such as "one who desires heaven should sacrifice," it makes known the connection of that property with the sacrifice through the force of semantic fitness (*yogyatā*) and other factors; thus, there is no need to postulate a denotative power (*śakti*) for the substrate (*dharmin*) itself in the Veda.

Furthermore, the status of being a means to heaven—which is perceived [in the injunction]—is otherwise inexplicable for a sacrifice that is not a direct means unless there is an intervening operation (*vyāpāra*); therefore, [the scripture implies] that which brings about that [status].

[The opponent] postulates an unprecedented operation (*vyāpāra*). [Objection: But what is the meaning of the claim that "causality is the state of being a preceding factor without any substrate, and that is accomplished by means of an operation"? Is something produced, or is it made known? It cannot be the first, because since the operation occurs subsequently, it lacks the capacity to act upon that [prior state]. Nor can it be the second.

If it is argued that the cause, though long destroyed, is pervaded by its operation because that [operation] is understood through the inferential mark (*liṅga*), we say no; for this is unproving (*aprayojaka*) due to the absence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary case. Otherwise, since one observes that a perceptible cause possesses an imperceptible operation—as in the cases of sacrifice and experience—one would have to assume such a thing [for all causes].

Furthermore, the very purpose of penance and the like is to remove obstacles to the fruit [of one's actions]. Regarding the scriptural statement, "He becomes purified from that sin," the meaning is that the performer does not experience the result arising from the prohibited act.
This is the sense of the saying: "Merit perishes through [the failure to] proclaim it."

If it is argued that there can be no secondary figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) for the word *dharma* in the expression "it flows" (*kṣarati*) unless there is a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), we say no; for the very fact that the word *dharma* has its primary denotation (*śakti*) grasped as referring to the enjoined action (*vihita-kriyā*)—which is what is most immediately present—acts as the subverting factor against any other sense.

Nor does this word have a power (*śakti*) toward another object-entity (*padārtha*) merely to preserve its primary status, because that would lead to the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of figurative usage (*lakṣaṇocchedāpatti*). Furthermore, the term *dhārmika* (righteous) is employed precisely through the cognition of one being the agent of the enjoined action. By this [argument], the following inference is refuted: "The body of Devadatta and others is preceded by elements impelled by the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of Devadatta, because, while being produced, it is a means to his enjoyment, like a garland fashioned by him. For from such an inference, the existence of those [qualities] is not established.
This is refuted:

[the objection that] there is a *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) because that which is intended to be the producer [of the result] is simply the knowledge and so forth belonging to another birth— do not say this, for the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been ascertained through untainted positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that "that which has long since perished possesses causality provided its operation (*vyāpāra*) exists," [and this applies] to the sacrifice.

If it is argued that because the cause has long since perished, one must postulate an operation (*vyāpāra*), and that the perception of the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the operation with respect to the effect is a limiting condition (*upādhi*) for its being the possessor of that operation—this is not so. For even in the absence of such [perceptible] operation in the case of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), experience possesses that operation.

Nor is the argument unconvincing (*aprayojaka*); for there is a sublation (*bādhaka*) in the counter-example: "If a sacrifice, despite having long since perished, were not possessed of an operation, it would not be a means to attain heaven, just like a jar."

Nor can the absence of a grasper of causality (*kāraṇatāgrāhaka*) here be an *upādhi*, because if one were to determine the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with that [absence] as well, it too would be subject to the same logical consequence. Furthermore, there is no rule that whatever is perceptible (*aindriyaka*) must possess a supersensible operation (*atīndriyavyāpāra*); for even if an operation exists, the fact of being non-existent at the time immediately preceding the effect serves as an *upādhi*, rendering such a rule non-conclusive (*aprayojakatva*).

[Objection: But surely, since scripture declares that the non-performance of the twilight prayers (*sandhyāvandana*) is a cause of suffering, the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of that performance is the cause of suffering; and since that [non-existence] is stable, it is possible for it to produce suffering. Thus, [the argument against the stability of sin] does not hold.
[Objection: It is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Nor is there a futility of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), because it is precisely the destruction of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) that is effected by it; for if that were not so, since the time unconditioned by the destruction and the prior non-existence would be the time of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), the performance [of the rite] at that time would be impossible. [Response: No, because the non-performance during the twilight period (*sandhyā-kāla*) is a producer of suffering.
It cannot be argued that because the qualified [non-performance] does not persist after the time of *saṃdhyā* has passed,
and because the qualification pertains to the non-performance during the *saṃdhyā* time rather than to its opposite— performance— the absence of the qualified remains constant;

for the connection with "not performing twice during *saṃdhyā*" belongs to the [negation], which is the primary meaning of the word, whereas "performing" is subordinate as it is merely one part of the word's referent.

Even so, let destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) itself be the operation (*vyāpāra*), since even that which does not admit of coexistence can be a cause; and although it is endless, by its very nature it produces a result that has a temporal limit.

If it is argued that "wherever there is a cause for the destruction of X, there is also the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of X," we say no, because this would lead to a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of curd produced from the destruction of milk, and in the case of liberation (*mukti*) accomplished through the destruction of false cognition.

If it is argued that since [the absence of an obstacle] is a cause by virtue of being an "absence of an obstructor," there is an inconsistency regarding its destruction (dhvaṃsa), and how that could be resolved by that very same [principle], we say: no. For when destruction has occurred, the inconsistency is resolved through the postulation of its being an operation, without the need for the knowledge that it is an operation. Do not say so.
Because the counter-positive and its destruction do not produce [an effect] in the same locus;
for it is not the case that, necessarily, when X is destroyed, Y becomes its cause therein.
(Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,2, p. 431)
Nor should it be said that [the absence of obstruction] is not the cause by virtue of being a non-occurrent absence (*saṃsargābhāva*);

for, due to the absence of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), that too is a necessary factor. Now, since the causality of the sacrifice derived from scripture would otherwise be untenable without an intermediate operation (*vyāpāra*), one must postulate that the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) produced by it is the cause; thus, both [theories] are [required].

If it is argued that [the sacrifice] is not the producer [of the result] elsewhere because there is a lack of evidence, we say no; for the destruction of the sacrifice cannot be conceived—even through presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*)—as the producer of the heaven born of the sacrifice, since this would contradict other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If it is then argued that the propitiation of the deity (*devatāprīti*) alone is the mediating operation (*vyāpāra*), we say no, because there is no evidence for the sacrifice being the cause of the deity's propitiation, and because there is no evidence for the propitiation of a deity being the cause [of the result] in cases such as bathing in the Gaṅgā.

Because that [result] is impossible in the absence of a deity; nor is there satisfaction for the deity even in that case, as there is no evidence for its being the cause of such satisfaction, and because—by the principle of parsimony—it is more reasonable to postulate an operation residing in the agent or the enjoyer. But is this not a restrictive rule? For, through the *gayā-śrāddha* performed by a son, an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) arises in the father, and through the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice performed by a father, it arises in the son.
Furthermore, even in that case, the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resides in the agent alone, because the enjoined action—just like a sacrifice—produces an unseen merit that inheres in the agent.
Nor should it be argued that when the son is liberated, heaven would not accrue to the father due to the destruction of that unseen merit;

for since unseen merit is destroyed only by its fruit, the unseen merit is not destroyed merely by the absence of heaven for the father, [because the merit] produces an experience that inheres in itself.

Because it would be contrary to liberation, no unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in the father is produced; for when the father is liberated, there is an absence of defects, and thus, as in the case of yogis, the performed ritual does not generate unseen merit in the father. If that were the case, even a *śrāddha* rite performed with all its constituent parts would be fruitless, which would result in the invalidation of the injunction for such rites. Furthermore, if pleasure were to arise in the liberated father through unseen merit residing in the son, [it would be untenable].

There is no contradiction, because, as in the case of the arising of pleasure for yogins, a fault is not a cause [of suffering]. Now, if it is argued that the father's pleasure is produced by the father's merit—since that [pleasure] is impossible without merit residing in the father, and not in the son—[we reply: ...

Regarding the point that this follows from the discussion of the fruit [of action]: if it is argued that an action performed by those desiring the father’s heaven is a cause of merit for the father, and therefore a rite performed by the son is also a generator of that [merit], then likewise a rite performed by the father would also be a generator of merit for the father; thus, without that [action], there would be no merit in the father. Furthermore, since the rite of the son generates merit for the son, let the merit in the son be the cause of the father’s heaven by virtue of being a merit produced by the desire for the father’s heaven.

If it is argued that this merit belongs to the father because it is merit that causes his happiness, and not to the son because it is merit that causes his happiness, we say no. That merit does not belong to the father because it is merit produced by an action performed by him; nor does it belong to the son because it is merit performed by him.
Therefore, since it is merit produced by the desire for the father’s heaven, it is the cause of the father’s heaven; thus, the merit itself resides in the son.
Not so;

for the *apūrva* that brings about heaven is postulated as residing in the locus of heaven, because it is the first thing to present itself, because of the parsimony of the postulation, and because the object of the postulation must be the direct producer [of the result].

It is not postulated as residing in the locus of the desire for heaven, nor in the agent of the action produced by the desire for heaven, because these are presented later, involve greater complexity (*gaurava*), and produce heaven only through an indirect succession.

Moreover, if through the merit performed by a son the body and so forth were produced for a liberated father, and he were to experience happiness, then— by way of being a witness— the father who is liberated would also incur the state of hell as taught in such passages as, "Having become a worm in ordure, he is cooked together with his ancestors," due to the sin generated by the son's actions, such as the speaking of untruths.
Furthermore, due to such a suspicion on the part of the son, no one would subject themselves to the hardships of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and so forth for the sake of liberation;

this would also contradict the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) which states, "He who moves about completely liberated from suffering does not return again. Thus, it is observed that pleasure, pain, and a body belong to the liberated one; and when the father is liberated, no unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) arises precisely because there is an absence of fault through the performance of *śrāddha* and other rites.

Nor does this imply that even a *śrāddha* performed with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*) is fruitless; for while the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) arises, it is due to the deficiency of a constituent part that exists in its own right (*svarūpasat*) as a defect.

This is just as an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) performed by one who is already free from the demerit (*durita*) that causes obstacles does not produce the destruction of sin, because [that demerit] exists only in its own nature [and is absent].
And thus, because the sinful limb is absent, the operation of the sacrifice as well will have a different locus [from the agent]. It is said in reply:
the general rule is that the fruit, which occurs at a later time, is produced by the enjoined action through the medium of an operation residing in the agent; and that...

[A result] is set aside by a powerful sublation (*bādhaka*); however, in the present case, no such sublation exists. For example, it is taught in the scriptures that the fruit [of an action] accrues to the performer; thus, heaven [is attained]. And that [attainment of heaven] is set aside by a powerful sublation; however, in the present case, no such sublation exists. This is because the scripture teaches the causality of the *gayā-śrāddha* performed by a son toward the father’s attainment of heaven, and likewise the causality of the *jāteṣṭi* performed by a father toward the son’s purity and so forth.

Is it not the case that this very rule applies even in the case of the *pitṛyajña* (ancestral sacrifice), the *jāteṣṭi* (sacrifice on the birth of a son), and so forth, where the fruit resides in the agent through a mediated relationship? For the fruit does not belong to just anyone’s father or son; rather, it belongs to one’s own father and son.

Thus, the mediated relationship with the fruit for the son consists in the fruit residing in his own father, or in his having a father who partakes of heaven. In the same way, qualities such as having a purified son (*pūtaputrakatva*) also reside in the father alone.
Nor should it be said that the state of being an object of protection (*palasya*) resides in the agent only through a direct relationship;
for there is an inconsistency, as villages, cattle, sons, gold, and so forth reside in the agent only through a mediated succession.
Indeed, villages and the like are not directly connected to the agent.
Thus, the general rule (*utsarga*) of the scripture pertains to making known that the fruit goes directly to the agent, but not to making known that the fruit [inheres] in the agent [as its locus].

As for the state of having a father who partakes of heaven, that is not the fruit, because there is an absence of a desire for that [state] as a qualification of the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikārin*); this is because of scriptural texts such as "one desiring heaven for one's father" (*pitṛgatasvargakāma*).

Furthermore, if one were to engage in the performance by such a desire on one’s own initiative, there would be the undesirable consequence of the fruit being absent due to a deficiency in the auxiliary elements (*aṅgavaiguṇya*), since the desire as it was heard in the scripture would be lacking in the performance.

Furthermore, in that [compound] "having a father who possesses heaven" (*svargabhāgipitṛkatva*), the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) is "having that [specific] father. This is neither something to be desired (*kāmya*) nor a fruit (*phala*), because it is already established and cannot be brought about [by the rite]. Rather, it is the qualifier—the heaven residing in the father—and thus that [heaven] alone is the fruit.
That is not so;
for the result is not "having a father who possesses heaven," but rather it is as stated—that it consists in a mediated relationship (*paramparā-sambandha*) of the son with heaven.

It is replied: if the father’s attainment of heaven were to reside in the son through a mediated relationship, then by means of *saṃyukta-samavāya* (inherence in what is conjoined) and other such relations, the result would accrue to anyone other than the son as well.

If it is argued that this relationship is not taught by the scripture (*śāstra*), then likewise, the state of having a father who is entitled to heaven is also not [taught] by the scripture; furthermore, since villages, cattle, gold, and so forth are already established [prior to the act], they are not the desired object (*kāmya*). Rather, it is the ownership (*svatva*) regarding those things that is the desired result, and that very ownership is directly situated in the agent; thus, the desire for the result resides in the agent.
The fruit taught in the scriptures belongs exclusively to that [recipient].

For this very reason, heaven—the object of desire—is the fruit of sacrifices and the like, and it belongs to that [recipient] alone; furthermore, since heaven, purity, and so forth are desired by virtue of their relation to the father or the son, the fruit of rites such as the *śrāddha* or the *jāteṣṭi* belongs exclusively to the father or the son.

And thus, when a son or other relative performs such acts as the construction of a lotus pond or great gifts out of a desire for the heaven of his parents and so forth, these very acts become the cause of heaven for the parents;

for it is heard in scripture that they are the means for attaining heaven, which is the object of their desire. Indeed, the injunction does not teach that the lotus pond and such things are to be performed by one who desires heaven for oneself, because such is not what is heard in scripture; rather, for one who desires heaven, "heaven" refers to heaven attained by oneself.

Or, as for the phrase "gone elsewhere," the state of desiring heaven (*svargakāmatva*) is not restricted [to one's own self]; furthermore, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the injunction *yajeta* (one should sacrifice) merely indicates that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent.

Moreover, in cases such as *svargakāmo dadyāt* (one desiring heaven should give), because the desire for heaven residing in oneself is more intimate (*antaraṅga*) and is the general rule (*autsargika*), the term "desirer of heaven" refers specifically to one who desires heaven for themselves. This is because there is no evidence to justify a shift toward a specific meaning when a general sense is available and no sublation (*bādhaka*) exists.

However, some say that since it is heard in scripture that the attainment of the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) is the fruit of properly maintaining the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*), then even for the *jāteṣṭi* and *pitṛyajña* sacrifices—which are duties of the householder—that same fruit applies. Thus, they maintain that while there is a general rule (*niyama*) that the fruit goes to the agent, this is a general statement (*utsarga*) intended to refer to specific fruits [of individual rites].

But one might object: that fruit belongs to the lifelong maintenance [of the stage], not to optional rites such as the *kāmya-śrāddha*, because there is no evidence for including them within the category of "optional" (*kāmya*), and because it is impossible to perform every optional rite.

Even that which can be performed is not included here, because it may not be performed due to the absence of desire and so forth; furthermore, if all obligatory rites were included, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of their fruit [in cases of non-performance], and because the obligatory rite alone presents itself as being mandatory and thus enters into the connection [of the injunction]. Moreover, it is not the case that those individual acts produce an originary *apūrva* (unseen potency) and those in turn produce a supreme *apūrva*, for that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) and lack of evidence.

Rather, [the result arises] from the final action or from another action consisting of the maintenance [of the ritual]; thus, not every ritual act has the attainment of the world of Brahman as its fruit.
Not so;

for it is heard in scripture that the attainment of the world of Brahmā is the fruit of any ritual whatsoever—whether optional (*kāmya*) or obligatory (*nitya*)—performed with the Blessed One as its objective. Therefore, when the *jāteṣṭi* and the *pitṛyajña* are performed in that same manner, they too have that very same fruit.
And so it is said in the Bhagavadgītā: "The knot of karma is dissolved for one who performs action for the sake of sacrifice;
for other than action performed for the sake of sacrifice, this world is bound by karma. (Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,2, p. 456)

Thus, that action, by virtue of being for the sake of a sacrifice, is capable of producing its respective fruit individually; however, their combination is useful like auspicious rites (*maṅgala*), otherwise there would be an impossibility due to the interruption of a single performance. The reason is simply that [the gift] must be preserved. As it has been said: "I give what is to be given," and "I am he who is to be sacrificed to in the sacrifice."
As for the claim that "correctness" consists solely in the non-connection with what is prohibited, rather than the performance of merely what is prescribed—
that is not so;

because there is no such thing as the non-connection with some particular prohibited act (since one might always be connected with another), whereas the non-connection with all prohibited acts is easily attainable everywhere— such is the traditional doctrine (*sampradāya*).
To this we reply:

Is it the case that any action whatsoever performed with reference to the Blessed One—whether it be every optional (kāmya) act, every obligatory (nitya) act, or all acts collectively—that [yields the desired result]?

Not the first alternative; for if the fruit were accomplished by performing even a single such optional or obligatory act, such as bathing, then what would be the point of those rites which require great wealth and other resources?
For [otherwise] there would be the consequence of non-engagement in ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and the like;
nor the latter two, because they are impossible;
nor the fourth, because the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice and others lack the quality of being obligatory (*nityatva*).
