Therefore, the fruit of properly maintaining the householder stage of life is indeed its proper and complete fulfillment; consequently, it has been rightly stated that the attainment of the world of Brahmā is not the fruit of rites such as the *gayā-śrāddha*, because "the fruit taught by the scripture accrues to the performer" is the general rule (*utsarga*).
Furthermore, that fruit is sometimes heard directly in the injunctive statement (*vidhi-vākya*) and sometimes found in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
(Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,2, p.
460) The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) against the theory that linguistic capacity (*śakti*) resides in the word as connected with the action to be performed (*kāryānvita-śaktivāda*):
But surely, since passages such as *arthavādas* have as their object an already established fact (*siddhārtha*), they lack authoritative validity (*prāmāṇya*).

Since the denotation of words can only be determined as being necessarily connected with an action (*kāryānvita*), the primary acquisition of linguistic competence for all persons occurs solely through the linguistic usage of elders; this is because no other means of acquiring word-knowledge is independent of such usage. For instance, a child, observing the activity of the person being prompted immediately after the utterance of the prompter’s sentence, and desiring to know the purpose of that utterance by a discerning person, perceives—due to its conformity with the presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [sentence] and due to its immediate proximity—that it is indeed the activity of the elder being prompted which constitutes the purpose.

One ascertains the purpose [of an action], and since it is not possible for something that does nothing to have that status [as a purpose], one postulates precisely the cognition of "taskness" (*kāryatā*)—which is produced by that [purpose] and is conducive to activity.

Furthermore, in one's own activity, one postulates that very cognition of taskness, because through that [activity] one ascertains that the cognition of taskness is the cause; there is no other [cause], because activity is already accounted for by the cognition of taskness.

Nor is it the case that a word functions as a cause for activity through the mediation of cognition; for, in one's own activity, a child does not ascertain that the cognition of the task to be accomplished (*kāryatājñāna*), as qualified by the word, is the cause.

Furthermore, since it is observed that cognition has various means such as perception and so forth, one might conclude that the word is also a cause for the cognition of the task to be accomplished, and thus [conclude] that [activity] occurs only in that regard.

Because it is what is immediately present, one first postulates a capacity [for the sentence as a whole]; subsequently, through the method of joint presence (*āvāpa*) and joint absence (*uddhāra*), one grasps the capacity of the words denoting actions and factors of action (*kāraka*) with respect to their respective meanings as conjoined with the effect (*kārya*), in accordance with the previously grasped general capacity.

It might be argued: although at first, from the usage of elders, a cognition of [meaning] conjoined with an effect was inferred, nevertheless, by means of a capacity for mere connection (*anvita-mātra*) alone—

Since the cognition of an object as connected to an action (kāryānvita) is possible through the co-occurrence of words expressive of "being an effect" (kāryatā) and by the power of expectancy (ākāṅkṣā) and other factors, there is no denotative power (śakti) even in the aspect of the "effect" itself. This is because the word, even indirectly, is conducive to the knowledge of an object connected to an action; thus, in the case of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), there is also the possibility of its being explained otherwise. Furthermore, the causality of expectancy and the rest is necessary, for even if there were a denotative power in the aspect of the "effect," there would be a rule that the absence of such expectancy would entail the absence of the expression of the connected meaning (anvitābhidhāna).

Furthermore, since a deviation from the effect is observed even when expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other conditions are present, there is nowhere any [function] distinct from the expression of the related meaning (*anvitābhidhāna*).

Otherwise, the word-potencies for "cow" and so forth would belong to the individual (*vyakti*) alone; however, that is not the case, because it is observed that the individual is obtained solely through mental impression (*saṃskāra*).

If, at that time, the requirement of being related to an action (kāryānvita) is obtained from the very word denoting the action itself, what is the use of [postulating] a primary expressive power (śakti)? For it is observed in the linguistic usage of elders (vṛddhavyavahāra) that there is invariably a cognition of something related to an action; thus, if one were to postulate a power there based on that observation, then—since in the usage of elders it is seen that the understanding of a relation arises only through that which is presented by a word—it would be more reasonable to postulate that the cause of the understanding of a relation is simply the proximity of a word.
Consequently, in cases such as "dvāram" ("the door"), it is the word itself that is supplied (adhyāhriyate).

If it is argued that, because the initial acquisition of linguistic competence arises from the usage of elders, verbal cognition is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*) even with respect to incomplete sentences, then [we reply]: since the cognition of a relation (*anvaya*) is observed even in the case of established facts (*siddhārtha*), the status of being a "thing to be done" (*kāryatva*) is likewise deviant.

Furthermore, there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) to justify figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in that case. For while figurative indication is accepted elsewhere out of fear of postulating a primary denotative power (*śakti*), here it is more parsimonious to accept the primary meaning itself, as it is appropriate to assume a power residing in the word-meanings alone, which is common to both types of objects.

Furthermore, it must necessarily be admitted that words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*), which denote an action to be accomplished (*kārya*), convey their own meaning as related to the meanings of other words endowed with expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth; therefore, by virtue of this specific property, let other words also possess the same character for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*).
To this, we say: not so.

For, when the cognition of an action to be accomplished is inferred as the cause of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), one determines through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the word is the direct cause [of that cognition].
Since directness (sākṣāttva) is the natural state rather than being mediated by a succession, and since it is improper to assume such a succession when that [directness] is possible,

one postulates the expressive power (śakti) in that very [word] itself; it is not postulated in the cognition of the related meaning or in the cognition of the word-meanings, because those two are not presented as the causes of activity due to their lack of efficacy in prompting action.

Nor should it be argued that, even if the word has the power to produce a cognition of the related [object], a cognition of its being an effect (kāryatva) is possible through a mediated sequence; therefore, by means of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), that [power] alone should be postulated due to parsimony (lāghava), and not the power to produce a qualified cognition (viśiṣṭajñāna), because that is obtainable through other means.

For presumptive testimony, having as its object only that which directly accounts for the fact to be explained, does not grasp what is either less or more than that; thus, it applies only to the cognition of the related effect, which is the direct account for the fact.

The capacity [of words] is postulated for the sake of the inferential signs (*liṅga*) and so forth, because the capacity is simpler [to assume], because it is not obtainable through other means, because there is an absence of reasoning [to the contrary], and because the first acquisition of linguistic usage (*ādyavyutpatti*) is subject to investigation.

Furthermore, it is improper to postulate a capacity for a mere cognition of connection that is not present, while abandoning the cognition of connection with an action (*kārya*) which is present as the cause of activity; this is because there is no reason [for such a postulation] and because there would be prolixity (*gaurava*) regarding another mode of presentation.

Now, even when the cognition of connection with an action is presented, the cognition of connection is also presented; therefore, by parsimony (*lāghava*), one should abandon the "action" portion and [postulate the capacity] in the connected [meaning].

If it is argued that "let the capacity [of words] be grasped [as residing in the cognition]," we say no; for the capacity of words resides in the cognition of the word-meanings (*padārtha*), because they are what is capable of being denoted, and not in the external objects themselves. Furthermore, the cognition of a meaning as related to an action (*kāryānvita-jñāna*) is one thing, whereas the cognition of a mere related meaning (*anvita-jñāna*) is another, since cognitions differ according to their distinct objects. As it has been stated in the *Abhāvavāda*: "The cognition of a bare floor is one thing, and the cognition of a floor possessing a jar is another. Thus, to claim that the capacity is grasped after having first established the cognition of a related meaning involves nothing but excessive complexity (*gaurava*).

If it is argued that while a meaning obtainable through another means may be grasped when it is possible to do so, a heavy (guru) meaning is not grasped in that way, we say no; for such [a distinction] applies only when two meanings present themselves simultaneously.
Nor is there a non-presentation of that [heavy meaning], since it is understood by everyone in the initial acquisition of language despite the defects of particular individuals.

Furthermore, if it is argued that the word’s expressive power (*śakti*) does not reside in that which is connected to an action (*kāryānvita*) because of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers which denote the action itself, we say no; for all words generate a cognition qualified by "being an action" (*kāryatva*).
And that [cognition] occurs either by not conveying its own meaning as connected with an action, or by conveying its own meaning as connected with another action.

Thus, once the linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) regarding connection with an action is established, since there would otherwise be deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases lacking expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, expectancy and the like function as limiting conditions (*upādhi*).

Consequently, in accordance with the primary and foundational convention of connection with an action upon which it depends, one must supply (*adhyāhāra*) an action even when no injunctive suffix (*vidhi*) is heard.

The argument that—since we observe the cognition of a relation even in the case of established entities (*siddhārtha*), where sometimes there is *lakṣaṇā* (indication) and sometimes there is the non-apprehension of non-relation—one should rather assume that the expressive power (*śakti*) resides only in the related [word] after the fact, and that the previously held notion of the word as denoting what is related to an action (*kāryānvita*) must be sublated—is refuted for this very reason.

For it would entail the fault of postulating a different assumption than the prior one; furthermore, the subsequent usage of words in established entities is compatible with *lakṣaṇā* and other mechanisms, and since it lacks the quality of being "unestablished otherwise" (*ananyathāsiddha*), it cannot sublate the prior cognition.
Furthermore, it would result in the subversion of that upon which [linguistic usage] depends.

Now, if it is argued that linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) exists even with respect to established facts—for instance, consider a child who has already perceived the birth of Caitra’s son and, having gone to Caitra’s presence together with such a messenger, hears the messenger’s words: "A son has been born to you, O Caitra."

If it is argued that one, perceiving the brightness of Caitra’s face, infers the joy of the hearer; and from that joy, postulates the knowledge of the birth of a son as its cause—because that [knowledge] is immediately present, because it serves as a sufficient ground, and because postulating another [cause] would involve complexity—and then, due to parsimony (*lāghava*), postulates the sentence itself as the cause of that knowledge: [we reply] no, because there are many possible causes for joy, and because the knowledge of the birth of a son is not necessarily established by the mark of joy.
Because it is impossible for a child to infer [the cause], and because it is impossible to exclude the knowledge of some other pleasant thing as the cause;

and if it is argued that there is an inference of the knowledge of the son’s birth from observing specific actions such as the increase in wealth which is invariably concomitant with the knowledge of the son’s birth—

then, in that case, the sentence "A son has been born to you" would merely be directed toward the performance of those actions, and thus it would only produce a cognition associated with an action to be accomplished (*kāryānvita-jñāna*).
First, that [word] is grasped, and subsequently there is the inference of the cognition of the son's birth; thus, the capacity for linguistic usage does not abandon its function as an effect.

Even in cases where linguistic usage occurs here through the coreferentiality with words of well-known meaning—such as "the *pika* (cuckoo) sings sweetly in this mango tree"—there too, the understanding of usage is preceded by [the knowledge of] the effect, and it is logical that the power of the word *pika* resides only in what is associated with an effect, since it was not previously determined [otherwise].

If that were not so, then in cases such as "bring the crow there," since for some people the linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) is established only with respect to what is connected to an action (*kāryānvita*),

and because that [initial understanding] is stronger by virtue of being the basis upon which subsequent cognition depends; furthermore, it is generally understood through the reason "because it is a word" that this [word] is capable of conveying knowledge connected to an action,
though its specific meaning has not yet been apprehended— that specific meaning is now understood through the instruction of a friend and other such means.

Therefore, it is established that words directed toward activity (*pravṛtti*) generate a cognition that prompts action; and this occurs either directly through a connection with an effect (*kārya*), or indirectly through a connection with an effect. For this very reason, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) that serve as supplements to injunctions (*vidhi*), as well as those that establish the denotative power (*śakti*) of words such as "heaven" (*svarga*), do not convey their own meanings as connected to an effect, because they are directed toward activity and thus connect with an effect only indirectly. In cases where there is a scriptural statement of a fruit (*phalaśruti*) in the recitation of the *Purāṇas*, the *Mahābhārata*, and so forth, [the meaning is understood] by virtue of those passages being supplements to injunctions postulated from the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
Their capacity to convey their own meanings as connected to an action (*kāryānvita*) arises through a long tradition of being intent upon activity (*pravṛttiparatva*).

However, in the case of poetry, drama, and the like, which are intended merely to describe the nature of things (*svarūpākhyānapara*), there is a conventional usage of "connection" based on the non-apprehension of a lack of connection between word-meanings; it is not, however, an actual apprehension of connection.
(Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,2, p. 484)

The doctrine that the word-meaning is the capacity [of a word] to denote an object as connected with an action (*kāryānvita-śaktivāda*) is addressed here: upon hearing the sentence "Bring the jar," the child infers through the resulting activity of the person being prompted—directed toward the bringing of the jar—that there is a cognition of the jar-bringing as something to be accomplished (*kāryatā-jñāna*), but not a cognition of it as connected with an action (*kāryānvita-jñāna*). This is because such a cognition is not the cause of a specific kind of activity, and because it is of no use in grasping the word-potency (*śakti*) of words such as "jar."

In that context, having ascertained that the specific sentence "Bring the jar" (ghaṭam ānaya) is the cause for that specific cognition, and having understood through the process of insertion and deletion (āvāpodvāpa) that each individual component— the word *ghaṭa*, the accusative case-ending, the verbal root, and the injunctive suffix— is the cause for the respective cognitions of the jar being the object, the act of bringing, and the task to be performed, he postulates their expressive power (*śakti*).

Subsequently, by means of the generality of activity (*pravṛtti*), one infers that the sentence as a whole possesses the power for the cognition of an object related to an action (*kāryānvitajñāna*). Since this [cognition] is obtainable from other sources, one sets aside the "action" portion and postulates the power [of the sentence] only for the cognition of the related object (*anvitajñānamātra*);
however, one does not first postulate that the sentence as a whole is the cause of the mere cognition of an object related to an action.
Then, because the action of bringing a jar is first known to be an action, one infers mere activity; and by means of that, having inferred the cognition of an object related to an action—

If it is argued that one first postulates the causality of the sentence as a whole and then postulates its power, and only thereafter arises the cognition of the causal relation between the two specific [word and meaning]— this is not so; for there is no evidence that a child’s inference of mere activity and mere knowledge associated with an effect occurs sequentially in this manner,
since the apprehension of the word-powers of "jar" and so forth is possible even without that [sequential process].
Nor should it be said that the causal complex for that inference is not present at that time; for there is no evidence for the recollection of pervasion and so forth at that moment.

If it is argued that the apprehension of the causal relation between two universals is the cause for the apprehension of such a relation between two particulars, we say no; because that [relation] between two particulars is apprehended precisely through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

If it is argued that—just as when the causal relationship between two specific instances of smoke and fire is grasped, the relation of cause and effect also appears between their general forms, otherwise pervasion (*vyāpti*) could not be apprehended through a single observation; and likewise here, the existence of the general forms in that same way is known precisely by the cognition of the causal relationship between the specific instances—[we reply: no, for when the specific instance is grasped by perception, the universal is also [grasped] due to its perceptual fitness (*yogyatva*).
In the present context, when a specific cause is inferred from a specific effect, it is not the general [form] that is apprehended; thus, there is no simultaneous presentation [of both].

If it is argued that because there is a causal relation between two particulars, this also leads to the inference of such a relation between their two general forms, then the comprehension of the causal relation between the two particulars must be primary; consequently, based on that, [the cognition] first occurs regarding the specific word.

There would be the apprehension of the word’s expressive power (*śaktigraha*) itself, because there is no evidence for an intermediate inference on the grounds that it would be purposeless. As for the argument that it is improper to postulate an expressive power for the cognition of a related object (*anvitajñāna*)—setting aside the cognition of an object related to an action (*kāryānvitajñāna*) which is present as the cause of activity—on the grounds that both [postulations] involve complexity (*gaurava*), that is not so; for the property of being a cognition of a related object (*anvitajñānatva*) exists within the cognition of an object related to an action, since the latter is a specific instance of the former. Therefore, [the expressive power resides] in that very [cognition].
The apprehension of the word's expressive power (*śaktigraha*) does not even pertain to the aspect of being an effect (*kāryatva*).

For this very reason, you yourself have accepted that in the cognition of a ground as "possessing a jar," the cognition of the bare ground is also present; therefore, that cognition—which is distinct from the former—is the cause for the linguistic usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*).

This is indeed so; however, even when that [bare ground] is presented, the state of being a cognition of something related (*anvitajñānatva*) is not its object, and thus there must be a further presentation of that very [bare ground].

If it is argued that [the object] is what is to be conceptualized (*kalpya*), we say no; for in the cognition of something as qualified by an action (*kāryānvita-jñāna*), the cognition of the qualifier (*anvita-jñāna*) is not the substantive (*viśeṣya*). Thus, when that [qualifier] is presented, the former [the qualified] must also be an object of cognition, because the appearance of the substantive necessarily follows from the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for the cognition of the qualified. Otherwise, if the cognition of the universal (*jāti-jñāna*) were one thing and the cognition of the universal-qualified were another, then a cognition of the universal would never be presented apart from a cognition of the individual (*vyakti-jñāna*).
The universal (*jāti*) alone cannot be the word-meaning; for if only the universal were presented, it could not be cognized through the same cognition as the individual (*vyakti*).

Now, if you hold the view that—despite the fact that the presentation of a cognition qualified by the universal has the individual as its object—the property of being a "cognition qualified by the universal" is not the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) because it is cumbersome and because the individual is obtainable from other sources, and instead the property of being a "cognition of the universal" is [the delimitor] due to parsimony (*lāghava*), then the same logic applies here.
Nor should it be argued that there is no application of parsimony (*lāghava*) when two things are simultaneously present, for in this case there is no simultaneous presentation;

because a qualified cognition is necessarily restricted to having the qualificand as its object. Furthermore, the cognition "this is my duty" is directly productive [of activity] and is inferred to be its cause by means of the activity itself; therefore, one would grasp the expressive power (*śakti*) therein, since the object of that power is that which directly produces the effect.
One might grasp the capacity [of the effect] through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), because conceptual construction has as its object that which directly establishes [the conclusion];

however, this is not the case regarding the cognition of the effect itself, because that [cognition] is what directly establishes it. Alternatively, in the cognition "this is my effect," the possibility of the cognition "this is my effect" arises through the capacity itself, by way of a mediated inference.

If it is argued that a separate expressive power (śakti) is not postulated because [the meaning] is obtainable elsewhere—since the cognition of an action connected with something else is possible simply through the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of words denoting the action, by means of the very power of [the word] to convey a cognition connected with another [word]—then this is equally true for the other case as well. Now, one might object: "The cognition 'this is to be done' (*kāryam*) is the direct motivator; its auxiliary cause is the recognition (*pratisandhāna*) of all the qualifiers that necessitate the duty (*kartavyatā*) as residing within oneself. Therefore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)."

If it is argued that direct instrumentality (*sākṣātsādhanatva*) does not cease even when the effect is not produced due to a delay in auxiliary factors (*sahakārī*), we say no; for activity proceeds from the very cognition "this is my task" (*kāryam*) out of parsimony (*lāghava*). Furthermore, how there can be an inference of taskhood (*kāryatā*) regarding a future object has been explained below. Moreover, the cognition "I am such a person for whom this is to be accomplished by unobjectionable effort" is not the cause of activity.

This is because a cognition of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatā*) regarding an object that has already been done or is currently being done does not produce a desire for an object that is already established; furthermore,

since desire is produced by a cognition whose qualifier is its own object, a desire in the form "I shall achieve this through effort" is produced by a cognition of being achievable through effort whose qualifier is its own object,
and such a cognition of being achievable through effort consists in the fact that the object will come into existence immediately after one's own effort.

Moreover, let it be granted that first there is the apprehension of the word's expressive power (*śakti*) with respect to the cognition of an action-qualified object, because the sentence is directly understood to be its cause; nevertheless, subsequently, through the process of insertion and deletion (*āvāpodvāra*), one postulates the expressive power of a specific word for the cognition of its own meaning as connected to something else, on account of parsimony (*lāghava*).
This applies even to the factor of "action-ness" (*kāryatva*), because [the inclusion of this factor] would involve complexity (*gaurava*) and because it is obtainable from other means.

Nor should it be argued that there would be a sublation of the cognition of the direct causality of the first instance of activity, nor of the apprehension of the word’s capacity (śakti) as related to the effect based upon that [cognition]; for this is indeed desired. For a child who perceives no other way to account for the situation (anyathāsiddhi), that [first cognition] has occurred; yet, because it is weak, the subsequent cognition is stronger, being produced by a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) assisted by the arguments of complexity (gaurava), availability through other means (anyalabhyatva), and logical inconsistency (tarka). Nor should it be argued that such a cognition does not arise because it would involve the sublation of what was previously relied upon (upajīvya-bādha).
There is no evidence for its being a source of livelihood (*upajīvyatva*).
For that conduct occurs first by chance; it is not a cause for the apprehension of the specific word-powers, since that apprehension is possible even without it.
Nor does its status as being "first" entail its superiority, as there are instances where this is not the case.

Nor can strength be established by being perceived first by everyone, because there are counter-examples: in the case of the notion of "I" with respect to the body, and in the case of everyone perceiving the small size of the moon, stars, and so forth.
For this very reason, the objection that it would lead to an infinite regress of alternative hypotheses from one prior hypothesis to another is refuted.

This is because where the strength of the prior assumption lies in its being either not otherwise established (*ananyathāsiddha*) or being that upon which [the other] depends, it remains so [in the case of the latter]. Furthermore, at first, only the general causality of the sentence toward the cognition of an object as connected with an action is apprehended—directly or indirectly—and not even its specific nature; for since the means, such as positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), are common to both specific possibilities, they give rise to doubt regarding that [specificity].
Even the presumption (*utsarga*) is determinative only when accompanied by the ascertainment of the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*).
Furthermore, a child is not able to ascertain the absence of a subverting factor—which consists in its not being obtainable through other means—merely by seeing it for himself at first glance.

For this very reason, although validity is presumptive (*autsargika*), certainty arises only from an ascertainment accompanied by the absence of a subverting factor; otherwise, there would be doubt everywhere as to whether it is a valid cognition or an invalid one, or whether it is a direct or indirect means of proof.
It would not be so.

As for the argument that it is because of the possibility of many causes for joy and so forth—that is incorrect; for, since there is no sublation of the suckling of the breast and other such things which are themselves causes of joy, and because no other cause of joy is apprehended, and because [the former] is present and capable of being established as a cause, it is the cognition of the son’s birth itself that is postulated as the cause of joy.

If it is asked how there can be such a doubt—namely, that "the knowledge of something else being dear [to the speaker] will be the cause of joy"—it is not so; for even in the case of the knowledge of an action as related to a purpose (*kāryānvita*), the word's expressive power (*śakti*) is not grasped. This is because the causes for the hearer’s knowledge of the purpose are manifold, and because the conformity to the word (*śabdānuvidhāna*) is equally established as being non-otherwise-accounted-for (*ananyathāsiddha*). Furthermore, there is no knowledge of what is dear to another; or even if there were such knowledge, there is no evidence for a rule that it must be present at that specific time.

This is because the absence of doubt is established, and because it is possible to infer the knowledge of a son’s birth from the sign of great joy—just as one might infer a cognition through a fortuitous correspondence produced by a fallacious sign (*liṅgābhāsa*). Furthermore, even if the inference were erroneous due to its being non-concomitant (*asāṃsargika*), the apprehension of the causal capacity (*śaktigraha*) would not be erroneous; for since the object exists in that very way, both [the inference and the apprehension] are consistent with reality (*yathārtha*).

For example, suppose someone commands a wooden puppet operated by strings, "Bring the jar," and it brings it; then, like a child observing this, one becomes proficient in the linguistic usage of consciousness, thinking:

"This action is produced by an effort (kṛti), that effort is produced by a cognition (jñāna), and that cognition is produced by the sentence. Although this chain of inferences is erroneous, the apprehension of the word's expressive power (*śaktigraha*) which is its cause, as well as the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) produced by it, are indeed valid (*yathārtha*), because the object exists in that very manner.
The apprehension of the word's power (śaktigraha) is established even with respect to a goal that has already been accomplished.

For this very reason, it is said: "That pleasure which is unmixed with pain, not followed by its immediate cessation, and brought about by desire—that is happiness, the referent of the term *svarga*."

Thus, since pleasure is presented by the *arthavāda*, the apprehension of the word "svarga" (heaven) as denoting that [pleasure] occurs solely from the Veda; it is not because the word "svarga" is applied to sandalwood and the like through a secondary association with pleasure, nor because it is not applied when pleasure is in a state of being abandoned. Therefore, pleasure alone is the primary denotation (*śakya*). Since one who seeks mere pleasure would not engage in a ritual action that is accomplished only through great expenditure of wealth and effort, the intention (*tātparya*) of the word "svarga" refers to the pleasure presented by the *arthavāda*.

Nor can it be argued that because an *arthavāda* (explanatory passage) is a necessary support, the apprehension of the word’s denotative power (*śakti*) regarding heaven arises from that very source; for since the *arthavāda* has as its intended object the status of being the word "heaven" itself, it cannot serve as the basis for [defining] heaven as consisting of "excessive pleasure. Nor can "excess" be the qualifying attribute of the usage, because excess is relative and would lead to the cognition, "This heaven is superior to this pleasure from sandalwood," whereas in the case of taste and the like, excess is a genus (*jāti*) and thus not dependent on a point of comparison.

If it is argued that the use of the term "excess" depends on a prior knowledge of something else, we say no; for since such an excess is produced by diverse causes, there are multiple distinct types of excess, and thus no single commonality (*anugama*) can be established.

Even if there were a concomitance [of the word "heaven"] with this [particular pleasure] by way of a subordinate excellence within the genus of pleasure (*sukhatva*), activity would result in non-occurrence because the capacity [of the word] would not be grasped due to a lack of ascertainment.

Furthermore, since a subordinate genus within the genus of pleasure is common to all pleasure in general, the qualifying adjunct (*prayogopādhi*) must be rejected; moreover, in common worldly usage, there is metaphorical indication (*lak�ṣaṇā*).

Now, if pleasure unmixed with suffering were the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*), then the application of the word "heaven" to sandalwood and the like would not even be possible through metaphorical indication.

If it were possible for there to be a pleasure that possesses excellence (*sātiśaya*), then there would be a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of sandalwood and the like by virtue of their connection with that [pleasure]. Therefore, what must be denoted is simply a sub-class of the genus "pleasure" (*sukhatva*) as characterized by its being unmixed with suffering and so forth. Even if a single genus exists, there is no evidence for a single genus in the case of heaven (*svarga*), which is produced by diverse causes and consists of various desired objects. Furthermore, being produced by enjoined rituals (*vihitakarman*) is restricted to those specific [causes] alone, since even a non-universal property can serve as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of being produced. And it will be stated later that a mere relation is the basis for secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).

Similarly, regarding a deity as well—in passages such as "one should worship Indra"—since there is no fixed usage in common parlance and since the term is employed only in a figurative sense, the meaning remains undetermined. Consequently, the apprehension of the word-power (*śakti*) of words like "Indra" with respect to a non-worldly being such as the "Thousand-eyed One" is based on the *arthavāda* itself, which is co-uttered with an injunction, such as "Indra is the thousand-eyed one. This is just like the case of the word "heaven" (*svarga*). Now, in the case of the word "heaven," because its application would otherwise be inexplicable and because of the scriptural statement, "That happiness is the locus of the word 'heaven'," the meaning is indeed derived from the *arthavāda* alone.

If it is argued that there is no apprehension of the word’s power (*śaktigraha*) here in this manner because the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is intended merely for incitement through praise— as in "Indra is thousand-eyed" and so forth— this is not so; for when one hears a scriptural statement of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with well-known words such as "Indra is thousand-eyed," one determines,
in the absence of any sublation, that the very thousand-eyed one is the denotation of the word "Indra" and other such terms, by the force of the connection with those well-known words.
For these [words] function as motivators only by taking up an implied object that is not contradicted;

for the ritualists employ the term "deity" with respect to that very [object] when they offer oblations directed toward one endowed with the moon-crested [Śiva] and other attributes revealed by the mantras.

Moreover, from such scriptural injunctions as "One should give a cow to Śiva," there is the hearing of Śiva and others being the recipients (*sampradāna*) of the deity, as evidenced by the thousand names of Śiva and so forth.

Because the Vedic revelation is authoritative due to its synonymy and its acceptance by the great multitude of people, and because the scripture declares that a propitiated deity is a bestower of boons,
the deity must be conscious in the absence of any subverting evidence.
Now, regarding the position that the deity is conscious:

If it is argued that the very pleasure [derived from the sacrifice] constitutes the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the sacrifice and thus there is no need to establish an *apūrva* (unseen potency), we say no; for pleasure (*prīti*), which is happiness, and its experience perish immediately. Furthermore, the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by that [pleasure] cannot be the cause of a result with respect to its own object.

Therefore, when there is a requirement for a lasting operation as the cause of the result, it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) to postulate an operation that has the same locus as the effort (*kṛti*).

Furthermore, the simultaneous presence [of multiple deities] at various sacrifices during the invocation of bricks is merely a specific mental construction (*buddhiviśeṣa*), just as the sense of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*) is superposed upon an image through the ritual of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).

Now, although Indra and others are indeed conscious beings because the Veda declares them to be the fruits of rites such as the *Rājasūya*, they do not possess actual "deityhood" (*devatātva*), as there is no evidence for it.

Rather, deityhood consists in being designated by a word ending in the dative case that functions as an instructor of the instruction; thus, it is the very word "to Indra" (*indrāya*) and so forth that constitutes it.

For this very reason, immediately after the manifestation of the fire by means of a mantra that illuminates the fire, the offering (*havis*) must necessarily be relinquished with the words "To Agni," and not by any other synonym. Nor should it be argued that the relinquishment of the offering intended for Indra does not produce anything residing in Indra, because—while not producing its [Indra's] own nature—it is performed with him as the object, just like giving to a Brāhmaṇa.
This is not tenable, because the argument lacks probative force (*aprayojakatva*) and because "being performed for the sake of that" is a limiting condition (*upādhi*).

In the expression *indrāya svāhā*, the dative case is not used in the sense of "being for that purpose" (*tādarthye*); rather, it is simply a case governed by a co-occurring word (*upapada-vibhakti*) due to its connection with words such as *svāhā*. Otherwise, the rule beginning with *namaḥ-svasti-svāhā* (Pāṇini 2.3.16) would be rendered useless.
This is not so.
There is no evidence that a word ending in the dative case constitutes a deity (*devatātve*). Even without the dative case, one employs the conventional designation "Indra is the deity."

Because in cases such as "To Agni Kavyavāhana," there would result the contingency of two deities; because the explanatory passage (arthavāda) "Indra, the thousand-eyed," when construed as a single syntactical unit with an injunction such as "One should worship Indra," establishes that very [passage] as the means [of knowledge]; and because even when something is offered to Mahādeva in the case of "One should not take Śiva’s property," cultured people (śiṣṭas) continue to treat it as "Śiva’s property."
Because by the word "to Agni" (*agnaye*), the act of renunciation is necessarily indicated by the scriptural injunction, and because such renunciation is the cause for the attainment of the fruit;
nor should it be argued that the potency of words such as "Śiva" is grasped only in those [mantras] where the seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*) constitute the deity,
since there is no rule that seed-syllables must always end in the dative case.

Even when that [Śiva] is not directly perceived, the ritualists' practical usage (*vyavahāra*) occurs precisely there by means of the offering of oblations directed toward the one endowed with the moon-crested deity and so forth as revealed by the mantra;

for the seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*) do not constitute the intended object (*uddeśya*) of the offering, and because the seed-syllables differ for each mantra, it is impossible to grasp the denotative power (*śakti*) of the word "Śiva" through a universal concomitance (*anugama*).
Nor should it be argued that, because the bodies of Śiva differ in form and thus lack a commonality, you too cannot grasp the word’s denotative power (*śaktigraha*).

For just as the universal "Caitra-ness" persists across bodies differentiated by childhood and other stages, so too does the universal "Śiva-ness," or rather, the state of being favored by a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣopagṛhītatva*), persist.

Furthermore, the Lord (*Īśvara*) who is devoid of unseen merit does not possess the status of a deity; rather, the Sovereign (*Īśāna*) is indeed distinct from him. Therefore, [the deity] is the intended object (*uddeśyatva*) by virtue of being the recipient of the oblation offered with the employment of a mantra.

The status of being a deity [is determined] because for others, the mantra is not the cause in relation to the sacrificial oblation (*havis*). Furthermore, in some cases, the apprehension of a word's power (*śaktigraha*) occurs through the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), as in: "The sacrificial pap (*caru*) consists of barley; a boar-skin is the footwear; on a mat of *vetasa* reeds, he prepares the *prājāpatya* sacrificial pap. In this context, do the words *yava*, *varāha*, and *vetasa* refer to *kaṅgu* millet, crows, and *jambu* trees? Or do they refer to barley, boars, and *vetasa* reeds? [The latter is the case, based on the explanatory passages.]

Regarding the words *dīrghaśrūka*, *sūkara*, and *vañjula*, there is a disagreement due to observing their usage among both Mlecchas and Āryas; because one cannot determine the primary meaning, the authority of those words is not certain. However, linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) arises from usage, and that [usage] is no different for words such as *pika* since proficiency is acquired through the usage of Mlecchas. For just as it is possible to make shoes from the hide of a pig, it is likewise possible to make them from the hide of a crow.
In the first fortnight of spring, the falling of leaves occurs for all crops; the barley grains are seen rejoicing, adorned with their ears.
"The cows run after the boar.
"The reed grows in water."

Thus, when the usage of the Mlecchas—which contradicts the Veda as represented by the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*)—is rejected as something to be discarded (like a Smṛti that contradicts the Veda), the apprehension of the word’s power (*śaktigraha*) proceeds from the unopposed usage of the Āryas. If it is objected: "The determination of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) from the remainder of the sentence does not determine the primary power (*śakti*), because the application of a word to a *śūkara* (boar) and the like can occur through secondary indication (*gauṇī*) and so forth, due to its similarity to a crow (*kāka*) and other such animals," we reply: No, for just as there is an ascertainment of the intended meaning in the case of the *śūkara*, there is likewise an ascertainment of the primary power.

For instance, although the capacity for beginningless usage is not restricted to *śakti* (denotative power) because it deviates in the case of Vedic secondary (*gauṇī*) and other usages, nevertheless, *śakti* is restricted to beginningless usage. Therefore, it would be more cumbersome to postulate both the capacity for beginningless usage and the *śakti* for the word "boar" (*varāha*) in a crow; whereas, since there is a beginningless connection with the Veda regarding the state of being a boar (*śūkara*), the usage is already established as beginningless, and only the *śakti* needs to be postulated—this is parsimony (*lāghava*). Thus, due to this beginningless intention, the *śakti* resides solely in the boar.

Now, if it is argued that the crow is also dissimilar [to the boar] because there exists a bovine animal such as the *gavaya* which is highly similar [to the boar], and thus some degree of similarity exists even for the crow—[we reply: no. For when both the crow and the boar are present in the mind through the word "boar" (*varāha*), for one who desires to know which of these two is the denotation, the crow is excluded because it is merely an object of memory; otherwise, [the exclusion would not occur] even in the case of a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) that serves to apprehend the intended meaning (*tātparya*).

There would be a lack of purpose [in postulating a separate power for *anvaya*] because similarity exists everywhere in some way, and thus the intended meaning (*tātparya*) cannot be determined. Furthermore, the claim that "the power resides in the word as connected with another" is merely a "sugar-coated pill" (*guḍajihvikā*); in reality, there is no power in the connection itself.

[Objection: But surely, since one grasps the word's denotative capacity (*padaśakyatva*) within the cognition of a thing as connected with another—which is inferred through linguistic usage—one grasps the power in that very [connection], because it is what is present [to the mind].

Nor can its abandonment [of the function of denoting] at the outset be justified due to a lack of reason; for linguistic usage does not depend on the mere cognition of word-meanings, as such a meaning is not present [in that context].

Furthermore, there is no evidence for postulating another means [of cognition] to bring about that other presence [of the meaning]. Therefore, if it is argued that "Anvitābhidhāna" (the theory of denotation of related meanings) holds because a word known to possess the capacity to denote its own meaning as related to others brings about the experience of the relation of its own meaning, we say: no, because in the case of the presence of the cognition of a word-meaning as related to others...

Since the cognition of the word-meaning is the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*), it is also an object when that [cognition] is presented; for there is a rule that a qualified cognition necessarily has the qualificandum as its object.

Therefore, one postulates the expressive power (*śakti*) in that [meaning] alone due to parsimony (*lāghava*), and not even in the aspect of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*), because that would involve complexity (*gaurava*).

Alternatively, let it be that the expressive power is first grasped with respect to the cognition of the word-meaning as related to others, and later that [power] is abandoned, because one realizes that [the relation] is obtainable through other means.

Since the meaning of a word must be something not obtainable through any other means, it has already been stated that what is apprehended for the first time alone does not constitute [decisive] strength; therefore, it has been stated by all that what is apprehended for the first time alone is not strong. Consequently, because the status of being the cause of the word is grasped in the cognition of the related (anvitajñāna)—which arises from the initial linguistic usage of all people, whether as a cognition of the related or simply as a cognition of the effect—the apprehension of its expressive power (*śakti*) occurs therein. Even later, when one reflects upon its complexity (*gaurava*) and the fact that it could be obtained through other means, there is no abandonment of that [apprehension of power].
To claim that [the word "pot"] is redundant because the previous conceptualization is erroneous is merely a delusion of one's own disciples.

Now, if it is argued that this is not so because "being an effect" (kāryatva) is obtainable from other words—since in such a syntactic connection (*anvaya*), that [property] cannot be denoted by other words, or if it could be denoted, there would be no dispute [regarding its presence]—we say no. For a word known to possess the power (*śakti*) to denote a pot brings about the recollection of its own meaning through the mediation of memory, by virtue of auxiliary factors such as expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).

Since a word, by its very nature, causes the experience of its own meaning as connected with the meanings of the words uttered alongside it—since the cognition of such a connection is obtained through this very process—what is the use of a separate power (*śakti*)?

Even if the word possesses the power for mere connection, one must necessarily depend upon expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors to obtain the cognition of a specific connection. Furthermore, if each word denoting an action or a factor were to convey its own meaning as already connected with the other, there would be the undesirable consequence of two distinct sentence-meanings being cognized simultaneously.
Nor can it be argued that only one word expresses the connected meaning while the other merely serves to remind one of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
Because there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if one were to experience the connection with something impossible due to a lack of distinction;

and if it is argued that the capacity (*śakti*) resides in the connection itself, we say no, for even that which is impossible causes the cognition of what is connected to the possible, and nothing else, since the state of being connected to the possible is not a restrictive factor by its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*); otherwise, you too could not avoid this consequence.

Now, if it is argued that since words produce the cognition of things as already connected, they must indeed possess a capacity (*śakti*) therein—because that which lacks capacity does not produce [cognition]—this is true even for you.

It is true that the understanding of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) arises from the word because of the existence of God’s will; however, in the production of the understanding of the relation, that [will] is required as something existing in its own right (*svarūpasatī*), not as something known. For the understanding of the relation with a jar is established simply from the knowledge of the word’s capacity for the jar, just as in your view, a word whose power resides in a universal (*jāti*) brings about the knowledge of its own individual instance (*vyakti*). Furthermore, it is observed that even in the case of an instrument where the cognition is already known, that which is known merely as being related to a general property serves as the means for a specific cognition.
Just as smoke, having been apprehended as being pervaded by the universal "fire-ness," generates a cognition of a specific fire; now,

if it is argued that since the property of being a "cognition of a jar" exists even in a cognition of a jar as connected with something else, the known potency must therefore operate toward that cognition of a jar as connected— this is true, however, the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is merely "the state of being a cognition of a jar," and not "the state of being a cognition of a jar as connected."
This is due to [the word's] gravity and because it cannot be obtained through other means.

Thus, just as a word denoting a genus (jāti) has a single power with respect to the individual (vyakti), so too, in the case of the element of logical concomitance (anvaya), that power exists by its own nature (svarūpasatī), while in the case of the referent (padārtha), it is known and pervaded. Since the genus and the individual are cognized by the same cognition, the knowledge of a jar and the like is not necessarily restricted to having concomitance as its object.

If it is argued that there is deviation (vyabhicāra) with regard to recollection, [we reply: the status of being a cause for a specific experience of a jar resides in the word "jar" as such; and that verbal experience is necessarily restricted to having positive concomitance (anvaya) as its object, since a solitary [word] is never experienced through a [verbal] expression. Furthermore, the status of being a cause for recollection does not reside in [the word] as a mere "word," because of deviation, but rather in its being known as a related entity (sambandhin).

It might be argued as follows: there is no dispute that the word conveys its meaning through the intention (*tātparya*) directed toward the syntactic connection (*anvaya*); and the function (*vṛtti*) that fulfills this intention is neither figurative (*gauṇī*) nor metaphorical (*lakṣaṇā*), thus establishing the existence of primary denotation (*śakti*).

Alternatively, it may be that there is indeed metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the connection itself, because the intention is directed toward that which is related to the word’s own primary meaning, and because the connection is logically established immediately after the presentation of the individual word-meanings.
Nor is there a contradiction between two functions, since the presentation of the word-meanings occurs as qualifiers of the connection.
Nor should it be argued: "Since words with secondary meanings (lākṣaṇika) do not produce cognition, how can there be a cognition of the syntactic relation (anvaya)?

For, because the word-meanings are remembered and because words possess the capacity for syntactic relation, words do not produce cognition through their primary power (śakti); rather, in all cases, it is only that which has a secondary meaning (lākṣaṇika) which produces the cognition.
This is not so.
For it is the function (*vṛtti*) that is required for cognition, not the actual existence of the essential nature [of the word], because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Nor is the connection here previously understood as being related to its own meaning, since the sentence-meaning is something not previously known (*apūrva*). Furthermore, if the connection were based on being related to what is denotable (*śakya*), then rather than postulating a denotative power (*śakti*) in the word-meaning—which is the referent of indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—it is better to postulate it in the connection itself, due to parsimony (*lāghava*).

"Let there be even such a power; why postulate two distinct functions? This being the case, even in actual usage, the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) is the word-meaning (*padaśakya*), because it is conveyed by the word without requiring any other function, just like the individual word-meanings (*padārtha*).
It is replied:

Since the intended meaning (*tātparya*) can be established even without a linguistic function (*vṛtti*), what is the use of such a function? For it is possible for words to generate the cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya-bodha*) through the aforementioned sequence [of operations] without [direct] function; otherwise, if the intended meaning were seen to be established only through primary denotation (*śakti*), then the doctrine of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) would be abolished. Now, if it is argued that the intended meaning is established through the relation to the primary meaning (*śakyasambandha*) even without primary denotation, and thus there is no primary denotation in that case, then [we reply]: if it is established without a linguistic function, what is the use of a function at all? For this very reason, the inference [proposed by the opponent] is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*). Otherwise, if one were to prove primary denotation merely on the grounds that something is conveyed by the words, then other linguistic functions would be abolished.

For this very reason, in the statement "there is smoke," although the word "smoke" intends to convey the cognition of fire, there is no indication (lakṣaṇā) with respect to fire; for once smoke is presented through its primary power (śakti), the cognition of fire is possible by means of inference. Likewise: "Go, O beloved, if you go; may your paths be auspicious.
May my birth also occur in that very place where you have gone."

Even though the intention (*tātparya*) of the sentence "Do not go" lies there, there is no indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because the meaning of the sentence is that going is a cause of the beloved's death; thus, the intention is fulfilled simply by making known the non-performability of going through inference alone, namely: "Going must not be performed by me, because it is a cause of the beloved's death."
For where the intended meaning cannot be established—either directly through the primary sense, or indirectly through a succession [of meanings]—there is *lakṣaṇā* (indication).
Now, one might object: in the case of "Bring the jar," there arises a desire to know the specific relation for each individual word.

If it is argued that a particular cannot exist without the comprehension of its universal, and therefore the power [of words] must reside solely in the universal of the relation (*anvaya-sāmānya*), we say no. This is because the universal of action and the universal of the factors of action (*kriyā-kāraka-sāmānya*) are necessarily implied by their respective causes; thus, the [particular] is established, just as when one perceives the fruit and so forth, there arises a desire to know the specific taste.

By this, the following argument is refuted: "In my view, there is a single power for each word in the related object, whereas in your view, there is one power for the object and another for the relation."
Because there is no capacity [of words] with respect to the synthesis [of meaning].
Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, there would be no application of words in the experience of synthesis;
for the capacity of words is postulated with respect to word-meanings precisely for the sake of the experience of synthesis.

Therefore, the word (*pada*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*), the recollection of the word-meaning (*padārthasmaraṇa*) is the operation (*vyāpāra*), and the experience of the connection between the recollected meanings—by virtue of auxiliary factors such as expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth—is the result (*phala*). The recollection of the word-meaning is not the productive cause (*vyadhāyaka*), because it is itself an operation;

nor is the word-meaning itself the cause by way of being the medium for recollection, because, due to its being future and so forth, it lacks the capacity to produce its own recollection or the experience of the connection.

Even so, let the recollection of word-meanings (*padārtha-smaraṇa*) alone be the instrument (*karaṇa*), because it is indispensable; for this very reason, since the cognition of syntactic relation (*anvaya-bodha*) arises from word-meanings brought forth by reflection (*cintā*), [the cause] is poetry and the like—if this is argued, we say no. For recollection, being devoid of causal efficiency (*nirvyāpāra*), cannot be an instrument. By means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that are not otherwise established, words possessing expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other conditions are the cause of the specific experience of syntactic relation (*anvaya-anubhava*). This is because the presentation of word-meanings (*padārthopasthiti*) is merely a cause for the cognition of relations (*saṃsarga-dhī*) in general.

Furthermore, since the word itself is the cause regarding the object of the cognition of verbal relation— even when there is knowledge of word-meanings in the case of "cow," "objectness," and "bringing," the cognition of the relation does not arise— because if the cause were the knowledge of word-meanings presented by specific words, then the specific word itself must necessarily be the cause. And in the case of poetry, it is the mind alone, assisted by poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) and other factors, that acts as the instrument for the experience of the relation, with the knowledge of word-meanings serving as its mediate operation (*vyāpāra*).

Nor indeed is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because, like the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, it belongs to a class of fallacious cognitions; because it lacks a non-overlapping, recurring form that delimits its status as an instrument of knowledge (*pramākaraṇatāvacchedaka*); and because it is devoid of any operation (*nirvyāpāratva*).
Rather, it is an auxiliary to a means of valid cognition.
For this very reason, in the case of mental consideration of the inferential mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*), the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth are not separate means of valid cognition.

Now, since the cognition of syntactic connection (*anvayabodha*) occurs even without a word when there is knowledge of semantic competency (*yogyatā*) and so forth, the function of words is exhausted merely in the recollection of word-meanings (*padārthasmaraṇa*).
As it has been said: "For one who sees the white form, hears the sound of neighing, and hears the sound of the trampling of hooves, the cognition arises: 'A white horse is galloping.'"

If this is argued, it is true that because the activity of the person being prompted is observed immediately after the utterance of the prompter’s sentence, the capacity (śakti) of the word itself is postulated for the sake of accounting for the cognition of the related meaning. For it is simpler to postulate a single capacity for the word in its primary sense than to postulate a separate capacity for each individual word-meaning. As they say: "Because of primacy, because of being the denoter, and because of the acceptance of intentionality (tātparya), it is better to admit that the capacity belongs to the words alone."

Thus, the cognition "the white horse runs" is born from a *liṅga* (inferential mark), because there is an absence of the word whose status as a cause [of such cognition] has been established [as being based on the universal].
This concludes the discussion on the theory that the expressive power resides in the universal (*jātiśaktivāda*).

Thus, the capacity [of a word] is determined with respect to the object itself. Regarding this, the Prabhākaras hold that although it is appropriate for the capacity to reside in the individual (vyakti) alone, because of its utility in activities such as bringing [an object].

Nevertheless, because of infinity and deviation, there can be no apprehension of the denotative power (*śakti*) therein. If the capacity were [to apply] through a collective conjunction (*samuccaya*), there would be an inability to include all [individuals] in cases such as "one should give a cow" (*gāṃ dadyāt*). If the capacity belonged to only one [individual], there would be uncertainty (*anadhyavasāya*).

Nor is the mere individual cow (*govyakti-mātra*) the meaning; for if the word "mere" (*mātra*) meant "all," the aforementioned fault would follow, and if it meant "universal" (*sāmānya*), the individual would not be perceived. Furthermore, if it had multiple meanings, it would be impossible to know each and every one of them, whether regarding the power itself or the object of that power.
Furthermore, there is no linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) for a cow that has never been seen before, and thus no gravity of meaning (*gaurava*).

Nor can it be argued that the individual (*vyakti*) characterized by "cowness" (*gotva*) is denoted—just as in the case of the word *dhenu*—because [if that were so], it would follow that there is no capacity [to denote all cows] immediately thereafter, nor would there be any deviation (*vyabhicāra*), nor any failure to include all individuals (*asarvasaṅgraha*), nor any polysemy (*nānārthatva*), since they are unified by "cowness.
This is what must be stated.

For an object is perceived through one form while it is cognized by means of another form; just as a particular house is distinguished by a crow, or a particular individual cow by its "cowness" (*gotva*), which is inherently distinct [from the crow]. However, the cognition of that [cow] does not occur solely through the form of the crow and so forth. Nor is there any single other form belonging to individuals apart from the universal (*jāti*), nor is such a thing known, since from the word "cow" there arises the cognition "this is a cow" alone.

Furthermore, because the connection with the action occurs in that which is qualified by "cowness" (*gotva*), cowness is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and not a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). When the connection with the action occurs through something other than that [qualifier], it is an indicator, as in the case:
"This one who possesses a garment is the referent of the word Devadatta," where the garment is an indicator.
Nor is the unity of individual instances produced by the unity of cowness, because that is impossible.
Nor is it made known [by the individual], because it does not exist;
nor is the oneness of that [universal] itself the oneness of the manifestation, because that is impossible.

Nor can the manifestation be capable of delimiting "cowness," just as a staff [cannot delimit the person it belongs to] when it serves as the cause [of cognition]; for in that case, from the word "cow" (go), there would be no cognition qualified by "cowness" (gotva).

If it is argued that, just as from the word *go* itself—assisted by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the apprehension of its denotative power (*śakti*)—there arises a cognition qualified by "cowness" (*gotva*), and that the awakening of this [impression] occurs through a transitive relation just as in the case of the word *dhenu*, [we reply: no; for in that case, since a specific individual instance of the act of milking (*dhāna*) must necessarily be the denoted object (*śakyārtha*), "cowness" is merely the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) for the sake of generalization, and not the reverse, because "cowness" exists even in a bull. But here [in the case of *gauḥ*], [it is not so].

However, since the individual instance (*vyakti*) would lead to over-extension (*atiprasakti*), it must be the individual as qualified by the universal (*jāti*) that is the denotable object (*śakya*).

In reality, however, because the universal is necessarily required either as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the denotable or as its delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), and on account of parsimony (*lāghava*), the universal alone should be the denotable object, not the individual; yet this is not the case with the word *dhenu* (cow), where "cowness" (*gotva*) does not function in that way.

This would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is argued: "Let it be that the capacity [of a word] is qualified by the universal (*jāti*), because through its own conventional usage and by being its own cause, the cognition qualified by the universal is inferred"—we say no. For if individual instances were the denotable objects, they would be infinite due to the difference between the qualificands (*viśeṣya*), and this would entail the aforementioned faults.

Since the identity of the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) follows from the identity of its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), it is as faulty as the view that the word denotes a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, if the individual (*vyakti*) is not the meaning of the word, the universal (*jāti*) alone must be the word-meaning. In reality, however, since the universal is necessarily both the recurring factor and the differentiator within the individual, it is the universal itself that is denoted by the "maxim of the unapprehended qualifier" (*nāgṛhītaviśeṣaṇanyāya*). Now, even regarding the universal, the individual alone is its specific feature because there is no other property [to serve as a differentiator]; for even a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), such as "existing in all cows while not existing in non-cows," is merely a particular instance of the individual.

Because it is constituted by individuals, the principle that "the qualifier must first be apprehended" applies to the individual as well; thus, both [the universal and the individual] must be denotable. This is because the universal is not excluded *per se*.

Otherwise, there would be a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*) in the cognition of their mutual exclusion based on the cognition of the exclusion of the universal from the individual and vice versa.
Furthermore, being "differentiated by itself" does not mean that it is its own differentiator, because a thing cannot reside within itself;
nor does it mean being differentiated even without a differentiator, for that is impossible.

Rather, it means having a nature that generates the cognition of differentiation with respect to itself, just as it does with respect to its own substratum, like the ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣa*) of other schools.

If even the differentiating property were to produce a cognition of exclusion only through another property, there would be an infinite regress; therefore, they say that some entity is indeed distinct by its own nature.

Or rather, let it be that the universal (*jāti*) alone—when understood as excluded by the individual—is the word-meaning, because of parsimony (*lāghava*), and not the reverse or both together, due to the excessive complexity (*gaurava*). But then, how does the cognition of the individual arise? It arises from that which has the power [to denote] the universal. How can there be a cognition of one thing from that which has the power to denote another? It is due to the very nature of things (*svabhāvāt*).

If it is argued that its very nature as having that [universal] as its essence cannot be established without a power (śakti) directed toward the individual (vyakti), we say no. For the word "cow" (go-pada) invariably causes both the universal and the individual to be understood; in this case, only the cognition of its power toward the universal is postulated as the auxiliary cause, because of parsimony (lāghava) and necessity, and not even the cognition of a power toward the individual, due to the resulting complexity (gaurava).

If it is argued: "Since there is no delay in the cognition of the individual when the power residing in the universal is known, just as for you [the Mīmāṃsakas] the cognition of syntactic relation arises from the word's power over the object itself;

or rather, the word whose power resides in the universal causes the cognition of the individual, even though that is not its primary denotation, because being the substratum of the universal is the restrictive factor—just as [a word] causes the cognition of another meaning that is not its own denotation;

therefore, let the power already established as the motivator remain as such, since it is more cumbersome to assume that being the substratum of the universal functions in that way"—we say: No, because that which is obtainable through other means is not the word-meaning (apadārtha); otherwise, even the syntactic relation would have to be a primary denotation.
Otherwise, there would be the annihilation of the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth.
Alternatively, the cognition of the universal (*jāti*), arising from the knowledge of the power residing in the universal, also takes the individual (*vyakti*) as its object;
for since the universal does not exist without the individual, that which causes the cognition of something makes known that [thing] without which it does not appear, just as [in the case of a lamp].

Or, just as your own *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (the established conclusion based on the subject) holds that the cause of the cognition of knowledge has that [knowledge] as its object— otherwise, even a word would not convey a universal (*jāti*), since a universal is never perceived in isolation— so too, the power postulated for the purpose of conveying the universal conveys the individual (*vyakti*) as well, because of the rule that they must be cognized by a single act of cognition.

By this, the argument that the very fact of being known by a single cognition would not be possible without the power of manifestation (*vyakti-śakti*)—because of the absence of a means of cognition—is refuted. For the cognition of the individual (*vyakti*) is neither causeless, as that would entail its being eternal, nor is it caused by the universal (*jāti*), for that would entail its being eternally present;
nor is it caused by the cognition of the universal, as that would result in a distinction between cognitions. Thus, [the objection] is rejected.
Because it is the power of the universal (*jāti*) alone that makes the individual (*vyakti*) known.

[Objection: But surely, since the individual is known through perception and other means even without the universal, the causal complex for the cognition of the individual is distinct; and the cognition of the individual as qualified by the universal would arise from the conjunction of these two separate causal complexes that make each known.

Therefore, the following [position] is refuted: "Since the recollection of a universal (jāti) without its individual (vyakti) necessarily has the individual as its object, it is postulated that whatever makes the universal known is itself what makes the individual known; for there is no subverting argument against such a postulation of a commonality.

This is because one can also recollect an individual even without the universal; thus, in that case, the causal complex (sāmagrī) is entirely different, and the recollection of the qualified [individual] arises from the conjunction of those factors that cause the recollection of both parts.
To this we reply:

while in the case of the perception of universals and particulars, two distinct causal complexes are grasped through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), in verbal cognition, however, the knowledge of the word's power (*śakti*) with respect to the universal alone is the cause for the cognition of the particular, due to parsimony (*lāghava*). There is no other causal complex [required], because when that [knowledge of the universal] is present, there is no delay in the absence of it.
And thus, a word known as having the capacity for a genus (jāti) is both the recollector and the producer of the cognition of that which is qualified by the genus.

Now, one might object: "Since capacity resides in the cognition [of the object], it is because of being an object of cognition (śakyatva) that something is so designated; and since the capacity resides in the cognition of both the genus and the individual (vyakti), the individual must also be the denoted object (śakya) just like the genus. To this we reply: no, for it is only when capacity is known as having a certain object as its domain that it functions within the cognition.

In that cognition of the denotative power (*śakti*), the genus (*jāti*) alone is the denotable (*śakya*), because it is the delimiting factor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) by virtue of being its object; and the cognition of the genus is likewise [the cause].
Individuality (*vyakti*) is not the delimiting factor even for the cognition [of the denotable], due to the principle of complexity (*gaurava*).

Nor is denotability merely the state of being a restricted object within the cognition of the denotable, in the case of the syntactic connection of those objects of the denotable experience inferred from linguistic usage.

Otherwise, there would be the contingency of [the word] being capable of denoting even the mothers and other relatives of that [person]. Thus, since it generates knowledge of both the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), the word's power (*śakti*) resides in both.

Regarding the universal aspect, that power is known (*jñāta*); regarding the individual aspect, it is a cause by virtue of its own existence (*svarūpasat*). This is the theory of "crooked power" (*kubjaśaktivāda*), because of parsimony (*lāghava*).

And so, there is no contradiction in the fact that the very same power is at one and the same time both known and unknown, denotative and non-denotative, due to the distinction between the universal and the individual as delimiters; for you too accept "crooked power" in the case of syntactic relation (*anvaya*).

Even though the individual (vyakti) is the denotable object (*śakyārtha*), it does not possess "denotability" (*vācyatva*) characterized as being the object of a cognition produced by a word whose power [to denote it] has been known.

Nor is this a mere technical convention (*paribhāṣā*); for if denotability were defined simply as being the object of a cognition produced by a word, then even metaphorical meanings (*lākṣaṇika*) and the like would result in being denotable.

Furthermore, even if the individual is the denotable object, the knowledge of the word's power with respect to the individual is not the cause [of its cognition], and the property of being "the knowledge of the power with respect to the individual" is not the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*); thus, there is parsimony (*lāghava*).
As for the claim that the cognition of an object arises only from knowing [the word] as possessing that capacity (śakti)— since a cognition is observed even from a delusion regarding capacity—

and likewise that the presentation of an individual (vyakti) from a word, which occurs even without the compatibility (yogyatā) or syntactic connection (anvaya), is accomplished by capacity (śakti), and therefore the individual is also denotable (śakya): that is not correct.

Because one does not postulate a capacity for that which can be obtained through other means; otherwise, even in your view of *anvaya* (syntactic connection), there would be a capacity [for every word], and there would be the total abolition of *lakṣaṇā* and so forth.
