Now, it may be argued that the universal (*jāti*) is not the meaning [of a word], because its acquisition (*vyutpatti*) is not established due to the absence of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*); for it is action qualified by a *kāraka* (participant in an action) that is the domain of linguistic usage, and the universal is not such.

If it is argued that [the universal] is not an agent because it is eternal, because it is not a *kāraka* since action does not inhere in it there, because it lacks participation in the fruit of an action inherent in another, because it is not the locus of the activity of agency, because it is insentient, and because there is no disjunction from it [the action], nor is it the substratum of action— [we reply: no, for by the very usage regarding individuals, the capacity (*śakti*) is grasped in the universal according to the stated reasoning, since the universal is excluded from non-conceptual cognitions and so forth.

When an individual is cognized, its connection with action occurs through conceptualization (*savikalpaka*), which arises from the universal (*jāti*) by way of indeterminate perception (*ālocana*); thus, the universal is also connected [to the action] as an instrument (*kāraka*) through a mediated sequence.

Alternatively, it is not the individual alone that possesses the status of an instrument; for in the case of "the cow goes," no one perceives that the mere individual is going, but rather that the individual qualified by the universal is so. Therefore, both [the individual and the universal] are instruments.

Śrīkara, however, maintains that because the word denotes only the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), the connection with the action belongs to the individual by way of being its locus, while it belongs to the universal by way of being its delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), just as in the case of "redness" (*āruṇya*) and so forth. Thus, from a word whose power resides in the universal, there is a verbal cognition (*śābda-anubhava*) of the universal, whereas the cognition of the individual is obtained through implication (*aupādānika*), since it cannot itself be the direct denotation.
(Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,2, p. 470)

Others, however, maintain that a word endowed with the power to denote the universal (*jāti*) is both the reminder and the producer of the cognition of both the universal and the individual (*vyakti*); thus, the individual also possesses the status of being denoted by words (*śābdatva*).

Nor can it be argued that the individual lacks the status of being denoted by words because it does not enter into the experience of syntactic relation (*anvaya*) without a formal semantic function (*vṛtti*), for even without a *vṛtti*, the individual is experienced through the very same word that denotes the universal, due to the rule that they must be cognized by a single act of awareness (*ekavittivedyatvaniyama*). Otherwise, there would be no syntactic relation of the universal either, since the universal cannot be experienced without the individual.
For this very reason, the teachers (guravaḥ) maintain that the power residing in the genus (jāti-śakti) itself brings about the cognition of the individual (vyakti).

Furthermore, words function as causes for the experience of syntactic relation (anvaya-anubhava) only with respect to that which has been presented by their denoted object (śakya); therefore, the experience of the individual presented by the word occurs through the genus, but not through the presentation of each specific individual denotation, because that would involve unnecessary complexity (gaurava).

Nor is there figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) when the primary power (*śakti*) is impossible; for just as there is no primary power because the cognition [of the object] arises from something else, so too there is no figurative indication. Why then would there be a primary usage even for the impossible? True, it is primary because it is directly presented by the power; however, the phrase "by its own power" is redundant. In reality, since the cognition of the individual (*vyakti*) is possible from the power residing in the genus (*jāti*) alone, there is no power in the individual.
And if the cognition of that [object] does not arise from that [word], then there would be causal power (śakti) in that [word] alone; otherwise, the cognition of it would not occur at all.

If it is argued: "But surely, by means of both the word and the universal (jāti), a single experience of both the universal and the individual (vyakti) is produced; in this case, the word is the cause of the experience regarding the universal-part, while the universal is the cause regarding the individual-part—this very [distinction] constitutes the meaning of 'appropriation' (upādāna)," then, in relation to the status of the universal as a cause, there must be a cognition of its causal power.

It is far more parsimonious to postulate that the individual already present [in cognition] possesses the status of a delimitor (avacchedakatva) alone, rather than admitting that the universal (jāti) constitutes a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

For this very reason, in the injunction "one threshes the rice-grains" (vrīhīnavahanti), there is no figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) with respect to the individual, because the presentation of what is to be accomplished by the action is established through the very power residing in the universal.

Alternatively, let it be that threshing is connected to the state of being rice (vrīhitva) as well, by virtue of its being the delimitor of the cow, just as in the case of the quality of redness (āruṇya) and so forth.
To this it is replied:

the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*) takes the form "the word is capable of [producing] the cognition of cowness" or "the word is capable of [producing] the cognition of the cow"; and thus, [it occurs] when there is the cognition of the object of that power (*śakya*).

The fact that a universal (*jāti*) functions as a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) by way of being an object of cognition is understood only by taking an individual (*vyakti*) into account, not in isolation, because a universal is never perceived without an individual. Thus, since the universal serves as the delimiting factor, the principle that "the qualifier is not grasped [without the qualified]" ensures that the individual's status as a delimiting factor becomes as firm as a diamond coating (*vajralepa*). Therefore, because it functions as a delimiting factor by way of being an object of the cognition of the word's power (*śakti*), the individual is also denotable (*śakya*), just like the universal. Consequently...
Either abandon the restriction that [the word-meaning] is cognizable by a single cognition, or accept that the individual (*vyakti*) is the denotable object.

Furthermore, when the cognition of something occurs only when another thing is known as possessing a certain property, that [property] is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) therein; since the cognition of the word's power (*śakti*) occurs in the cognition of the object only when the individual is known as possessing that [power], the individual is also denotable.

Now, one might argue: "In the first instance of learning the word, it is known that the capacity to prompt action resides in the cognition only when that cognition is known as having the object and the subject (*miti-mātṛ*) as its content, and not otherwise. But this is not so.

The cognition of those two [the object and the self] is what prompts action; therefore, there is no deviation [in the rule that the word's power resides only in the cognition of the object]. Otherwise, by means of the prompter's action, one could infer the cognitions of the knower and the self, and a child would then grasp the word's power even with respect to those.

If you argue that, for you as well, the power must reside only in the cognition of the object as connected to an action, because the power is grasped only when the cognition is known as such [i.e., as connected to an action], then [we reply that] the state of being a cognition of the knower and the self, and the state of being a cognition of the object as connected to an action, are both [cognitions].

Even without the motivating cognition (*pravartakajñāna*), it is possible to cognize "being a cognition of a jar" (*ghaṭajñānatva*) and so forth; therefore, those two [the motivating cognition and the object] do not possess the status of delimiters (*avacchedakatva*).
Rather, it is "being a cognition of a jar" and so forth that [possess this status], due to parsimony (*lāghava*) and because those two are obtained from that very source.

Furthermore, a word, for the purpose of cognizing an individual (*vyakti*), postulates only the status of being a delimiter of the individual as the objective content (*viṣayatā*) within the cognition of the denotable object (*śakyajñāna*).

Due to parsimony (*lāghava*), the fact that the word refers to the individual (*vyakti*) is necessarily and more rapidly presented to consciousness—just as its referring to the universal (*jāti*) is—because it is known through the very awareness of the cognition itself (*jñānavittivedyatva*).

It is not the case, however, that the power resides in the universal (*jātiśakti*), nor is there any other cause for that cognition, nor is there any delimitor (*avacchedaka*) thereof; this is because such would involve complexity (*gaurava*) and because their presentation would have to be postulated at the time of grasping the word's power (*śaktigraha*).

Others, however, first determine that the word possesses a power (śakti) with respect to the cognition of an individual inferred from linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), because [the word] conforms to that [individual] (*śabdānuvidhāna*); they do not [determine it] with respect to the cognition of the universal (*jāti*), because at that time the universal is not present, since it does not produce the linguistic usage. Subsequently, having understood through another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) that the universal is also the object of that word—for the sake of excluding other individuals and for the sake of [their] inclusion—they [conclude] that the word has power even with respect to the cognition of the universal.

One understands that [the cognition of the individual] is the cause; likewise, the cognition of the power residing in the individual is also a cause, and it is not rendered superfluous (anyathāsiddha) by the cognition of the power residing in the genus (jāti).

This is because the apprehension of the causality of the cognition of the genus depends upon the apprehension of the causality of the cognition of the individual; thus, there would be a contradiction with what is being depended upon (upajīvya-virodha).

By this, it is also shown that the genus is the denotable object (śakya), owing to parsimony (lāghava), since the latent impression (saṃskāra) produced by the apprehension of the power is necessarily restricted to having the individual as its object.

When the recollection of a birth (*jāti-smaraṇa*) is produced from a word, it must necessarily have an individual (*vyakti*) as its object. Even though the awakening of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is not restricted to a specific trigger, one must assume a rule that the awakening of the individual aspect occurs precisely from the same trigger that awakens the generic aspect (*jāty-aṃśa*). This is just as the recollection of a specific power (*śakti*) is restricted by the very same impression awakened by a word; for even without the word, all such recollection of a birth has the individual as its object, otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of remembering the mere universal (*jāti*) alone.
The experience of an object qualified by its universal (*jāti*) arises from the word itself, accompanied by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), just as recognition arises from the sense organs.

For this very reason, the view inferred in the *Bhāṣya*—that there is an experience of a qualified object through both mental impressions and the power of the word—is refuted; for, according to the aforementioned principles, the individual (*vyakti*) is as much the denotable object (*śakya*) as the universal is.

Furthermore, although there is an infinity of names for qualified objects, one may set aside the specific identity (*tattva*) of a single qualified instance and, taking up "cowness" (*gotva*), [denote] that which is qualified by cowness.
The apprehension of this capacity is possible; just as in some instances there arises the cognition that "smoke is pervaded by fire," or just as in the same way,

despite the infinity of effects, one sets aside the specific nature (*tattva*) of a particular effect and, taking up the agent's effort (*kṛti*) with respect to the substratum, apprehends the capacity of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth for the "unseen potency" (*apūrva*), thinking "the effect is possible"— in that very manner, the unity of the capacity follows from the unity of its delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*).

Or, just as in the case of words such as "cow" which denote an individual, the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*) occurs by taking the universal "cowness" (*gotva*)—which is known through its general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*)—in every cow; and just as omniscience (*sārvajña*) is indeed accepted with respect to all cognitions insofar as they possess the property of being knowable (*prameyatva*), but it is not accepted [to apply] to a single indifferent cow insofar as it possesses the knowledge of all modes such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*); for if only one [instance] were taken up, there would either be no determination (*anadhyavasāya*).

Otherwise, even for you, since everything is cognizable by a single cognition, what would be the recourse when the aforementioned fault arises regarding the theory that everything is ultimately one? Or what would be the recourse for words such as "animal" (*paśu*), which denote individuals? In the Bhaṭṭa school’s view, however, the universal (*jāti*) alone is the denotable meaning due to parsimony (*lāghava*); the individual, on the other hand, is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*). But surely there is no implication, because those two are cognized by a single cognition; for a universal is the state of commonality among things, and that cannot exist without the individual.

If it is argued that [the universal] does not appear, we say no; for a universal cannot exist in its own right (*svarūpeṇa*), nor is "universality" its intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), because that is a property (*dharma*) of it.
Otherwise, it would not appear even in pure sensory intuition (*ālocana*).

If it is asked how a universal, which is not cognized as a universal, can be denoted by a word as being distinct from the individual, we say no, because the word does not convey the universal as being distinct from the individual.

If it is argued that—since a genus, being itself excluded [from others], cannot imply specific individuals without an excluded cognition, the individual alone must be the differentiator therein; and since even the state of being "concomitant" does not appear without something concomitant, the individual is known only through the cognition of the genus—[we reply]: no, because the nature of the genus, which is inherently excluded, is what is denoted.
If another property (*dharma*) were the differentiator of the individual (*vyakti*), there would be either mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) or an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
[Objection: But surely from the word "cow" (*gauḥ*), there is a simultaneous cognition of both the genus (*jāti*) and the individual.

Nor is that cognition erroneous due to the non-perception of a subtle difference in time, because there is no sublation (*bādhaka*); and thus, from the word "cow," there arises the cognition of cowness (*gotva*). From that—

If it is argued that it is better to assume that the individual is cognized through the cognition of the universal—rather than postulating a succession of cognitions where first there is the knowledge of pervasion and the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), and from that, the inference of the individual—it is not so; for the capacity of a word to convey meaning depends upon linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). Therefore, when considering such convention, simultaneous cognition [of both] is unestablished.

For this very reason, the postulation of a succession of cognitions is also logical; otherwise, there would be no implication of an agent either, since from a word one understands only an action that possesses an agent.

Nor is there a rule that the cognition of a universal must necessarily have an individual as its object, because in the case of perception and so forth, that [cognition of the universal] depends on the convergence of the causes for the cognition of the individual.

For this very reason, there is no rule that the cause of the cognition of a universal must be assisted by the cause of the cognition of the individual, because such a requirement is established only by convention. Furthermore, [the universal] is established as a mere cognition of the universal through the inference: "Cowness is the object of a cognition whose object is not the cow, because it is a universal, or because it is an entity distinct from the cow"; and because the cognition of the universal alone is thus established. Now, whatever is dependent upon something else must be cognized by the same cognition as that thing, just as knowledge, which is dependent upon an object, is cognized along with the object.

If it is argued that "universality (jāti) is dependent" and thus appears only when the individual (vyakti) appears, we say no. For "dependence" (paratantratva) cannot mean "inherence in another," because that would lead to a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of smell and other qualities. Nor can it mean "being defined by that [the individual]," because that is unproven (asiddhi). Nor can it mean "appearing only when that [the individual] appears," because that would be no different from the point to be proven (sādhyāviśeṣa). Nor can it mean "being known only as a qualifier," for [the universal] is known simply as "cow."
If it is argued that someone perceives "cowness in the cow," we say no; for even without its being a qualifier, there is a perception of it by its own nature.

From a word whose power resides solely in the universal, there arises a mere recollection of the universal, which is indeed an indeterminate perception (*ālocana*). This occurs through the word acting upon a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) whose object is the universal as qualified [by the individual].
Because when there is the awakening of the aspect of the universal (jāti), there is the recollection of the universal alone;
for this very reason, from that [awakening], there is sometimes a recollection of the individual (vyakti) even without the universal.

Or, let it be that even indeterminate perception (ālocana) generates a latent impression (saṃskāra), like that of a teacher, since the recollection of the universal alone is established through the power of linguistic proficiency (śabdavyutpatti).

Furthermore, it is not the case that remembrance (*smaraṇa*) is exclusively a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), for if experience (*anubhava*) were also thus [restricted], it would entail the non-establishment of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*).

Even if [remembrance] were known by the same means of knowledge [as its object], like the first sight [of an object], the remembrance of "cowness" from a word is merely a bare observation (*ālocana*); this is because it cannot have as its object the qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) such as the subsistence of cowness in an individual cow, since such a qualification is impossible [to be conveyed by a word].

Nor is it the case that indeterminate perception (*ālocana*) cannot be a memory because it is produced by the sense organs; for the property of being a memory (*smṛtitva*) resides in indeterminate perception as a property directly pervaded by the property of being a cognition (*jñānatva*). If it is argued: "The cognition of an individual arises through implication (*ākṣepa*), neither as an individual (*vyaktitva*) nor under another form, since the cognition is simply 'this is a cow' (*gaur*); nor is it as 'cowness' (*gotva*), because there is no implication of cowness through its distinction from what is qualified by cowness," we say: No, for there is no contradiction with inference due to the distinction between the qualifier and the qualified.

For this very reason, by the force of the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) in the inference "Cowness is dependent on an individual, because it is a universal (*jāti*)," the existence of an individual that is the substratum of cowness is established; or else, its establishment occurs through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

If it is asked: "What is unaccountable without the individual (vyakti)? Since the universal 'cowness' (gotva) and the cognition thereof are established even without the individual, how can there be presumptive testimony (arthāpatti)?"—we reply: No, for the pervaded (vyāpya) cannot be established without the pervader (vyāpaka). It is said: from the sentence "Bring the cow" (gām ānaya), because one understands the connection of the action with that which is qualified by cowness, the cognition having the individual cow as its object in the form "cow" (gauḥ) is the cause [of the understanding]. And that [cognition] does not arise without the word; through implication (ākṣepa), one has the notion that "cowness resides in an individual," but not the cognition "it is a cow."

Nor is it the case that the individual (vyakti) is likewise connected with the action, because [the cognition] is already satisfied by its dependence on the genus *gotva*, just as in the case of "bring the king's man," where [the action] relates to the king; otherwise, there would arise the thought "bring the individual," but not "bring the cow.

Furthermore, the genus *gotva* is not pervaded by the individual, for there is no rule that wherever or whenever *gotva* exists, the individual must exist, nor that whatever is a universal is an individual, since such a rule is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Nor can there be an inference that "the genus *gotva* is dependent on a cow because it is *gotva*," because this would involve the very process of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) itself.

Furthermore, being a universal (*jātitva*) is not a logical mark (*liṅga*) for [establishing] the dependence on an individual (*vyakti*), because a universal is not presented from the word; or, if it were so presented, the individual would be cognized by the very cognition of the universal. Moreover, a logical mark, being pervaded (*vyāpya*), when found untenable [without its correlate], makes known the pervader (*vyāpaka*) which establishes its own substratum.
And here, there is no cognition of an individual as the substratum of "cowness" (*gotva*).

We, however, say this: if the individual (vyakti) were not the meaning of a word, then the number, objecthood, and so forth—which are the meanings of case-endings—could not be construed with the individual; for it is established by linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that suffixes convey their own meanings as being construed with the meaning of the stem (*prakṛti*). If one were to maintain that such construction occurs only with respect to what is the intended referent of the stem, then there would be an abandonment of the principle of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and there would be excessive complexity (*gaurava*).

The number denoted by the meaning of the verb (*ākhyāta*) does not connect with that which is merely inferred; rather, it connects with the pure *bhāvanā* (efficient force) as presented from another word in the nominative case. In this context, "implication" (*ākṣepa*) refers simply to its presentation [from that other word]. For this very reason, there is no implication of the individual (*vyakti*); rather, according to Maṇḍana, the cognition of the individual arises through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) from the word "cow" as "the cow.
As he said: "For existence and non-existence do not qualify the universal (*jāti*)."
It is said:
Metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs when something is known through a form other than its own primary meaning, as in the case of the word "Ganges" when it is known as a riverbank.

However, in this case, there is no presentation of the individual (*vyakti*) through a form other than "cowness" (*gotva*); rather, while the individual is indicated by "cowness" itself, as well as by its being an individual and its possessing a dewlap and so forth, the cognition from the word "cow" would not arise in the form of "individuality" (*vyaktitva*) and the like.

But [the word] "cow" [does not function thus]. Nor is there a secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) regarding that which is related to cowness—that is, the individual qualified by cowness—for cowness does not directly connect with actions such as bringing. If it were to connect [with the action], it would do so only by way of delimiting the individual, and thus its status would be non-primary.

Even through secondary signification, it is the individual as delimited by cowness that is understood as connecting with the action, not the individual alone. Therefore, if the individual qualified by cowness were the object of signification, there would be a contradiction of two simultaneous functions (vṛtti-dvaya-virodha) regarding cowness.
Or rather, there is *lakṣaṇā* (indication).

Furthermore, there is no primary denotative power (*śakti*) in the universal alone, nor is there *lakṣaṇā* in the individual, because the primary usage occurs with respect to the universal, and both [secondary usage] are rooted in that. For usage has as its purpose the knowledge that serves as the cause for linguistic practice (*vyavahāra*). Nor does linguistic practice occur regarding the universal alone from a non-conceptual cognition of the universal alone, which does not apprehend the individual, because such practice is accomplished by means of a qualified cognition—as in "Look at the cow," "The cow exists," and so forth, where it is precisely the [cow] qualified by cowness [that is the object].
There is both cognition and linguistic usage.
Therefore, because of the rule that [an object] must be cognized by a single act of consciousness, it is possible for the genus (*jāti*) to be qualified [by the individual].

And if, as in the case of the instrument being singular in the instrumental case, the cow and the cowness were both possible objects of the third case, then the cognition would be "the cowness and the cow-individual."

It might be argued that [the word "cow"] does not denote "cowness" (gaur), but rather its qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) or its relation; however, this is a separate matter, similar to how in the cognition "this is a jar," the status of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatā*) or a distinct entity is another question altogether. Furthermore, the configuration (*ākṛti*)—consisting of the conjunction of parts—possessing a specific genus is also denotable by the word "cow. From the word "cow," there is a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward a configuration resembling the genus and the configuration, because a specific conjunction of flour-particles cannot be denoted. If the word were intended to refer to each of the triad—genus, configuration, and individual—separately, there would necessarily be secondary indication for each, since each is distinct from the others qualified by genus and configuration; just as, according to the Guru (Prabhākara), the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in common usage, while capable of denoting the "thing-to-be-done" (*kārya*), ultimately refers to the "state-of-being-a-thing-to-be-done" (*kāryatva*).

For this very reason, the aphorism of the Great Sage (Pāṇini), "The individual, the configuration, and the genus are the meaning of a word" (*vyaktyākṛtijātayas tu padārthaḥ*), employs the singular number in the term *padārthaḥ* to indicate that they are cognizable by a single cognition through a single power. This is the theory of the power residing in the genus (*jātiśaktivāda*). Thus, the lotus (*padma*) is the denotation of the word *paṅkaja* because there is invariably the cognition "the lotus is produced from mud," since the individual components [of the etymology] lack the capacity for that [specific meaning]; furthermore, were it not for conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the word being used based on etymological derivation (*yoga*) alone.

"Now, even if there is conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), why would those two [the meanings 'lotus' and 'mud-born'] not apply to the *kumuda* (white water-lily) through etymological derivation (*yoga*)? The ancients say: 'Because of the obstruction by conventional usage. We, however, hold that the lotus alone, which is invariably recalled by the conventional usage, is experienced as the agent of the production from mud (*paṅkaja-nikartṛtā*) by means of the suffix *ḍa*, which denotes the individual object;

for words denoting individuals necessarily refer to the specific entity present, provided there is no subverting factor (*bādhaka*), just as in the case of the word ending in the suffix *ḍhak* in 'āgneyī'."

By means of context and other factors, the specific *ṛc* verse denoted by the suffix *ḍhak* is understood as being present; thus, in all cases, the causal complex for the experience of the word-meaning is complete, and consequently, there is no cognition of a water-lily (*kumuda*), nor is there any usage of the word for that purpose. Objection: In that case, let it be a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) alone, since both [the specific and general meanings] are obtained from that very source; what is the use of a "conventional-yogic" (*yogarūḍhi*) meaning? Reply: No, because the power of the individual components (*avayava-śakti*) has already been established, and because there is an experience of the etymological meaning (*yaugika-artha*).

If only the conventional meaning (*rūḍhyartha*) or only the etymological meaning (*yaugikārtha*) were experienced, then there would indeed be a dispute, because that [dispute] would be severed by experience itself.
On this point, the Mīmāṃsakas say:

First of all, the word has no power (*śakti*) for the sake of remembrance (*smṛti*), because in the case of the application of the word *paṅkaja* (mud-born), remembrance is established solely from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the certain experience of the lotus; for there is a rule that remembrance is necessarily produced by that [experience].

Nor is it for the sake of experience that the word *padma* is necessarily remembered; for, according to the principle of expressing the individual (*vyaktivacana*), the experience "the lotus is the agent of the production from mud by means of its parts" is possible through its components. Furthermore, whether the remembrance [of the word] occurs through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or otherwise, there is no distinction.

If it is asked, "Why is there a necessity of usage without a [direct] power (*śakti*)?", the answer is: no, because there is a necessity of generating the experience of the lotus by depending on prior usage, according to the principle of the release of the components.
The prior application [of a latent impression] is also dependent upon its own prior application; thus, there is indeed beginninglessness.

If it is argued that—since there is no cause for the definite awakening of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) whose awakening is otherwise indefinite—a definite recollection could not occur at all without such a power (*śakti*)—we reply: No, for even when a power exists, recollection is impossible if awakening does not occur; therefore, definite recollection can indeed occur even without a [permanent] power.
And because the recollection of the word's power (*śakti*) occurs invariably.

Furthermore, the excitant (*udbodhaka*) is not restricted to specific [factors] such as similarity, the word itself, the power, or the knowledge of related items, since each of these individually deviates;

rather, it is postulated that wherever recollection occurs, there is an unrestricted excitant produced at that very moment, due to the force of the result, for properties are to be inferred from their effects.

Because it is inferred according to its specific effect, there is no risk of the memory of its pervader and so forth occurring in the same way as the memory of "lotus-ness" [does]. Since the postulation of an awakening factor depends on the force of memory, and since that memory is absent in those other cases, there is no awakening of them; therefore, without a specific capacity (*śakti*), the memory of "lotus-ness" occurs with necessity, just like the memory of that capacity itself.

Nor should it be argued that, for this reason, there would likewise be no expressive power (*śakti*) even in words such as "cow" (*go*), since the recollection of "cow" and so forth could arise from the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) existing at the time of linguistic usage. For in that case, the expressive power does not exist for the sake of recollection; rather, it exists for the sake of direct experience (*anubhava*). This is because for one who has not mastered the language, direct experience of "cow" and so forth cannot arise from anything other than the word, and the direct experience of the word itself arises only through its connection [to its meaning]. Thus, the collection [of letters] is not the cause [of the experience], as it would be otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*).

Therefore, the postulation of a word’s expressive power (*śakti*) with respect to a collection [of phonemes] cannot be based on the force of experience. If it is argued that, in this way, let there be the expressive power of words such as "cow" (*go*) with respect to the property of being cognizable (*prameyatva*), and that the recollection of the cow arises from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), we say no. It is by means of the linguistic usage of "cow" that the expressive power of the word is postulated with respect to the cognition of a cow—which serves as its own justification—but not with respect to a cognition of a cow as the property of being cognizable, which does not so justify it. Thus, [the power resides] in the cognition of a cow arising from the word "cow."
Furthermore, because there is no experience [of the word] "cow" as the object of cognition (*prameya*).

Now, if it is argued that the recollection of the bank and so forth occurs from the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) alone, then figurative (*gauṇa*) and indirect (*lākṣaṇika*) usage would be abolished; for that [figurative usage] is not postulated for the sake of experiencing the bank and so forth, since such experience is established by other words alone, as those two [figurative and indirect meanings] do not themselves produce the experience. Therefore, [the connection] is restricted.

If it is argued that memory is accomplished by a linguistic function (*vṛtti*), and thus, because of the conceptualization of those two [functions], it is necessary to postulate a primary power (*śakti*) even for the word *paṅkaja* (lotus) as its function, in order to ensure the certain recollection of the lotus—since there is no secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or other such function here—we say: no. For in cases such as *gaṅgāyām* ("in the Ganges"), if the bank and so forth were not the meaning of the word (*padārtha*) due to the absence of a function, there could be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*). This is because of the established linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that case-endings convey their own meanings as connected to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*).
However, since the lotus (*padma*) is denoted by the word *paṅkaja*, its connection with the meaning of the case-ending is established, just as in the case of [the word] *pācaka* and others.
